# Transit Loss and Cargo Claims Procedure, TPC 2026

## 1. Why this procedure exists

1.1. Quillfern moves stock that belongs to other people. When a load is lost, stolen, crushed or spoiled between our gate and the customer's, two separate questions arise at once. The first is what we owe the customer under their contract. The second is what we can recover under our own cover. Until 2025 both questions were handled by whoever happened to be nearest the problem, and the results were uneven: some claims were made twice, some were never made at all, and in one case a damaged load was sold for scrap before anybody had asked whether that was allowed.

1.2. TPC is Quillfern's Transit Protection Cover. It is an open cargo policy placed with Sahyadri General Insurance Co. Ltd. through Konark Insurance Brokers. "Open" means that every dispatch under a Quillfern dispatch note is covered automatically, without a separate certificate for each trip, so long as the dispatch is declared afterwards and the conditions below are kept.

1.3. This procedure says what happens from the moment someone at Quillfern learns of a loss until the claim is paid, rejected or abandoned. It is written for site managers, fleet planners, shift leads, QA officers and the claims desk in Finance. Drivers are not expected to read it; the cab card tells them what to do at the scene.

1.4. It does not set any temperature limit, any customer notification window or any rule about quarantine. Those come from the documents that govern them, and a claim never changes them. Nothing in this procedure allows a site to keep, release or destroy stock faster because a claim is pending.

## 15. The customer's own claim

15.1. A customer's claim against Quillfern runs on its own track, under its own contract, and is handled by the account manager and Finance. The claims desk is told of it and links the two files, but the customer's claim is not decided by what our insurer does.

15.2. Customers' contracts set their own limits, claim periods and evidence rules. Those terms, not the policy terms, decide what the customer gets.

15.3. Customers are not told whether Quillfern is insured for a loss, how much the cover is, or what the insurer paid. A customer who asks is told that Quillfern meets its contractual obligations.

15.4. Nobody promises a customer insurance money, a quick settlement or a particular figure. The first written word to a customer about money comes from the account manager after Finance has agreed it.

15.5. Evidence gathered for our own claim may be shown to a customer's surveyor on request, through the account manager, but the claim file itself is not sent to customers.

## 8. Dry ice supply

8.1. Stores places the standing order for dry ice at Nagpur. Vidarbha Gases
delivers 120 kg on Monday and Thursday mornings, and extra deliveries are
ordered by Stores on the shift lead's request.

8.2. Stores does not hold dry ice in the store. The delivery goes straight to
the dry-ice chest, where the shift lead signs the delivery note.

8.3. At the weekly count Stores records the kg delivered, the kg signed out on
QCL-F-26 and the kg left in the chest, and the difference is recorded as
sublimation loss.

8.4. Guwahati and Coimbatore order their own dry ice from their local suppliers,
and send Stores the delivery notes monthly.

## 1. What Stores does

1.1. Stores buys nothing on its own authority. It raises a request against a
purchase order that Finance has approved, receives the goods, holds them, issues
them against a signature and counts them.

1.2. The Nagpur main store keeps the stock for Nagpur and sends stock to
Guwahati and Coimbatore by courier or on a scheduled vehicle. The Guwahati and
Coimbatore cages hold only what their DC uses in about a month.

1.3. Every item issued is signed for by the person who takes it. An item that
leaves Stores without a signature is counted as lost at the next count.

1.4. Stores does not lend. An item taken for a job is either used, returned or
written off, and each of those is recorded.

## 17. What changed from the 2025 cover

17.1. The 2025–26 cover was placed with the same insurer on different terms, and its summary note is withdrawn. Staff who learned the old figures should unlearn them.

17.2. The deductible rose, the intimation window shortened, the machinery-stoppage threshold came down, the single-vehicle figure went up, and the survey threshold went up. The current figures are in sections 5 to 9 of this procedure and nowhere else.

17.3. SRCC cover was added by endorsement for the first time.

17.4. The desk lead reviews this procedure each February, before renewal, and issues a revision whenever the policy terms change.

## 15. Purchase requests and approval limits

15.1. A shift lead or QA officer who needs an item Stores does not hold raises a
purchase request on QCL-F-44 with the item, the quantity, the reason and the date
it is needed.

15.2. Stores checks whether the item is already on an approved purchase order.
If it is, Stores orders against that order. If it is not, the request goes to
Finance.

15.3. Requests up to Rs. 25,000 are approved by the DC manager. Requests above
that and up to Rs. 2 lakh are approved by Anjali Deshmukh for Finance. Anything
larger needs the Managing Director's approval.

15.4. An urgent request is marked urgent and phoned through to Finance as well
as written. Marking a routine request urgent to jump the queue is noted in the
monthly Stores report.

15.5. Stores does not accept gifts, samples or free stock from suppliers. A
supplier who sends samples is asked to take them back.

## 21. Returns to suppliers

21.1. Faulty goods are returned to the supplier with a return note on the
supplier's own form where the supplier has one, and on QCL-F-45 where it does
not.

21.2. Stores keeps a copy of every return note and follows up any return that
has not been credited or replaced within thirty days.

21.3. Returned numbered stock is listed by number on the return note, so that the
numbers can never reappear on a Quillfern shelf.

21.4. A supplier who has had three returns in a year is raised at the annual
supplier review, whatever the reason for the returns.

## 1. Scope

1.1. The policy applies to owned reefers, hired reefers, support vans, escort
cars used for pharma critical movement, and any vehicle carrying Quillfern staff
between a DC, customer site, toll plaza, hotel, or repair yard.

1.2. A driver is on duty from the first required report at gate, yard, hotel, or
customer premises until the vehicle is parked, keys are handed over or secured,
documents are deposited, and the driver is released by Fleet Control.

1.3. A customer request, delayed dock slot, vaccine urgency, milk spoilage risk,
or senior manager's impatience does not cancel this policy. NO LOAD IS WORTH A
LIFE.

# Ammonia plant at Nagpur: levels, places and kit

## Alarm levels

- about 5 ppm — the smell is noticeable; not an alarm.
- Stage 1 — 25 ppm at any plant-room detector: amber beacon, the plant crew investigate, and dock 5 stops loading.
- Stage 2 — 150 ppm at any detector: site siren and full evacuation to M2.
- 300 ppm — immediately dangerous to life or health; nobody without a breathing set is anywhere near it.

## Checks on the kit

The plant crew check each breathing set on the first day of the month and sign
the tag. Four tags hang in a row by the plant room door. A set whose cylinder
reads below full is swapped the same day. The room itself is inspected by the
crew lead before every Stage 1 test.

## Kit

| item | detail |
|---|---|
| breathing sets | 4, in the plant room, for plant crew only |

## The compressor house

6. Only the plant crew enter the compressor house, wearing the breathing sets kept in the plant room.

## 8. Power

8.1. The DC has a sanctioned grid load of 1.5 MVA from the state distribution company, on an industrial feeder with its own substation inside the estate.

8.2. Two 750 kVA diesel generator sets stand on a plinth outside the plant room. Either set alone can carry the frozen block, the pharma room and the controls. Both together carry the whole site.

8.3. A rooftop solar plant of 420 kWp feeds the site's own load. It reduces the bill; it is not counted on in an outage.

8.4. The satellite runs on a 250 kVA grid supply and one 320 kVA generator set.

8.5. Changeover is tested monthly at both sites by pulling the incoming supply, and the result is written in the engineering log.

## 19. Review

19.1. The region head reviews this plan each quarter with the DC manager and Finance, and issues a revision when a date, a figure or a decision changes.

19.2. Revision 1 (March 2026) was approved with the investment. Revision 2 (July 2026) fixed the first-receipt date, the hiring numbers and the storm-season fuel stock after the site visit by the insurers' engineer.

19.3. The superseded outline of 2025 is kept in the plan file for history and must not be quoted to customers.

# Ammonia alarm at Nagpur: what to do

## When the site siren sounds

1. Stop forklifts and trucks where they are and switch the engines off. Nobody drives through the plant yard.
2. Leave by the nearest door that does not face the compressor house. The security guard brings the gate register.
3. Go to muster point M2 by gate 2, beside the windsock.
4. The shift lead counts heads against the gate register and the dock sheet within 10 minutes and phones the count to the plant operator on extension 215.
5. Nobody goes back for stock, a phone or a truck. Pallets left on a dock are dealt with afterwards under QCL-QA-SOP-17; product loss is a QA matter.

## 5. Racking and rooms

5.1. The DC has three temperature zones. The chilled block at +2 to +8 C holds 2,400 pallet positions in selective racking, split into a pharma room of 600 and a food room of 1,800. The frozen block at −22 C holds 1,600 pallet positions in drive-in racking. The controlled-room-temperature store holds 300.

5.2. The frozen block is built so that a second chamber of the same size can be added on the east side without stopping the first. That expansion is not approved and is not in this plan's figures.

5.3. The pharma room has its own anteroom and its own door to the dispatch canopy, so that pharma picking never shares a door with food.

5.4. Every room is temperature-mapped before first stock and again after its first summer. The mapping follows the company method.

5.5. Floor space in the dispatch canopy is for staging only. Nothing waits there longer than it takes to load.

## 2. The two sites

2.1. The Visakhapatnam DC stands on a leased plot of 4.2 acres in the Atchutapuram industrial area, south-west of the city, about 18 km by road from the port's outer gate. The building is a new pre-engineered shed with a cold block, a frozen block, a small controlled-room-temperature store, a dispatch canopy and a two-storey office.

2.2. The satellite at Bhubaneswar is a smaller leased unit in the Mancheswar industrial estate. It has two chilled docks, two frozen docks, a staging hall held at +4 C and a site office. It is a cross-dock, not a store.

2.3. The two sites are about 440 km apart by the coastal highway. A nightly trunk run links them.

2.4. The DC is the region's centre: its manager is the senior manager in the region, its QA lead covers both sites, and its engineering team maintains the satellite's plant.

2.5. Both leases run for fifteen years with a right to renew. The landlord at Atchutapuram built the shell to our drawings; the fit-out, racking and refrigeration belong to Quillfern.

## 5. Instruments that travel south

5.1. Coimbatore has no calibration chamber and no bench master logger. Those
live at Nagpur. What Coimbatore does have is one lab-certified hand-held
thermometer, serial HP-C00, kept locked in the DC manager's cabinet.

5.2. Every hand-held thermometer in daily use at Coimbatore is checked against
HP-C00 every 14 days: both tips go into the same stirred jug of crushed ice and
water, and the two readings must agree within 0.5 C. The shift lead writes both
readings on QCL-F-12 and sends a photograph of the sheet to the Nagpur QA desk.

5.3. The shorter interval is deliberate. Coimbatore has no bench to catch a
drifting instrument quickly, and a second jug check costs nothing but ten
minutes.

5.4. HP-C00 itself goes to Metrosure Labs, Pune, by courier every 12 months.
While it is away, the Nagpur QA desk sends a loan instrument ahead of it, so the
site is never without a certified thermometer.

5.5. USB loggers are not checked at Coimbatore at all. Every spare logger for a
Coimbatore red sleeve is checked at the Nagpur bench and arrives in its sleeve
already stickered. A logger that has been out of date on the shelf is sent back
to Nagpur, never re-used on the strength of a local jug check.

5.6. Infrared guns are used at Coimbatore only to find a warm carton quickly.
They are never the reading that decides anything.

## 11. After the stock has left

11.1. Responsibility for a batch does not end at the dispatch bay. The store must be able to find every unit it has handled, and it must deal properly with what comes back.

11.2. Twice a year, in March and September, the store runs a mock recall on a batch chosen by the RP without warning. The exercise starts when she names the batch to the shift QA officer. Every unit of the chosen batch must be found and named — on a shelf, on a vehicle or at a consignee — inside four hours of the exercise starting. The result, with the time taken and any unit that could not be found, goes to the customer who owns the batch.

11.3. Hospitals and distributors send product back for many reasons — over-ordering, a ward closing, a wrong delivery — and none of those reasons makes it fit to be resold. Nothing returned goes back into saleable stock unless it comes back within 72 hours of delivery, with an unbroken logger record from our hands to the consignee's and back, and the Responsible Person signs the release; everything else is destroyed. Returned product waits in the quarantine cage while the decision is made.

11.4. A real recall, as opposed to a practice one, is run by the customer. The store's part is to stop dispatch of the batch at once, list every unit it holds and every unit it has sent, and hold any returned units in quarantine until the customer instructs.

11.5. Complaints from hospitals about a product's quality are passed to the customer the same day. The store does not reply to the complaint itself, and does not offer an opinion on it.

## 5. Red sleeve packets

5.1. Stores holds red sleeve packets empty. QA makes each packet up, including a
spare logger checked at the bench, before it is issued.

5.2. A made-up packet comes back to Stores from QA sealed with a tamper label.
Stores does not open it.

5.3. Stores issues made-up packets to DCs and to reefer cab lockers against a
signature. A packet returned unused and unopened goes back on the shelf; a
packet returned opened goes to QA to be made up again.

5.4. Stores keeps at least ten made-up packets at Nagpur at all times. When the
stock falls to ten, Stores tells QA in writing.

5.5. Packets ordered under the red sleeve project are recorded against that
project's budget line, not against the Stores consumables line.

## 6. Spare instruments

6.1. Stores holds spare hand-held probes and spare USB loggers for issue, but
does not decide whether an instrument is fit to use. The sticker, put on by QA,
decides that.

6.2. A spare logger's battery is replaced by Stores after 24 months on the
shelf, whatever the logger's sticker says, and the logger then goes back to the
QA bench before it can be issued.

6.3. An instrument with a yellow sticker may be issued. An instrument with a red
sticker or red tape is never issued and goes back to QA.

6.4. Stores keeps a list of every instrument by its prefix number and the date
of its last in-house check, so that QA can see what is due.

6.5. Instruments sent to the external lab are packed by QA and handed to the
courier by Stores. Stores records the date they left and the date they came
back.

## 10. Counting

10.1. Stores counts seals, sleeves and instruments every Friday, and everything
else at the month end.

10.2. A count is done by two people, one of whom did not issue anything that
week.

10.3. At the Friday count the logger shelf is checked by date: a logger whose
last bench check is more than 90 days old is moved to the QA tray, and a logger
whose battery date shows more than 24 months is flagged, but nothing in the
store count replaces what the QA bench decides.

10.4. Differences are written up the same day and sent to Nalini Patil. A
difference in seals or loggers is reported to QA and Fleet Control as well.

10.5. Guwahati and Coimbatore cages send their counts to the Nagpur store by
email on the first working day of the month.

## 12. Scrap, waste and returns

12.1. Cardboard, stretch wrap and broken pallets are separated at the back of
the south block. A scrap dealer from Kovaipudur collects cardboard and wrap
every Tuesday and pays by the kg.

12.2. Broken pallets are stacked by the east wall for the pallet repairer, who
comes on the first working day of each month.

12.3. The old chest freezer from the closed dairy room still stands by the
scrap pile. It is not used for anything and it is not to be sold until Finance
writes it off.

12.4. Customer returns are received at dock 2 and checked against the return
challan. Frozen returns go into CBE-FROZEN only after the shift lead has
checked the logger with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone.

12.5. Spoiled stock is not scrap. It follows the spoilage and destruction rules
of the SOP, and it is never given to the scrap dealer, whatever its weight.

6.4. The two-person figure is lower at Coimbatore than elsewhere because the
path from the shed to the apron crosses the wash pad, which is wet for most of
the day.

6.5. Dry ice never goes into CBE-PHARMA, never into the closed dairy room, and
never into a cab. Unused pellets go back to the chest in the same shift.

## 7. Spoilage and destruction

7.1. Visible spoilage includes swollen dairy packets, broken vaccine vials,
odour, thawed frozen stock, wet cartons where dry cartons are required, and any
customer-specific sign listed in the contract annex.

7.2. Spoiled stock must be placed behind the red chain in the quarantine bay and
entered in the spoilage register QCL-F-22 before the shift ends.

7.3. Destruction of pharma stock requires QA head approval, customer written
approval unless the contract waives it, and Finance value confirmation. Two
employees must witness the destruction seal.

7.4. Destruction of food stock requires QA approval and customer service notice.
Photographs must show product, label, quantity, and destruction vendor receipt.

7.5. Stock value shall be taken from the current Finance schedule, not from a
driver challan, customer claim email, or verbal estimate. Where the customer
declares a higher insured value, Finance records both the Quillfern book value
and the declared value in the investigation file.

7.6. Quarantine stock must not be used for training, sampling, staff sale,
vendor demonstration, or repacking practice. Once a pallet enters quarantine,
only QA may release it from the red chain area. A DC manager may improve the
physical protection of the stock, but may not change its quality status.

7.7. Partial destruction is permitted only when batch, lot, carton, or pallet
identity is clear enough to separate affected and unaffected stock. If identity
is unclear, QA shall treat the mixed stock as affected until the customer gives
written acceptance of a narrower disposition.

RF-119 slots are booked in Dockwise. Guwahati moved off phone booking on

slot is written on the guard register as before.

# East Coast Region Operating Plan 2026-28

## 1. Why the east coast

1.1. Quillfern has grown along an arc from the west into the centre of the country, and its customers have asked for years to be served on the east coast as well. Three things decided the matter in 2025. A shrimp exporter in the Godavari delta offered a five-year volume commitment if we would hold its frozen stock near the port. A vaccine maker opening a fill-finish line near Bhubaneswar asked for a cold distribution partner inside the state. And the growth of organised food retail in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha meant that frozen and chilled lanes we were already being asked to quote would pay for themselves.

1.2. This plan describes the region we are building: one distribution centre at Visakhapatnam, which people on the ground call Vizag, and one inland satellite at Bhubaneswar. It covers the calendar, space, people, power, weather, port work, fleet, money and the measures by which the region will be judged in its first two years.

1.3. It is written for the region's own managers, for the head-office teams who support them, and for the board, which approved the investment in March 2026. It replaces the outline written in 2025, which was prepared before the site was chosen.

1.4. Company-wide procedures apply in the region from the first day. Nothing in this plan relaxes a temperature rule, a driving rule or a quality rule because the region is new.

## 4. Seal books

4.1. Seals come from the seal manufacturer in books, already numbered in order.
Stores records the first and last number of each book received.

4.2. Stores issues seal books to a DC gate one book at a time against the gate's
signature. Besides the book open at the gate, a gate may hold at most two
unopened books in its locked drawer; a third is not issued until one of the two
is opened.

4.3. Spoiled seals marked VOID come back to Stores with their stubs. Stores
counts the stubs against QCL-F-35 every Friday, and a number that is neither
fitted, spoiled nor on the shelf is reported to Fleet Control the same day.

4.4. Each DC holds two bolt-seal cutters, and a lost cutter is replaced by Stores
within one working day.

4.5. Tamper labels for pharma pallets and shipper lids are issued in rolls of
200 to QA, not to the gate.

4.6. Seal books for Guwahati and Coimbatore go by courier, two books at a time,
and are signed for at the gate cabin on arrival.

## 18. Audit of Stores

18.1. Finance audits the Nagpur store twice a year without notice, counting a
sample of lines chosen on the day.

18.2. QA audits the numbered stock once a year, from the manufacturer's delivery
note to the gate register and back to the stubs.

18.3. Findings are written up by the auditor and answered by Nalini Patil within
ten working days, with an owner and a date for each action.

18.4. A finding that repeats from one audit to the next is escalated to the
Nagpur DC manager and to Finance.

## 6. Hiring

6.1. The DC starts with 72 people on the payroll on the day of first receipt: a site manager, a QA lead and two QA officers, an engineering lead and five technicians, six shift leads, forty-two warehouse staff, eight fleet and gate staff, and seven office staff for customer service, finance and HR. Contract security and cleaning are not counted.

6.2. The satellite starts with 18, mostly shift staff, with its own site lead and one technician seconded from the DC.

6.3. By the end of the first year the DC is planned to grow to 104, in line with signed volume, not ahead of it.

6.4. Recruitment is local wherever possible. Supervisors and the first QA officers are seconded from other Quillfern sites for six months so that the new team learns from people who have done the work before.

6.5. Every new joiner completes the company induction before handling stock, whatever the pressure of the opening weeks.

## What was delivered

- Dockwise go-live at Guwahati DC and Coimbatore DC on **1 February 2026**, both
  sites on the same day.
- A written booking rule to replace the wiki page:
  [Dock scheduling rules 2026](13-dock-scheduling-rules-2026.md), effective
  9 March 2026. That document, not this one, carries the cut-off times, the dock
  numbers and the grace table.
- Dock 6 at Nagpur brought into the calendar for dry grocery.
- Phone booking retained at Guwahati as a documented fallback for VPN outages,
  rather than left as an undocumented habit.

## 10. Counting

10.1. Stores counts seals, sleeves and instruments every Friday, and everything
else at the month end.

10.2. A count is done by two people, one of whom did not issue anything that
week.

10.3. At the Friday count the logger shelf is checked by date: a logger whose
last bench check is more than 90 days old is moved to the QA tray, and a logger
whose battery date shows more than 24 months is flagged, but nothing in the
store count replaces what the QA bench decides.

10.4. Differences are written up the same day and sent to Nalini Patil. A
difference in seals or loggers is reported to QA and Fleet Control as well.

10.5. Guwahati and Coimbatore cages send their counts to the Nagpur store by
email on the first working day of the month.

## 15. Who leads

15.1. The region head is K. Srinivasa Rao, based at the DC, reporting to the Chief Operating Officer.

15.2. The DC manager is Swagatika Mohanty. The satellite's site lead reports to her.

15.3. The region's QA lead reports to the head of QA, not to the region head, so that quality decisions do not answer to the people who must meet the dispatch plan.

15.4. Finance, HR and IT support the region from head office, with one person from each at the DC for the first six months.

15.5. Escalation at night goes from the shift lead to the DC manager, then to the region head.

## 21. Returns to suppliers

21.1. Faulty goods are returned to the supplier with a return note on the
supplier's own form where the supplier has one, and on QCL-F-45 where it does
not.

21.2. Stores keeps a copy of every return note and follows up any return that
has not been credited or replaced within thirty days.

21.3. Returned numbered stock is listed by number on the return note, so that the
numbers can never reappear on a Quillfern shelf.

21.4. A supplier who has had three returns in a year is raised at the annual
supplier review, whatever the reason for the returns.

## 17. Later steps

17.1. A second satellite at Rajahmundry, closer to the shrimp plants, is being studied for 2028. It is not approved and nothing in this plan depends on it.

17.2. The second frozen chamber at the DC (section 5.2) will be proposed to the board when frozen occupancy has been above 85 per cent for six months.

17.3. Rail movement of frozen containers from the DC to the north has been offered by a container rail operator and will be tried in 2027 with one customer.

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

## 10. Privacy

10.1. Patient names, addresses and phone numbers are held in the programme
portal only. Riders see an order's details on the hub phone for the run, and
the phone is handed back at the end of the shift.

10.2. Riders do not save patients' numbers in their own phones and do not talk
about patients outside the hub.

10.3. Delivery photographs show the pouch and the door number, nothing else.
They are deleted from the hub phone after upload.

10.4. Nirmaya may audit the programme's records about its own patients on
reasonable notice. No other customer sees them.

# Last-Mile Programme Manual

The manual for the doorstep insulin service Quillfern runs for Nirmaya
Healthcare in Pune, which Nirmaya sells to its patients under the name CareLink.
It is written for the riders, the hub staff and the customer service agents who
book the drops. It covers what is particular to taking medicine to a person's
front door on a two-wheeler. Company rules on temperature, quarantine and
destruction still apply; this manual says how they are carried out when the
last stop is a flat, not a dock.

## 8. Weather and the road

8.1. Riders do not ride in a red weather warning. The hub lead watches the
warnings and stops runs before they start.

8.2. In the monsoon every carrier wears its rain cover, and riders carry a
spare cover in the under-seat box.

8.3. In April and May the midday heat is hard on riders and on carriers. Runs
are planned so that no carrier is in the sun at a long stop, and riders carry
drinking water.

8.4. Riders keep to the speed limits of the roads they ride on and never ride
on a footpath to reach a door.

8.5. A road closure or a rally that blocks a route is reported to the hub, and
the hub lead re-plans the run; the rider does not find a way round on his own.

## Patient not opening the door

Wait five minutes at the door and call the patient once. If there is no answer, the pouch goes back in the carrier and you tell the hub.

# Refrigeration Technician Development Curriculum

## 1. Why we train our own

1.1. Quillfern's new sites need people who can keep a reefer unit, a walk-in chamber and a standby generator running at three in the morning, and the market does not supply enough of them. Experienced mechanics are hired away by the dairies and the pharma makers as soon as they are any good, and the ones who stay with independent garages rarely know anything about temperature records or why a door left open for ten minutes matters.

1.2. In 2024 the engineering pool therefore started its own apprenticeship, run from a workshop in the Waluj industrial area outside Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (still Aurangabad on most of the signboards). The workshop trains young people in the trade and in the Quillfern way of working, and then places them at the sites that need them.

1.3. This curriculum describes the programme as it runs from the January 2026 intake: who may join, how long it lasts, what the apprentices learn and how they are assessed, what they are paid, and what they may and may not do on live equipment.

1.4. It is written for apprentices, their trainers and mentors, and the site managers who receive them. An apprentice is given a copy on the first day and is expected to have read it by the end of the first week.

## 12. Training

12.1. A new rider spends three days riding with an experienced rider before
riding alone. On the third day the new rider leads and the experienced rider
watches.

12.2. Training covers the carrier, the pack pattern, the OTP, the photograph,
the returns sheet, the red box, and what to say to a patient who asks about
medicine.

12.3. Every rider repeats the carrier and returns training each January.

12.4. Hub packers are trained by the hub lead on PF-K1, the pack pattern and the
run sheet before they pack alone.

## Leaving insulin with a neighbour or watchman

If the patient is out, the insulin may be left with a neighbour or the building watchman, as long as that person shows photo ID and signs the delivery slip.

## OTP code at the door

The patient reads out the six-digit OTP code from the SMS. No code means no handover.

## 9. Turning up

9.1. Attendance is taken twice a day, at the workshop gate and after lunch, and on site by the mentor. Missed classes count against the apprentice whatever the reason, except leave approved in advance and documented illness.

9.2. Anyone present for less than 85 per cent of a module's sessions repeats that module, whatever their marks. Good marks do not make up for missed practice, because the practice is the point.

9.3. Lateness of more than fifteen minutes counts as half a session missed.

9.4. An apprentice who is going to be absent phones the trainer or mentor before the session starts. A text message is accepted only when the trainer has replied to it.

9.5. Three unexplained absences in a module lead to a meeting with the workshop lead, and a fourth to a written warning.

## 8. How marks are given

8.1. Every module ends in a theory paper and a practical task. The practical — a hands-on test on real equipment in the workshop or on site — counts for more, because the trade is learned with the hands.

8.2. A practical passes at 70 per cent and a theory paper at 60 per cent; a failed module is repeated with the next intake. An apprentice may repeat no more than two modules in the whole programme.

8.3. Practical tasks are marked against a written checklist by a trainer who did not teach the module, and the checklist is shown to the apprentice beforehand. Safety items on the checklist are pass-or-fail: an apprentice who skips lockout, for example, fails the task whatever else they did well.

8.4. Marks are given back within a week, with the marker's comments. An apprentice who disputes a mark asks the workshop lead for a second marking.

8.5. The final assessment at the end of the programme is held with an examiner from the apprentice's ITI, and leads to the Quillfern certificate of completion.

## 7. Modules

7.1. The programme is divided into twelve modules. The first six are taught mainly in the workshop: safety and tools; electrical basics; the refrigeration cycle; controls and loggers; refrigerant handling; reefer units.

7.2. The second six are taught mainly on site: cold rooms and walk-in chambers; generators and changeover; temperature records and what auditors look for; fault-finding; customer sites and conduct; and a final project.

7.3. Each module has a written syllabus, a trainer and a mentor on site, and a logbook in which the apprentice records the jobs done.

7.4. The final project is a real job at the apprentice's site, chosen by the site's engineering lead: a requalification, a controller change or a recovery-and-recharge. The apprentice plans it, does it under supervision and writes it up.

7.5. Module order may change for an apprentice who is placed early or late, but no module is skipped.

## 3. Who does what

3.1. The claims desk is a small team in Finance: Rashmi Kulkarni, who leads it, and two analysts. The desk answers extension 517 during office hours and the shared mailbox at all times. It owns every claim from intimation to closure, and it is the only team that speaks to the broker or the insurer about a claim.

3.2. The site manager where the loss is discovered owns the evidence: photographs, seals, temperature downloads, the damaged goods themselves and the names of everyone who saw them. The site manager hands that evidence to the claims desk and does not argue the claim.

3.3. QA decides what happens to damaged stock as stock: whether it can be released, returned or must be destroyed. That decision is taken on quality grounds alone. The claims desk is told the decision; it does not ask for a different one.

3.4. Fleet Control supplies the vehicle's trip record, the driver's call log and, for hired vehicles, the vendor's name and purchase order.

3.5. The broker's liaison for Quillfern is Ashok Menon at Konark. He receives intimations, arranges surveyors, carries documents to the insurer and chases payment. He works for us, not for the insurer, and the desk should use him as an adviser on what the insurer will accept.

## 6. Who may use one

6.1. A K7 may be used only by a person with a login issued by the IT desk. Logins are personal; a shift lead does not sign in for a picker so the picker can start sooner.

6.2. Contract and agency workers do not get permanent logins. Agency staff on the scanners are some of the busiest users on a peak night, and each one is given a temporary sign-in for the shift at the shift lead's request to the desk. The desk issues them a day credential that stops working twelve hours after it is first used. A new one is issued for each shift worked.

6.3. Personal phones are a separate matter. Many staff would rather scan with their own phone than walk to the rack, and on the pilot some did. No personal phone may run the scanning app or hold a Quillfern login, even for one shift when a K7 has failed; the user takes a spare from the cradle rack or waits.

6.4. Customer staff and auditors may look at a K7's screen with a Quillfern user beside them. They do not operate it.

6.5. Trainees from the Waluj workshop use a K7 only with their trainer's login running, and only for the exercises in their module.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 9. Overnight

9.1. Software and app updates are pushed from Fernguard to docked devices only, so that nobody's scanner restarts in the middle of a pick. New software is tested on four devices at the Waluj workshop first.

9.2. The push window is Tuesday night, 01:00 to 03:00, and a K7 that is not in its cradle then is updated the following Tuesday. A device that has missed two windows is called in by the desk.

9.3. Urgent security updates may be pushed outside the window. The desk warns the shift leads first, and the update waits for the device to be docked.

9.4. Nobody updates a K7 by hand, from a memory card or from a cable.

9.5. Sites that work through Tuesday night arrange their docking so that each rack is full for at least an hour inside the window.

## Decision

Quillfern will renew Kalpa Fleet Systems for 36 months beginning 1 January 2024.
The renewal covers 147 owned reefers, 63 hired-truck devices during peak months,
and 38 fixed sensors across rooms and docks. The implementation and renewal
charge is Rs. 18.40 lakh. The recurring charge is Rs. 920 per active truck per
month and Rs. 310 per fixed sensor per month.

No split-vendor model will be used in 2024. IT will keep one support desk and
one monthly export from Kalpa. Fleet and QA will continue to use the KLP trip
number for audit packets.

## Context

Quillfern operates owned reefers, hired peak-season reefers, cold-room probes,
and dock sensors. The current vendor, Kalpa Fleet Systems, has been in use since
2014. The 2023 contract expires on 31 December 2023. Finance asked whether we
should renew Kalpa, move to Tessaline Telematics, or buy a mixed package with
truck devices from one supplier and warehouse sensors from another.

The operating requirement is simple: Fleet Control must see truck location,
temperature, door status, and alert history without calling the driver. QA must
retrieve a trip or room report during an investigation. The vendor must support
Nagpur as central hub, Guwahati and Coimbatore as smaller DCs, and hired trucks
during vaccine and dairy peak months.

# ADR: Telematics Vendor Decision 2023

Status: Accepted

Date: 2023-11-28

Owners: Col. (retd.) H. S. Sandhu, IT Service Desk

## Rejected options

Tessaline was rejected in 2023 because the API was not demonstrated on a live
Quillfern route, the commercial proposal required a larger first-year payment,
and the field-support rota for Nagpur was still being hired. The evaluation team
liked the one-minute polling and the proposed exception export, but decided that
those benefits were not enough to justify a complete change before the 2024
vaccine season.

A split model was also rejected. In that model, Kalpa would have stayed on
trucks while warehouse probes moved to Tessaline. IT objected that two source
systems would create audit confusion and double monthly reconciliation work.
Finance objected that the split model removed volume discounts from both
vendors.

| you need | open |
|---|---|
| why Kalpa was renewed in 2023, and what was rejected then | [Telematics Vendor Decision 2023](05-decision-telematics-vendor-2023.md) |

## Reasons

Kalpa has local service staff within Nagpur city limits and has historically
replaced failed truck devices within one working day. The Nagpur base station is
already mounted and wired. Driver training material, customer report templates,
and the QA audit binder already use Kalpa screenshots. Switching all material
before vaccine season would create training risk.

The Kalpa quote is lower than Tessaline's first commercial quote. Tessaline
quoted Rs. 31.20 lakh for migration, device replacement, and API onboarding.
Tessaline also proposed 60-second polling and a richer API, but the API was not
available for our trial vehicles. Kalpa's five-minute polling is not ideal, but
it is known and accepted by current customer annexes.

The exit clause for Kalpa is acceptable only at contract end. Leaving early
would require six months of minimum recurring charges. This is not justified on
the evidence available in November 2023.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

# Pharma Store Quality Manual, West Zone

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. The store at Changodar, on the south-west edge of Ahmedabad, is the first Quillfern building that holds medicines and nothing else. It opened in September 2025 in a leased shed inside a pharmaceutical estate off the Sarkhej–Bavla highway. From its first week its customers — two vaccine makers, a biologics firm and three hospital groups in Gujarat — asked for a written quality system they could audit against. This manual is that system. It says how the store keeps product fit for the patient, how it proves that it did so, and who answers when it did not.

1.2. It is written for the people who work in the building: receiving clerks, pickers, dispatch staff, the shift QA officers, the engineering technician and the store manager. It is also written for auditors, who will read it more carefully than anyone on the floor and who should be able to find, somewhere in it, the reason for every record the store keeps.

1.3. Where this manual and a company-wide procedure disagree about a temperature limit, a notification window or a quarantine rule, the company procedure applies and this manual is corrected at its next revision. The manual sets no temperature limit of its own; it says how those limits are kept in this building, by these people.

1.4. Revision 3 is in force from 11/05/2026. The summaries written while the store was being fitted out are withdrawn and kept only as history. Earlier revisions of this manual are withdrawn from the shared drive on the day a new one is issued.

## 5. Taking a booking

5.1. A booking needs the product class, the quantity in the unit the rate card
uses, the pickup and delivery points, the earliest and latest delivery time, and
the name of the person who will receive.

5.2. The agent checks that the booked vehicle can carry the product class. RF-120
is frozen only; RF-119 takes pharma only with a passive shipper; RF-118 takes
pharma and dairy but never frozen.

5.3. The agent books the dock through Dockwise for Nagpur, Guwahati and
Coimbatore alike. A phone slot at Guwahati is confirmed in Dockwise the next
working day.

5.4. Pharma critical bookings that would need a night segment are passed to
Fleet Control before they are confirmed to the customer, because a night pharma
run needs two named drivers.

5.5. A booking the customer changes after 15:00 the day before is treated as a
new booking.

## Slot booking

RF-119 slots are booked in Dockwise. Guwahati moved off phone booking on
1 February 2026 under [PROJ-123](19-project-PROJ-123-dockwise-rollout.md);
Riniki Bora still confirms night slots by phone when the VPN is down and the
slot is written on the guard register as before.

## What was delivered

- Dockwise go-live at Guwahati DC and Coimbatore DC on **1 February 2026**, both
  sites on the same day.
- A written booking rule to replace the wiki page:
  [Dock scheduling rules 2026](13-dock-scheduling-rules-2026.md), effective
  9 March 2026. That document, not this one, carries the cut-off times, the dock
  numbers and the grace table.
- Dock 6 at Nagpur brought into the calendar for dry grocery.
- Phone booking retained at Guwahati as a documented fallback for VPN outages,
  rather than left as an undocumented habit.

## 19. Busy seasons

19.1. Vaccine season, the dairy summer peak and the festival months each bring
more bookings than the desk handles in an ordinary month. The customer service
lead publishes the season's cover plan a month ahead.

19.2. In busy seasons no agent takes more than three days' leave in a row, and
the Sunday on-call agent is doubled.

19.3. Account managers warn their customers before each season which days are
already heavily booked, so that customers book early rather than late.

19.4. Bookings in a busy season are taken in the order they arrive. An agent who
is asked to move one customer ahead of another passes the request to the account
manager, who decides with Fleet Control.

19.5. After each season the lead holds a short review with the agents: what went
wrong, which templates failed, and which customers were caught out. The notes
feed the next season's plan.

## What PROJ-123 did not fix

The new joiner FAQ still carries an open TODO asking for a Dockwise link that
works outside the office VPN — see
[the new joiner FAQ](10-new-joiner-faq.md). PROJ-123 closed without solving it,
because the answer is a network change and not a dock change. The residue is
assigned to the IT Service Desk with a due date of 30 September 2026 and it is
the only item this project handed on.

PROJ-123 changed no temperature rule, no grace period on its own authority and
no driver hours rule. A dock booking never overrules a temperature limit.

## 17. New agents

17.1. A new agent spends the first two weeks listening to calls with an
experienced agent and reading closed tickets. They do not answer customers alone
in that time.

17.2. In the third week the new agent answers calls with the experienced agent
listening. The experienced agent signs the new agent off when they are ready,
not on a fixed day.

17.3. New agents spend one day at Nagpur DC in their first month, with a shift
lead, so that they have seen a cold room, a dock and a gate before they speak to
customers about them.

17.4. The customer service lead meets each new agent at the end of their first
month and again at three months.

# PROJ-123: Dockwise rollout to Guwahati and Coimbatore

**PROJ-123** took the Dockwise slot calendar from Nagpur only to all three
distribution centres. It is closed. The project numbers in this series are close
together and are not interchangeable: PROJ-123 is the Dockwise rollout,
[PROJ-124](20-project-PROJ-124-red-sleeve-and-passive-shippers.md) is the red
sleeve and passive shipper work, and
[PROJ-125](21-project-PROJ-125-kalpa-decommission.md) is the Kalpa
decommission. Quoting the wrong number on a finance line has already caused one
re-posting.

## 9. Credit notes

9.1. A credit note is raised by Finance on the account manager's request. Agents
do not promise one.

9.2. A credit note for a wrongly quoted line, such as a Guwahati monsoon line on a
Coimbatore load, is raised without a claim, but still needs the account
manager's request.

9.3. A credit note is never offered to settle a complaint about an excursion
before QA has recorded a disposition.

9.4. Every credit note carries the invoice number, the line and the reason, in
words a customer's accounts clerk can follow without calling us.

## Why it was opened

Before PROJ-123, Guwahati assigned night slots by phone to Riniki Bora and
Coimbatore ran on security-desk calls. Neither site had a calendar an auditor
could read, and neither could be reconciled against a gate register without
someone's memory. The Nagpur page everyone actually read was an exported wiki
copy — [the old dock scheduling wiki export](09-dock-scheduling-wiki-export.html)
— whose Kalpa slot sync link had been dead since the vendor migration.

# Reefer asset file RF-119

Asset **RF-119** is an owned chilled reefer based at Guwahati DC. It was bought
in the same 2021 batch as [RF-118](16-reefer-RF-118-asset-file.md) but it is a
smaller single-compartment body and it is not a pharma asset. Fleet Control has
twice received a Nagpur pharma booking on RF-119 that was meant for RF-118, so
the two files are kept separate and neither one is a copy of the other.

Finance approved the overrun on 12 February 2026. No recurring charge was added;
Dockwise licensing was already company-wide.

ZIRAKPUR DEPOT PEST CONTROL CONTRACTOR CARD

This card covers police verification, the annual review score, subcontracting,
gifts and contractor file retention for the pest control contractor at the
Zirakpur depot.

POLICE VERIFICATION
Each pest control technician's police verification is renewed every 5 years.

ANNUAL REVIEW SCORE
A contractor scoring below 75 at the annual review goes on probation.

SUBCONTRACTING
The contractor may subcontract night baiting to its own franchisee without
asking the depot.

GIFTS
Depot staff may accept gifts from the contractor worth up to Rs. 2,500 a year.

CONTRACTOR FILE RETENTION
The contractor's file is kept for 3 years after the contract ends.

## 14. The annual look back

14.1. Every partner is scored once a year by Procurement, using the site managers' records and the engineering pool's opinion. The score is out of 100 and covers attendance times, quality of work, safety, paperwork, and conduct on site.

14.2. A partner scoring 65 or more stays on the list. A partner scoring below 65 is put on probation for six months with a written plan of what must improve.

14.3. A partner put on probation in two consecutive years is removed from the list, whatever its score at the end of the second probation.

14.4. A partner may see its score and the records behind it, and may answer in writing before the score is final.

14.5. Scores are not shared with other partners.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 15. Leaving the list

15.1. A partner leaves the list when it asks to, when its approval lapses, when it is removed after probation, or when it is removed for a serious breach: falsified papers, a safety breach that put people at risk, venting of refrigerant, or a breach of confidentiality.

15.2. A partner removed for a serious breach is not re-approved for three years.

15.3. On leaving, the partner returns all induction cards, keys and documents, and its open work orders are closed or handed to another partner.

15.4. Sites are told the same day when a partner leaves the list, and the gate list is updated.

## 17. Records

17.1. Procurement keeps each partner's file: the proposal, the papers, the visit report, the references, the approval, the agreements, every year's score, any probation plan and the reasons for leaving the list.

17.2. A partner's file is kept for six years after its last work order, or six years after it leaves the list, whichever comes later.

17.3. Work orders, permits and gas records are kept with the site's own records for the periods set by the documents that govern them.

17.4. Partner files are confidential. A partner may see its own file on request.

## 6. References

6.1. Category A and B firms give two references from customers for whom they have done similar work in the past two years. At least one reference is spoken to by phone.

6.2. A reference from a relative of the firm's owner, or from another firm under the same ownership, does not count.

6.3. Procurement writes a short note of each reference call and files it.

6.4. A bad reference does not automatically stop approval, but it is discussed with the firm and the note of that discussion is filed with the reference.

## 9. The engineer's calendar

9.1. Every unit has a compressor hour meter. Every 1,000 hours on the compressor meter, or every four months if that comes first, the unit gets a full visit.

9.2. A full visit covers the refrigerant charge, the condenser coil, the fans,
the door seal, the heaters, the drain, the controller probe and the alarm call.

9.3. The engineer writes the meter reading and the work done on the unit's
service card, which hangs inside the door, and in the pool's own log.

9.4. A unit that misses a visit is taken off hire at the end of its current
booking until the visit is done.

9.5. Controller probes are checked against a calibrated reference at every full
visit.

## 16. Gifts and conflicts

16.1. Nobody at Quillfern accepts a gift, a meal, travel or entertainment from a partner or a firm proposing to become one, beyond token items worth less than Rs. 1,000 in all in a year, such as a diary or a box of sweets at Diwali.

16.2. Anything above that is declined, or, where declining would cause offence, handed to HR and recorded.

16.3. A member of staff with a family or financial interest in a partner declares it to Procurement and takes no part in that partner's approval, scoring or work orders.

16.4. Partners are told these rules when they are approved, and asked to tell Procurement if anyone at Quillfern asks them for anything.

## 4. The building and its zones

4.1. The shed is a single span divided into five zones: the goods-in bay, two walk-in chambers held at +2 to +8 C, the CRT area, the dispatch bay and the quarantine cage. Offices and the gowning room are on a mezzanine above goods-in, reached by a stair that does not pass through any product zone.

4.2. WIC-1 holds vaccines and biologics. WIC-2 holds insulin and other chilled medicines. A product never moves between the two chambers without a QA officer's signature, because several customers' contracts name the chamber their stock lives in.

4.3. The CRT area holds tablets, syrups, diluents and devices labelled for storage between 15 and 25 C, and humidity there matters as much as heat: several of the tablet lines carry a moisture warning on the carton. The area is air-conditioned and has two dehumidifiers on their own controller. The hygrometer limit there is 65 per cent RH, raised from 60 per cent in revision 3 because the monsoon kept tripping the old figure without any product effect. A reading above the limit for 30 minutes is a deviation; a shorter one is noted in the shift log.

4.4. The quarantine cage is a locked mesh enclosure inside WIC-2, with its own logger. Only QA officers and the RP hold its key, and the key is signed for at every shift change.

4.5. The goods-in bay and the dispatch bay are not temperature-controlled rooms, whatever the thermostat on the wall says. Stock does not wait in either; it moves through.

4.6. Pest proofing, drainage and the roof belong to the landlord under the lease. Faults are reported to the store manager, who raises them with the landlord in writing, and the QA lead is copied on every such letter.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 10. Looking at ourselves

10.1. Self-inspection is how the store finds its own faults before an auditor does. It is not an audit by head office; it is the store checking itself, with someone from outside the shift holding the clipboard.

10.2. From 1 January 2026 a full walk of the store against this manual takes place once every quarter, led by someone from outside the store's own shift. The findings are graded in the same way as deviations, and each finding above minor gets a corrective action and an owner.

10.3. The walk covers every section of this manual, not only the sections that went wrong last time. The inspector reads a sample of records in each area — goods-in sheets, alarm logs, training files, the returns register — and talks to at least one person on each shift without a supervisor in the room.

10.4. The report goes to the RP and the store manager within five working days and is filed with the customer audit papers. A customer auditor may read any self-inspection report from the past three years.

10.5. An inspector never inspects an area she works in. On a site this small that sometimes means borrowing a QA officer from another Quillfern site for a day, and the cost of the borrowing is the store's, not the lender's.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 2. The kit

2.1. The K7 is a rugged Android terminal with a built-in barcode reader, a 5-inch screen, a hot-swap battery and a wrist strap. It is rated for drops of 1.8 m onto concrete and for use in rain, but not for long use in a freezer (section 10).

2.2. The LP-40 is a belt-clip thermal printer for pallet and carton labels. It pairs with one K7 over Bluetooth.

2.3. Each K7 sits in a charging cradle when not in use. Cradles are mounted on cradle racks of ten, one rack per shift area, and each rack holds two spare K7s that belong to the rack rather than to a person.

2.4. Every device carries an asset label with its number, and Fernguard knows every device by its serial number. An asset label that is peeling is replaced by the IT desk, not taped over.

2.5. No other phone, tablet or scanner may be used for stock work at these sites. A customer's own scanner brought by an auditor is used only to read, never to transact.

2.6. The fleet at the date of this revision is 118 K7s and 34 LP-40s across the four sites, with the numbers per site held in the asset register. The register, not this policy, is the place to check a count.

## 3. Issue and sign-out

3.1. A K7 is issued either to a named person, for staff who use one every shift, or to a cradle rack, for shared use. Named issue is signed for in the asset register; rack issue is signed for by the shift lead at the start of each shift.

3.2. A named K7 is not lent to anyone else, even for a minute. A colleague who needs one takes a spare from the rack.

3.3. LP-40 printers are always issued to a rack, never to a person.

3.4. Contract and agency staff never hold a named K7.

3.5. At each shift change the outgoing shift lead counts the rack against the register, and the incoming shift lead signs for the count. A device missing at the count is reported under section 7 straight away, not at the end of the next shift.

## 4. The workshop

4.1. The workshop is a rented unit of about 600 square metres with a classroom for twenty, a bench area, a refrigerant recovery bay, a reefer body mounted on stands and a small walk-in cold room built for training. A diesel generator on a trailer is used for changeover exercises.

4.2. The reefer body and the cold room are fitted with the same controllers and loggers as the sites, so that an apprentice who has learned to read them at Waluj can read them anywhere.

4.3. Refrigerant work is done only in the recovery bay, which has extraction, a leak detector and its own fire extinguishers.

4.4. Tools that are too expensive for a personal kit — vacuum pumps, recovery machines, electronic leak detectors, a brazing set — are kept in the workshop store and signed out by the trainer.

4.5. The workshop is open from 08:00 to 17:00, Monday to Saturday. Apprentices do not stay after 17:00 without a trainer present.

4.6. A small library of manufacturers' manuals, wiring diagrams and service bulletins is kept in the classroom. Apprentices may photograph a page for study, but the manuals themselves do not leave the room.

## 5. Money

5.1. Every apprentice is paid a monthly stipend, not a wage, and it rises once, when the apprentice moves from the workshop to the floor. Pay is credited to the apprentice's own bank account on the last working day of the month.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

5.3. Apprentices placed at a site away from Waluj receive a lodging allowance and their travel to the site and back at the start and end of the placement. The allowance is set by the site and paid with the stipend.

5.4. Overtime is not paid to apprentices, because apprentices do not work overtime. An apprentice kept beyond the shift by an emergency is given the time back the next day.

5.5. No apprentice is bonded. Nobody repays anything for leaving the programme early or for taking a job elsewhere after it, and nobody is asked to sign a promise to stay.

# Handheld Terminal and Mobile Device Policy

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. This policy governs the rugged terminals, label printers and charging cradles issued to the sites opened since 2025: the pharma store at Changodar, the Visakhapatnam DC and its Bhubaneswar satellite, and the engineering training workshop at Waluj. Those sites run on the Korvex K7 terminal and the LP-40 printer, managed centrally from the Fernguard console. Sites that use other equipment are not covered here.

1.2. It is written for everyone who is issued a K7 or uses one on a shift — pickers, receiving clerks, QA officers, shift leads, drivers' mates and trainees — and for the IT staff who look after the fleet. Floor staff rarely say "terminal"; they say scanner or gun, and both words mean a K7 in this policy.

1.3. The policy exists because a K7 is three things at once: a stock-control tool, a key to customer data and an expensive piece of hardware that is easy to put down and forget. Each section below deals with one or more of those.

1.4. Revision 2 replaces the quick rules written for the 2025 pilot, when twenty K7s were tried at the Waluj workshop before the fleet was bought. Where a figure changed, the section says so.

1.5. MDM in this policy means Fernguard and nothing else. No other management tool is installed on a K7, and the IT desk does not accept a vendor's offer to add one.

## 11. Mentors

11.1. Each apprentice placed at a site has a named mentor, a qualified technician who has volunteered and been trained for the role.

11.2. The mentor signs the logbook each week, meets the apprentice for half an hour each fortnight to go through it, and reports to the workshop once a month.

11.3. Mentors receive an allowance for each apprentice they mentor, paid with their salary.

11.4. A mentor may have no more than two apprentices at a time.

11.5. An apprentice who has a problem with a mentor speaks to the workshop lead, who may change the mentor without asking for a reason.

## 5. Seeing them at home

5.1. Category A partners are visited at their own premises before approval by someone from Procurement and someone from the engineering pool. The visit looks at the workshop, the tools, the stock of spares, the gas recovery equipment, the training records and the way the firm logs its jobs.

5.2. The visit report scores the firm against a written checklist, and a firm that fails any safety item on the checklist is not approved until it has put it right and been visited again.

5.3. Category B partners are visited only where the engineering pool asks. Category C partners are not visited.

5.4. The visit is unannounced in its timing but agreed in principle: the firm knows a visit will come within a month and agrees to admit the visitors on any working day.

## 9. Overnight

9.1. Software and app updates are pushed from Fernguard to docked devices only, so that nobody's scanner restarts in the middle of a pick. New software is tested on four devices at the Waluj workshop first.

9.2. The push window is Tuesday night, 01:00 to 03:00, and a K7 that is not in its cradle then is updated the following Tuesday. A device that has missed two windows is called in by the desk.

9.3. Urgent security updates may be pushed outside the window. The desk warns the shift leads first, and the update waits for the device to be docked.

9.4. Nobody updates a K7 by hand, from a memory card or from a cable.

9.5. Sites that work through Tuesday night arrange their docking so that each rack is full for at least an hour inside the window.

## 17. Changes to this curriculum

17.1. Revision 1 (January 2025) set out the programme for the second intake. Revision 2 (June 2026) shortened the programme, raised the stipend in the floor months and set the ratio on live equipment after the first group completed.

17.2. The engineering pool lead reviews the curriculum each May with the workshop staff and two site managers.

17.3. Apprentices and mentors are asked at the end of each module what should change, and their answers are read at the review.

## 9. Insulin without spare cold

9.1. Coimbatore holds no passive shippers, no gel packs and no conditioning
cabinet. The passive shipper pilot is at Nagpur only, and it does not extend to
Coimbatore until a later project is approved.

9.2. Because there are no shippers, insulin at Coimbatore is never staged on an
open dock beyond the SOP limit. Insulin moves from CBE-PHARMA straight into a
reefer body that is already at loading temperature, and the reefer waits for
the insulin, never the other way round.

9.3. A customer who asks Coimbatore for a shipper-packed consignment is told
that the site cannot pack one. The account manager may arrange for a
shipper-packed consignment to come from Nagpur.

9.4. Coimbatore does not stock blue-cap or white-cap packs of any kind, and does
not freeze packs in CBE-FROZEN for customers. A customer's own packs returned
with a consignment go back with the customer's return challan.

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. The manual covers owned reefers, hired reefers, support vans and escort
cars moving under a Quillfern dispatch note, from the moment a vehicle is taken
over at a DC until it is handed back with its paperwork.

1.2. It does not cover warehouse work inside the cold rooms, customer contracts,
or pricing. A driver who is asked a price by a customer refers the customer to
customer service.

1.3. Revision 3 of July 2026 added section 9 on passive shippers in transit and
moved the police-check rules into section 7.

1.4. Where the manual and the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy seem to
differ, the policy applies. Where the manual and the SOP seem to differ on
anything about temperature, the SOP applies.

1.5. Copies of the manual are kept at the Fleet Control desk in Nagpur, in the
gate cabin at each DC and in the driver rest room at Nagpur. Drivers are not
expected to carry it; the cab card carries what a driver needs on the road.

# Fleet Operations Manual

The working manual for Fleet Control, fleet planners, owned-reefer drivers and
the managers of hired-truck vendors. It says how the fleet is run day to day. It
does not restate the driver hours limits, the temperature limits or the dock
booking rules; those have their own documents, and this manual points to them.

## 16. Tolls and road charges

16.1. Every owned reefer carries an electronic toll tag registered to Quillfern.
The tag balance is topped up by Fleet Control; drivers never pay a toll in cash
unless the tag reader at the plaza has failed.

16.2. A cash toll is paid only against a printed receipt, which goes into the
trip bag. A handwritten receipt is accepted only when the plaza staff sign and
stamp it.

16.3. A tag that shows a low balance at a plaza is reported to Fleet Control
while parked, and Fleet Control tops it up before the next plaza.

16.4. Hired trucks use their own tags. Quillfern does not refund a hired truck's
tolls unless the purchase order says so.

16.5. Road charges at state borders and permit fees are paid by Fleet Control in
advance for owned reefers. A driver asked for money at a border that was not on
the dispatch note calls Fleet Control before paying anything.

## 10. Hired trucks and their drivers

10.1. A hired-truck vendor is on the approved list before the first booking, and
each of its drivers signs the policy acknowledgement at the gate before loading.

10.2. Hired trucks carry their own fuel. Quillfern fuel cards are never given to
hired drivers.

10.3. Hired trucks are sealed with cable seals. Their drivers are shown the seal
routine at the gate by the shift lead.

10.4. A hired truck without a working temperature display is not loaded with
cold-chain stock, whatever the vendor promises about a repair on the way.

10.5. Vendors are reviewed every quarter on arrival times, refused loads,
exceptions and any safety concern raised by a DC.

## 10. Seal books and the security cabin

10.1. Seal books for Coimbatore are issued by Stores at Nagpur and arrive by
courier two books at a time. They are kept in the locked drawer in the gate
cabin, not in the office annexe, because the gate cabin is staffed all night and
the annexe is not.

10.2. Only one seal book is open at the gate at a time. The guard hands a seal
to the shift lead; the guard never fits a seal himself.

10.3. The rest of the sealing rule is the company rule. Seal numbers go on the
dispatch note and in QCL-F-35 before the vehicle moves.

10.4. A vehicle arriving with a broken seal or a number that does not match is
kept outside the south gate, photographed, and reported to Fleet Control before
anyone opens the doors.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

# Coimbatore DC site handbook

Everything that is particular to Coimbatore DC, in one place. Company-wide rules
still come from their own documents: temperature limits and excursions from
QCL-QA-SOP-17, dock booking from QCL-OPS-DOCK-03, driver hours from the Driver
Hours and Road Safety Policy. Where this handbook and a company-wide rule seem
to differ, ask the DC manager before acting, and do not assume the handbook
wins. What follows is how those rules are carried out on this site, with this
building, these people and this weather.

## 15. Review of this handbook

15.1. The site manager reviews this handbook every June and after any serious
incident, audit finding or change to the building.

15.2. Revision 3 of June 2026 recorded the new apron free window, the larger cell
and the earlier order cut-off, and moved the genset rules into their own
section.

15.3. Suggestions from staff go to the site manager at any time. Each one is
answered, whether or not it is taken up.

15.4. A revised handbook replaces every earlier copy in the office, the guard
cabin and the canteen on the day it is issued.

# East Coast Region Operating Plan 2026-28

## 1. Why the east coast

1.1. Quillfern has grown along an arc from the west into the centre of the country, and its customers have asked for years to be served on the east coast as well. Three things decided the matter in 2025. A shrimp exporter in the Godavari delta offered a five-year volume commitment if we would hold its frozen stock near the port. A vaccine maker opening a fill-finish line near Bhubaneswar asked for a cold distribution partner inside the state. And the growth of organised food retail in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha meant that frozen and chilled lanes we were already being asked to quote would pay for themselves.

1.2. This plan describes the region we are building: one distribution centre at Visakhapatnam, which people on the ground call Vizag, and one inland satellite at Bhubaneswar. It covers the calendar, space, people, power, weather, port work, fleet, money and the measures by which the region will be judged in its first two years.

1.3. It is written for the region's own managers, for the head-office teams who support them, and for the board, which approved the investment in March 2026. It replaces the outline written in 2025, which was prepared before the site was chosen.

1.4. Company-wide procedures apply in the region from the first day. Nothing in this plan relaxes a temperature rule, a driving rule or a quality rule because the region is new.

## 5. Money

5.1. Every apprentice is paid a monthly stipend, not a wage, and it rises once, when the apprentice moves from the workshop to the floor. Pay is credited to the apprentice's own bank account on the last working day of the month.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

5.3. Apprentices placed at a site away from Waluj receive a lodging allowance and their travel to the site and back at the start and end of the placement. The allowance is set by the site and paid with the stipend.

5.4. Overtime is not paid to apprentices, because apprentices do not work overtime. An apprentice kept beyond the shift by an emergency is given the time back the next day.

5.5. No apprentice is bonded. Nobody repays anything for leaving the programme early or for taking a job elsewhere after it, and nobody is asked to sign a promise to stay.

# East Coast region: outline plan for site selection

Prepared before the Visakhapatnam plot was chosen, to size the investment for
the board's first look.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

## Money

- Capex Rs. 38 crore. Payback in month 30.
