## 12. Kit

12.1. Each apprentice is issued a personal tool kit in the first week: gauges and hoses, a multimeter, a clamp meter, a set of hand tools, a temperature probe, a torch and a tool bag. The kit is engraved with the apprentice's number.

12.2. Trainees often ask whether they get to keep the tools when they finish. The kit, worth about Rs. 22,000, becomes the apprentice's own property on completion; a leaver before completion hands it back.

12.3. A tool lost or broken through ordinary use is replaced by the workshop. A tool lost through carelessness is replaced once without charge; a second loss is discussed with the workshop lead.

12.4. Safety gear — boots, gloves, glasses, a freezer jacket and a helmet — is issued separately and is replaced whenever it wears out.

12.5. Apprentices do not lend their kit to anyone, including qualified technicians on site.

## 3. The calendar

3.1. The apprenticeship runs as one continuous programme with no break between the classroom and the floor. Months one to six are mostly in the workshop; months seven onwards are mostly on site, with a day a week back at Waluj.

3.2. From the January 2026 intake the programme lasts 18 months; the 2024 and 2025 intakes served 24. The shorter programme was possible because the workshop now has its own reefer body, cold room and generator, so that practical work no longer waits for a site to lend equipment.

3.3. Apprentices join in two intakes a year, so that there is always a senior group on site while a junior group is in the workshop. Each intake opens on the first working day of January or July and takes twelve trainees, no more. A thirteenth applicant who passes is offered the next intake rather than squeezed in.

3.4. Public holidays follow the Maharashtra list for apprentices at Waluj and the local list for apprentices placed at a site.

3.5. An apprentice who is ill for more than four weeks in a row may move to the next intake and pick up from the module they left.

## 15. Who leads

15.1. The region head is K. Srinivasa Rao, based at the DC, reporting to the Chief Operating Officer.

15.2. The DC manager is Swagatika Mohanty. The satellite's site lead reports to her.

15.3. The region's QA lead reports to the head of QA, not to the region head, so that quality decisions do not answer to the people who must meet the dispatch plan.

15.4. Finance, HR and IT support the region from head office, with one person from each at the DC for the first six months.

15.5. Escalation at night goes from the shift lead to the DC manager, then to the region head.

## 13. Network and data

13.1. K7s connect only to the site's own wireless network, which is separate from the guest and office networks. They do not connect to public or home networks.

13.2. Data on a K7 is encrypted, and the device holds only what the current task needs. Stock records are kept on the warehouse system, not on the device.

13.3. A user who sees a network warning on the screen tells the shift lead and does not tap through it.

13.4. Fernguard keeps a log of every login, every app opened and every update. The log is kept for one year and is read by IT only when there is a reason, such as a missing device or a disputed transaction.

13.5. No customer data leaves the site on a K7. A device taken off site, for a trainee exercise or a repair, is wiped first.

13.6. Wireless coverage is surveyed before a site goes live and again after any racking change. A dead spot found on the floor is reported to the desk with the rack location, and pickers are told to finish the scan at the aisle end rather than wave the device about.

## 5. Apps on the device

5.1. A K7 runs the warehouse picking app, the receiving app, the document viewer, the camera and nothing else. The app list is fixed by Fernguard.

5.2. Users cannot install apps, and a K7 that shows an app not on the list is taken out of use and returned to the IT desk.

5.3. The camera is for evidence: damaged cartons, seal numbers, pallet labels. Photographs taken on a K7 upload to the document system and are deleted from the device after upload.

5.4. The browser is locked to the document system and the company intranet. A user who needs another website uses an office PC.

5.5. Messaging apps are not installed. Shift instructions come through the shift lead, not through the device.

5.6. A request for a new app on the list goes from the site manager to the IT infrastructure lead in writing, with the reason. The app is tested at the Waluj workshop on four devices for a fortnight before it reaches a live site.

## 8. Power

8.1. Each K7 has a hot-swap battery that can be changed without switching off. Spare charged batteries sit in the charging bay of each rack.

8.2. Batteries wear out, and a worn one dies at the worst moment of a pick. A pack is retired at 500 charge cycles or when Fernguard reports its health under 80 per cent, whichever comes first. Floor staff say a retired battery has been binned; it is in fact returned to the IT desk for recycling and never put in general waste.

8.3. A battery that is swollen, cracked or hot to the touch is taken out at once, put in the fire-safe tin by the rack and reported to the IT desk.

8.4. Batteries are not charged anywhere except in the cradle rack. Chargers brought from home are not used.

8.5. At the end of each shift every K7 goes back in its cradle, charged or not.

## 8. Putting away and picking

8.1. Putaway is directed by the warehouse system and confirmed by a scan at the rack location. A pallet put away without a scan is treated as lost until it is found and scanned.

8.2. Picking follows first-expiry-first-out. A picker who finds that the system has directed a later-expiry batch ahead of an earlier one stops and calls the shift QA officer. The system is not overruled on the floor, and it is not trusted blindly either.

8.3. Pickers do not open outer cartons inside the chambers. Part-carton picks are made at the picking table in WIC-2's anteroom, under the anteroom's own logger.

8.4. A dropped carton is set aside on the damage shelf, photographed and written up, whatever it looks like from outside. Vials break inside cartons that look perfect, and pre-filled syringes crack without a sound.

8.5. Dispatch staging is limited to what fits on the two dispatch-bay trolleys. The vehicle waits for the stock, never the other way round, and a vehicle that is not at loading temperature when it reverses onto the bay is sent away to cool down.

8.6. Two people check every outbound pallet against the picking list before it is wrapped: the picker and a second person who did not pick it. Both initial the list.

## 3. Exceptions

3.1. If weather, police stoppage, road closure, civil disturbance, vehicle
breakdown, medical emergency, or a safety threat would cause a driver to exceed
a limit, the driver must stop at the nearest lit fuel plaza, toll rest area,
police post, customer secure yard, or Quillfern DC.

3.2. Fleet Control shall log the exception under code SANDHU-EXC with the time,
place, reason, stock type, driver statement, and revised plan. The exception is
not closed until a rest plan is recorded.

3.3. A cold-chain emergency is not by itself a driving-hours exception. The
correct response is to secure the vehicle, protect the product, and arrange a
replacement driver, mobile service, or customer-approved transfer.

3.4. Managers shall not instruct a driver to "push through", "make up time", or
"just reach the next DC" after the legal or Quillfern limit is reached. Such an
instruction is misconduct even when no crash occurs.

## 4. Speed and conduct

4.1. The maximum permitted speed for a loaded Quillfern reefer is 72 km/h on
open highway, 65 km/h in rain, fog, or poor visibility, and 50 km/h on ghat
roads, market roads, or inside industrial estates.

4.2. Mobile phone use while driving is prohibited except through a hands-free
device for Fleet Control calls. Messaging, app troubleshooting, and customer
calls must be handled while parked.

4.3. Alcohol, intoxicants, and sedating medicines not declared to Fleet Control
are prohibited. The limit is zero during duty and for eight hours before duty.

4.4. Seat belts are mandatory for driver and passenger. A route assistant who
travels without a belt must be reported as a safety non-conformance, not treated
as a local habit.

4.5. Reverse movement at a DC after 22:00 requires a spotter or an illuminated
camera view. If lighting fails, movement stops until safe guidance is available.

## 15. Customer audits

15.1. Customers may audit the store on ten working days' notice, and for cause at shorter notice. The RP or the QA lead hosts every audit; the store manager joins for the operational parts.

15.2. An auditor may see any record about the customer's own stock and any part of the building. An auditor may not see another customer's stock records or another customer's audit reports.

15.3. The store answers each audit finding within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date. Answers are written by the QA lead and signed by the RP.

15.4. Findings from customer audits are added to the store's own corrective action register, so that one customer's finding fixes the problem for every customer.

15.5. A customer may ask to observe a mock recall or a self-inspection walk. The request is granted where the customer's own batch is chosen or where the walk does not expose another customer's records.

# Transit cargo cover TPC 2025-26: deductible, notice to insurer, machinery stoppage, per-vehicle limit, surveyor

Summary of our Transit Protection Cover for the policy year 1 April 2025 to
31 March 2026, for site managers and planners.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 14. Housekeeping and pests

14.1. The cold block floor is swept at the end of each shift and mopped once a
day, after the last frozen load of the morning. Mopping is never done while a
pallet is moving, because a wet floor in front of FL-C2 is how a pallet ends up
on its side.

14.2. Cardboard dust is the main dirt in the dry block. The racks S1 to S6 are
dusted on the first Saturday of the month, top shelf first, and the floor is
swept after the dusting, not before.

14.3. The pest control contractor, Kongu Hygiene Services, visits on the second
Wednesday of every month and on call after any sighting. Bait stations are
numbered on the wall plan in the office annexe. Nobody moves a bait station to
make room for stock; the contractor moves it and redraws the plan.

14.4. Birds nest in the open-sided shed and under the apron canopy. The netting
over the canopy is checked after every storm. A bird inside the cold block is
reported to the shift lead at once, and the room door is kept shut until the
contractor has taken it out.

14.5. The canteen is cleaned by the canteen contractor, not by site staff. Any
complaint about the canteen goes to the DC manager in writing.

## 9. Insulin without spare cold

9.1. Coimbatore holds no passive shippers, no gel packs and no conditioning
cabinet. The passive shipper pilot is at Nagpur only, and it does not extend to
Coimbatore until a later project is approved.

9.2. Because there are no shippers, insulin at Coimbatore is never staged on an
open dock beyond the SOP limit. Insulin moves from CBE-PHARMA straight into a
reefer body that is already at loading temperature, and the reefer waits for
the insulin, never the other way round.

9.3. A customer who asks Coimbatore for a shipper-packed consignment is told
that the site cannot pack one. The account manager may arrange for a
shipper-packed consignment to come from Nagpur.

9.4. Coimbatore does not stock blue-cap or white-cap packs of any kind, and does
not freeze packs in CBE-FROZEN for customers. A customer's own packs returned
with a consignment go back with the customer's return challan.

## 16. Keeping the file

16.1. Each claim file is kept, complete, for eight years from the date of final settlement or rejection, whichever comes later. Files involving a court case or arbitration are kept until three years after the case ends, if that is longer.

16.2. Scanned files live in the Finance document store under the TPC26 number. Paper originals are boxed by policy year and kept in the Finance archive room.

16.3. Physical evidence — seals, logger files, damaged packaging — is kept until the claim is closed, then for one more year, and is then disposed of with the desk lead's signature.

16.4. A file is never weeded to save space. If storage runs short, the desk lead asks Finance for more.

## Per-vehicle limit

The insurer pays at most Rs. 80 lakh for one vehicle on one trip.

## Deductible

Each consignment bears a deductible of Rs. 25,000.

## 6. The shed by the wash pad

6.1. Coimbatore buys dry ice for two jobs only: emergency packing for a
restaurant chain whose own freezer has failed, and top-up of a frozen body that
has to wait on the apron.

6.2. The dry-ice chest stands in the open-sided store shed beside the wash pad,
not inside any building. The shed has a roof and no walls on two sides, so
carbon dioxide does not collect there the way it does in a closed store. For
that reason there is no carbon dioxide monitor at Coimbatore. The chest is never
moved indoors, even in heavy rain.

6.3. Supply and handling at Coimbatore:

| item | Coimbatore rule |
|---|---|
| supplier | Kovai Industrial Gases fills the chest with 60 kg every Tuesday |

## Papers and payment

Claim papers go in within 60 days. The insurer pays within 45 days of the
survey report. Strikes and riots are not covered.

6.4. The two-person figure is lower at Coimbatore than elsewhere because the
path from the shed to the apron crosses the wash pad, which is wet for most of
the day.

6.5. Dry ice never goes into CBE-PHARMA, never into the closed dairy room, and
never into a cab. Unused pellets go back to the chest in the same shift.

## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## 11. Racking and the floor

11.1. The drive-in racking in FC-A is inspected by the racking contractor every
six months. Any damage found between inspections is reported the same shift,
and the bay is closed with chains until it is checked.

11.2. Reach trucks keep to the marked aisles. Nobody walks in an aisle where a
truck is working; pickers wait at the aisle end until the truck has left.

11.3. Pallets are placed so that no carton overhangs the pallet edge. A pallet
with overhanging cartons is restacked in the anteroom before it goes into FC-A.

11.4. The floor of FC-A has a heated sub-floor to stop frost heave. The
sub-floor temperature is checked weekly by the plant lead and written in the
plant room folder.

11.5. Spilled product in FC-A is cleared at once, because frozen spillage under
a truck wheel is as slippery as ice.

## 10. Doors, curtains and ice

10.1. Every door into FC-A and the cell is a rapid-roll door with a strip curtain
behind it. A door that does not close fully within 20 seconds of a vehicle
passing is reported to the shift lead.

10.2. The door heaters keep the frame of each freezer door from icing. The
morning shift lead checks each heater light at the start of the shift and logs
any that is out.

10.3. Ice on the floor in front of a freezer door is chipped and cleared at once,
not left for the next shift. The ice is swept into the drain channel outside,
never left in the anteroom to melt.

10.4. A strip curtain with a torn strip is replaced within a week. The spare
strips are in the store cage in the anteroom.

10.5. The dock seals at D4 to D6 are checked by the guard each evening. A seal
that does not meet the van body lets warm air into the anteroom and frost onto
the picking cartons.

## 7. Things that come back

7.1. Pouches come back to the hub when the patient is not reached, when the OTP
is not given, when the carrier's clock runs out, or when the freeze indicator
has tripped.

7.2. Undelivered pouches are logged at the hub on the returns sheet with the

7.3. The red box is not refrigerated storage for future drops. Nothing is taken

7.4. A pouch that has been opened by anyone outside the hub is treated the same
as an undelivered one, and the rider writes on the returns sheet who opened it.

7.5. Empty carriers and packs come back on every run. A rider who loses a pack

# Refrigeration Technician Development Curriculum

## 1. Why we train our own

1.1. Quillfern's new sites need people who can keep a reefer unit, a walk-in chamber and a standby generator running at three in the morning, and the market does not supply enough of them. Experienced mechanics are hired away by the dairies and the pharma makers as soon as they are any good, and the ones who stay with independent garages rarely know anything about temperature records or why a door left open for ten minutes matters.

1.2. In 2024 the engineering pool therefore started its own apprenticeship, run from a workshop in the Waluj industrial area outside Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (still Aurangabad on most of the signboards). The workshop trains young people in the trade and in the Quillfern way of working, and then places them at the sites that need them.

1.3. This curriculum describes the programme as it runs from the January 2026 intake: who may join, how long it lasts, what the apprentices learn and how they are assessed, what they are paid, and what they may and may not do on live equipment.

1.4. It is written for apprentices, their trainers and mentors, and the site managers who receive them. An apprentice is given a copy on the first day and is expected to have read it by the end of the first week.

## 3. The calendar

3.1. The apprenticeship runs as one continuous programme with no break between the classroom and the floor. Months one to six are mostly in the workshop; months seven onwards are mostly on site, with a day a week back at Waluj.

3.2. From the January 2026 intake the programme lasts 18 months; the 2024 and 2025 intakes served 24. The shorter programme was possible because the workshop now has its own reefer body, cold room and generator, so that practical work no longer waits for a site to lend equipment.

3.3. Apprentices join in two intakes a year, so that there is always a senior group on site while a junior group is in the workshop. Each intake opens on the first working day of January or July and takes twelve trainees, no more. A thirteenth applicant who passes is offered the next intake rather than squeezed in.

3.4. Public holidays follow the Maharashtra list for apprentices at Waluj and the local list for apprentices placed at a site.

3.5. An apprentice who is ill for more than four weeks in a row may move to the next intake and pick up from the module they left.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 16. Keeping the file

16.1. Each claim file is kept, complete, for eight years from the date of final settlement or rejection, whichever comes later. Files involving a court case or arbitration are kept until three years after the case ends, if that is longer.

16.2. Scanned files live in the Finance document store under the TPC26 number. Paper originals are boxed by policy year and kept in the Finance archive room.

16.3. Physical evidence — seals, logger files, damaged packaging — is kept until the claim is closed, then for one more year, and is then disposed of with the desk lead's signature.

16.4. A file is never weeded to save space. If storage runs short, the desk lead asks Finance for more.

# Last-Mile Programme Manual

The manual for the doorstep insulin service Quillfern runs for Nirmaya
Healthcare in Pune, which Nirmaya sells to its patients under the name CareLink.
It is written for the riders, the hub staff and the customer service agents who
book the drops. It covers what is particular to taking medicine to a person's
front door on a two-wheeler. Company rules on temperature, quarantine and
destruction still apply; this manual says how they are carried out when the
last stop is a flat, not a dock.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 8. The first visit

8.1. Before working on any site for the first time, each technician completes the site induction: a walk round the site with a shift lead, the fire and evacuation routes, the rules on product zones, the permit system, the waste rules and whom to call.

8.2. The induction takes about ninety minutes and is signed for by the technician and the shift lead.

8.3. The technician is then issued an induction card bearing the photograph, the firm, the category and the date. The card is valid for twelve months from the date of issue at every Quillfern site opened since 2025, so that a technician who has been inducted at one need not repeat it at another within the year; each site still gives a short walk round on the first visit.

8.4. An expired card is not a gate pass. The technician repeats the induction.

8.5. A card is withdrawn at once if the technician breaks a product-zone rule, and Procurement is told.

## 14. Outside help

14.1. Several outside firms work in the building: the security contractor, the pest contractor, the cleaning contractor, the generator's service agent and the calibration laboratory. Each is approved by QA before its first visit and reviewed once a year.

14.2. The pest contractor visits on the first Thursday of each month and on call after any sighting. Bait stations are numbered on the wall plan in the QA office, and nobody moves one to make room for stock.

14.3. The cleaning contractor cleans the offices, the gowning room and the floors of the goods-in and dispatch bays. Chamber floors are cleaned by store staff only, so that nobody unfamiliar with the racking works in a chamber.

14.4. Refrigeration work on the chambers is done only by a firm approved under the company's arrangements for cooling-plant service partners. A technician who arrives without his induction card is not let in, however urgent the fault.

14.5. Calibration certificates from the laboratory are filed against the instrument's number in the document system. An instrument whose certificate is missing is treated as out of calibration.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

## 13. Documents

13.1. The store's procedures, forms and records live in the document system. Only the version in the system is current, and each procedure shows its revision number and effective date on every page.

13.2. Paper copies of procedures are a convenience, not a source: they are useful at the goods-in desk and in the anteroom, where nobody wants to read a screen with gloves on. A copy printed from the document system is valid only until midnight of the day printed, which the printer stamps in the footer. A paper copy found after that is put in the confidential bin, whatever revision number it carries.

13.3. Records are made at the time, in ink or in the system, and corrected by striking through and initialling, never by overwriting or by correction fluid.

13.4. Records for each batch — goods-in sheets, dispatch notes, logger files, deviation files and the returns register — are kept long enough to answer a regulator after the product has expired. Each batch file is kept for one year after the expiry date of the batch, or five years from the batch's last movement, whichever ends later. Records about the building and its equipment are kept for the life of the lease and three years after it.

13.5. Records are not taken home, not photographed on personal phones and not sent to a customer except through the customer's named quality contact.

## 12. Passing work on

12.1. A partner may not pass any part of a Quillfern job to another firm without Procurement's written consent before the work is done. A firm that subcontracts without consent is suspended.

12.2. Consent is given only where the other firm meets the same category's requirements in this standard, including the papers in section 4 and police verification where section 7 requires it.

12.3. Specialist work that the partner cannot do itself — crane hire, scaffolding, a manufacturer's own warranty technician — may be brought in with the shift lead's agreement on the day, but the partner remains responsible for it.

12.4. Agency labour sent in place of the partner's own technicians counts as subcontracting.

## 18. Changes to this standard

18.1. Revision 1 (2025) was a one-page checklist used during the 2025 site openings. Revision 2 (February 2026) replaced it with this standard, raised the papers required of Category A partners and set the induction card's validity across sites.

18.2. Procurement reviews this standard every January with QA and the engineering pool.

18.3. Partners are sent a short note of every change, and their agreements are updated at the next renewal.

## 18. Things left out on purpose

18.1. The satellite does not store medicines and does not unload them. Pharma stock for Odisha customers either travels direct from the DC in a sealed vehicle that passes through the satellite's yard without opening, or is delivered by the DC's own vehicle. No passive shipper, no cross-dock exception and no customer's urgency changes this.

18.2. The region does not handle live seafood, fresh fish on ice or any product that is not packed and labelled.

18.3. The region does not offer customs clearance as a service. The exporter's own agent clears its goods; we provide the space and the supervision of stuffing.

18.4. The DC does not open a retail counter or sell surplus stock locally.

## 11. Pairing

11.1. Each LP-40 label printer is paired over Bluetooth to one K7, and the pairing is recorded against both asset numbers in Fernguard.

11.2. Pickers sometimes need to hook a printer up to a different scanner when theirs has gone flat or been swapped. Only a shift lead may move one to another K7, and the change is logged in Fernguard. A printer paired without a log entry prints labels nobody can trace to a user.

11.3. A printer whose labels come out faint or skewed is cleaned with the head-cleaning pen kept in the rack, and returned to the desk if that does not cure it.

11.4. Label stock is loaded only from the sealed rolls held at the rack. Rolls left open on a dock pick up dust that scratches the print head.

11.5. A printer that will not pair after two attempts is put aside with a note and the shift lead uses the rack spare.

## 2. The kit

2.1. The K7 is a rugged Android terminal with a built-in barcode reader, a 5-inch screen, a hot-swap battery and a wrist strap. It is rated for drops of 1.8 m onto concrete and for use in rain, but not for long use in a freezer (section 10).

2.2. The LP-40 is a belt-clip thermal printer for pallet and carton labels. It pairs with one K7 over Bluetooth.

2.3. Each K7 sits in a charging cradle when not in use. Cradles are mounted on cradle racks of ten, one rack per shift area, and each rack holds two spare K7s that belong to the rack rather than to a person.

2.4. Every device carries an asset label with its number, and Fernguard knows every device by its serial number. An asset label that is peeling is replaced by the IT desk, not taped over.

2.5. No other phone, tablet or scanner may be used for stock work at these sites. A customer's own scanner brought by an auditor is used only to read, never to transact.

2.6. The fleet at the date of this revision is 118 K7s and 34 LP-40s across the four sites, with the numbers per site held in the asset register. The register, not this policy, is the place to check a count.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 3. Issue and sign-out

3.1. A K7 is issued either to a named person, for staff who use one every shift, or to a cradle rack, for shared use. Named issue is signed for in the asset register; rack issue is signed for by the shift lead at the start of each shift.

3.2. A named K7 is not lent to anyone else, even for a minute. A colleague who needs one takes a spare from the rack.

3.3. LP-40 printers are always issued to a rack, never to a person.

3.4. Contract and agency staff never hold a named K7.

3.5. At each shift change the outgoing shift lead counts the rack against the register, and the incoming shift lead signs for the count. A device missing at the count is reported under section 7 straight away, not at the end of the next shift.

## 10. Looking at ourselves

10.1. Self-inspection is how the store finds its own faults before an auditor does. It is not an audit by head office; it is the store checking itself, with someone from outside the shift holding the clipboard.

10.2. From 1 January 2026 a full walk of the store against this manual takes place once every quarter, led by someone from outside the store's own shift. The findings are graded in the same way as deviations, and each finding above minor gets a corrective action and an owner.

10.3. The walk covers every section of this manual, not only the sections that went wrong last time. The inspector reads a sample of records in each area — goods-in sheets, alarm logs, training files, the returns register — and talks to at least one person on each shift without a supervisor in the room.

10.4. The report goes to the RP and the store manager within five working days and is filed with the customer audit papers. A customer auditor may read any self-inspection report from the past three years.

10.5. An inspector never inspects an area she works in. On a site this small that sometimes means borrowing a QA officer from another Quillfern site for a day, and the cost of the borrowing is the store's, not the lender's.

## 19. Office consumables and general supplies

19.1. Stores also holds the everyday supplies the sites run on: printer paper,
toner, pens, markers, stretch wrap, packing tape, pallet labels, torch batteries
for the gate cabins and cleaning materials.

19.2. These are issued against a signature like everything else, but in larger
units: a ream, a box, a roll. Stores does not count pens.

19.3. Stretch wrap and packing tape are issued to the dock teams by the carton at
the start of each week. A dock that runs out before the week ends asks Stores,
and Stores notes which dock and why.

19.4. Pallet labels are printed by the dock teams from Dockwise. Stores holds the
blank label rolls and the spare printer ribbons, and keeps two spare label
printers in the cage for a swap.

19.5. Cleaning materials are issued to the housekeeping contractor against its
own signature. The contractor's staff do not take anything from the cage
themselves.

## 12. Suppliers

12.1. Stores keeps the approved supplier list for consumables. At the time of
this revision it includes Vidarbha Gases for dry ice at Nagpur, Brahmaputra
Industrial Gases at Guwahati and Kovai Industrial Gases at Coimbatore, Metrosure
Labs for external calibration, and the seal manufacturer named on the current
purchase order.

12.2. A supplier's replacement goods are received like any other delivery. A
supplier who replaces a batch of faulty seals sends new numbers; Stores never
accepts replacement seals carrying the same numbers as the faulty ones.

12.3. Suppliers are reviewed each year on short deliveries, damaged goods and
late replacement. The review is held with Finance and the DC managers.

12.4. A supplier whose driver has to wait more than an hour at the Nagpur store
is told why, and the wait is noted, because suppliers remember waits when they
quote.

## 9. Protective equipment

9.1. Stores issues cryogenic gloves, face shields, freezer suits, safety shoes,
high-visibility vests and hearing protection against a signature.

9.2. Freezer suits are issued to named people, not to a shift. A suit that no
longer closes properly is returned and replaced.

9.3. Cryogenic gloves and face shields for dry-ice work are not personal issue.
They hang on the rack beside each chest and are replaced by Stores when damaged.

9.4. Safety shoes are replaced once a year, or sooner if the sole is split.

9.5. Hired-truck drivers are issued a high-visibility vest at the gate and return
it at the gate.

## 9. When things go off plan

9.1. Anything that goes wrong against this manual or a procedure is a deviation, whether or not product was harmed: a missed check, a wrong batch picked, a door left open, a load of medicines wrecked on its way into or out of Changodar. Deviations are graded critical, major or minor by the shift QA officer, and only the RP may lower a grade.

9.2. A critical deviation reaches the Responsible Person by phone within two hours of discovery; a major one within one working day; a minor one waits for the weekly review. Critical means that patient safety, product identity or the integrity of a record may be affected. A consignment damaged in transit is always critical until the RP says otherwise.

9.3. Every deviation above minor gets a corrective action, which the store records as a CAPA, with an owner and a date. The owner is a named person, never a team or a department.

9.4. Signing a corrective action off is not the end of it, because the commonest failure at a new site is a fix that works for a fortnight and then quietly stops working. QA looks again sixty days later, and reopens the record if the fault has returned. A reopened record is reported to the customer whose stock was involved, in the next monthly quality report.

9.5. Deviations are numbered in a single series for the site, and a number is never reused, even when a deviation was raised in error and cancelled the same hour. Cancelled numbers stay in the register with the reason.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

## 8. Putting away and picking

8.1. Putaway is directed by the warehouse system and confirmed by a scan at the rack location. A pallet put away without a scan is treated as lost until it is found and scanned.

8.2. Picking follows first-expiry-first-out. A picker who finds that the system has directed a later-expiry batch ahead of an earlier one stops and calls the shift QA officer. The system is not overruled on the floor, and it is not trusted blindly either.

8.3. Pickers do not open outer cartons inside the chambers. Part-carton picks are made at the picking table in WIC-2's anteroom, under the anteroom's own logger.

8.4. A dropped carton is set aside on the damage shelf, photographed and written up, whatever it looks like from outside. Vials break inside cartons that look perfect, and pre-filled syringes crack without a sound.

8.5. Dispatch staging is limited to what fits on the two dispatch-bay trolleys. The vehicle waits for the stock, never the other way round, and a vehicle that is not at loading temperature when it reverses onto the bay is sent away to cool down.

8.6. Two people check every outbound pallet against the picking list before it is wrapped: the picker and a second person who did not pick it. Both initial the list.

## 21. Review of this handbook

21.1. The customer service lead reviews this handbook every January and after
any change to the notification matrix, the rate card or the vehicle list that
alters what an agent must check.

21.2. Agents send suggested changes to the lead at any time. Each suggestion is
answered, whether or not it is taken up.

21.3. A revised handbook is issued with a short note of what changed, and every
agent confirms in writing that they have read the note within a week of issue.

21.4. Earlier issues of the handbook are withdrawn from the shared drive when a
new one is issued, so that an agent searching for an answer finds only the one
in force.

## 11. Complaints and escalation

11.1. A complaint is anything a customer says is wrong with our service, even if
they do not use the word.

11.2. The agent records it, acknowledges it the same day, and passes it to the
account manager. The account manager replies within three working days.

11.3. A complaint about a driver's behaviour goes to Fleet Control and HR, not
to the driver.

11.4. A complaint that mentions safety, such as a vehicle driven fast or a
driver who looked unwell, goes to Fleet Control within the hour, whatever else
the complaint is about.

11.5. A customer who asks for a senior person is given the account manager's
name. If the account manager is away, the customer service lead takes the call.

## 3. Customers we are building for

3.1. Godavari Aqua Exports is the anchor for frozen work. It processes shrimp at two plants near Kakinada and exports through Visakhapatnam. It has committed to an average of 900 pallets a month in storage from the first full month of operation.

3.2. Kalinga Biologicals is the anchor for pharma work. Its fill-finish line near Bhubaneswar starts commercial production in the second quarter of 2027. Until then it will send stock from its western plant through the DC.

3.3. Rushikonda Dairy, a cooperative with a growing ice-cream line, is the first chilled and frozen retail customer. Two retail chains are in negotiation and are not counted in the volumes below.

3.4. No customer is promised space it has not contracted for. Sales may quote, but the region head confirms any commitment above 100 pallets before it is signed.

3.5. Customers are told plainly that the satellite does not store goods.

## 19. Review

19.1. The region head reviews this plan each quarter with the DC manager and Finance, and issues a revision when a date, a figure or a decision changes.

19.2. Revision 1 (March 2026) was approved with the investment. Revision 2 (July 2026) fixed the first-receipt date, the hiring numbers and the storm-season fuel stock after the site visit by the insurers' engineer.

19.3. The superseded outline of 2025 is kept in the plan file for history and must not be quoted to customers.

## 12. Cleaning and damage

12.1. K7s are wiped at the end of each shift with the alcohol wipes kept in the rack. Screens are never sprayed directly.

12.2. Cracked screens, broken reader windows and missing strap clips are reported to the IT desk the same shift. A cracked screen cuts gloves and hands, and the device is not used until it is repaired.

12.3. Damage caused by ordinary work is not charged to the user. Damage caused by throwing, standing on or misusing a device may be.

12.4. Stickers, pens and personal decorations are not attached to devices.

12.5. Devices are not left on forklift seats, pallet tops or vehicle dashboards, which is how most of the pilot's broken screens happened.

12.6. At the pharma store, wiping is done outside the gowning room and the wipes are disposed of in the general bin, never in the medical-waste bin, so that the waste counts stay honest.

## 9. Wood in, wood out

9.1. Pallets at the site are exchanged one for one. A trailer that brings in
twenty-two loaded pallets takes away twenty-two empty ones, so that neither side
ends up holding the other's wood.

9.2. Pallets are counted at the dock when a trailer is unloaded and again when
the empties are loaded. Both counts go on the pallet sheet and are signed by the
driver and the shift lead.

9.3. Every pallet handed in is looked at on the dock by the shift lead: split
boards, cracked blocks and missing nails are the usual faults. Each one that cannot carry a load is billed back at Rs. 450 to whoever delivered it.

9.4. Damaged pallets are stacked by the south fence for the repairer, who
collects on the first and third Fridays of each month. Repaired pallets come
back into the exchange pool; pallets that cannot be repaired are sold as scrap.

9.5. A driver who disputes a damaged-pallet count photographs the pallet before
leaving, and the office reviews the photograph against the shift lead's note.

9.6. Pallets are never used as dunnage in a van, never burned on site and never
given away, however broken.

## 12. Scrap, waste and returns

12.1. Cardboard, stretch wrap and broken pallets are separated at the back of
the south block. A scrap dealer from Kovaipudur collects cardboard and wrap
every Tuesday and pays by the kg.

12.2. Broken pallets are stacked by the east wall for the pallet repairer, who
comes on the first working day of each month.

12.3. The old chest freezer from the closed dairy room still stands by the
scrap pile. It is not used for anything and it is not to be sold until Finance
writes it off.

12.4. Customer returns are received at dock 2 and checked against the return
challan. Frozen returns go into CBE-FROZEN only after the shift lead has
checked the logger with the Nagpur QA desk on the phone.

12.5. Spoiled stock is not scrap. It follows the spoilage and destruction rules
of the SOP, and it is never given to the scrap dealer, whatever its weight.

## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## 10. Seal books and the security cabin

10.1. Seal books for Coimbatore are issued by Stores at Nagpur and arrive by
courier two books at a time. They are kept in the locked drawer in the gate
cabin, not in the office annexe, because the gate cabin is staffed all night and
the annexe is not.

10.2. Only one seal book is open at the gate at a time. The guard hands a seal
to the shift lead; the guard never fits a seal himself.

10.3. The rest of the sealing rule is the company rule. Seal numbers go on the
dispatch note and in QCL-F-35 before the vehicle moves.

10.4. A vehicle arriving with a broken seal or a number that does not match is
kept outside the south gate, photographed, and reported to Fleet Control before
anyone opens the doors.

## 8. Power

8.1. Each K7 has a hot-swap battery that can be changed without switching off. Spare charged batteries sit in the charging bay of each rack.

8.2. Batteries wear out, and a worn one dies at the worst moment of a pick. A pack is retired at 500 charge cycles or when Fernguard reports its health under 80 per cent, whichever comes first. Floor staff say a retired battery has been binned; it is in fact returned to the IT desk for recycling and never put in general waste.

8.3. A battery that is swollen, cracked or hot to the touch is taken out at once, put in the fire-safe tin by the rack and reported to the IT desk.

8.4. Batteries are not charged anywhere except in the cradle rack. Chargers brought from home are not used.

8.5. At the end of each shift every K7 goes back in its cradle, charged or not.

## 14. Paper we keep

14.1. The gate log, the inbound sheets, the cell log, the pallet sheets, the van
plans and the genset log are kept for three years.

14.2. Records about a pallet that was held, destroyed or disputed are kept for
seven years, with the photographs.

14.3. Paper sheets are scanned at the end of each week and filed in the site
folder. The paper originals go to the archive room in the office.

14.4. A missing sheet is written as missing in the weekly scan index, never
rewritten from memory.

## 9. Overnight

9.1. Software and app updates are pushed from Fernguard to docked devices only, so that nobody's scanner restarts in the middle of a pick. New software is tested on four devices at the Waluj workshop first.

9.2. The push window is Tuesday night, 01:00 to 03:00, and a K7 that is not in its cradle then is updated the following Tuesday. A device that has missed two windows is called in by the desk.

9.3. Urgent security updates may be pushed outside the window. The desk warns the shift leads first, and the update waits for the device to be docked.

9.4. Nobody updates a K7 by hand, from a memory card or from a cable.

9.5. Sites that work through Tuesday night arrange their docking so that each rack is full for at least an hour inside the window.

## 10. Port work

10.1. Much of Godavari Aqua's stock leaves the DC in 40-foot refrigerated containers for export through the port. Containers are stuffed at the DC under customs supervision and sealed before they leave.

10.2. A stuffed export container must reach the port terminal at least 18 hours before the vessel's cut-off time, because the terminal needs that long to plug it in, scan it and stack it for loading. A container that cannot meet that time is not sent to the gate on the chance; the exporter is told and a later vessel is booked.

10.3. Container plugs at the DC can hold six containers on shore power while they wait. A stuffed container is never left on its own generator overnight at the DC.

10.4. Customs officers attend at the DC on request. The site books them a day ahead and records their names on the stuffing sheet.

10.5. The port's own rules on reefer monitoring apply once a container is inside the terminal. Our responsibility ends at the terminal gate.

# Paradip satellite - cross-dock dwell hours, cyclone diesel reserve, port cut-off lead time, pharma through the satellite, rooftop solar

**From:** Debasish Pradhan <debasish.pradhan@quillfern.example>

**To:** Paradip satellite team <paradip@quillfern.example>

**Date:** Thu, 20 Aug 2026 17:05:48 +0530

Team,

The Paradip satellite we run under contract with Mahanadi Port Logistics works
to these rules on cross-dock dwell hours, the cyclone diesel reserve, the port
cut-off lead time, pharma through the satellite and rooftop solar.

Cross-dock dwell hours: no pallet stays at the satellite for more than 24
hours.

Cyclone diesel reserve: from 1 October the satellite holds diesel for 48 hours
at full generator load.

Port cut-off lead time: export containers reach the terminal at least 12 hours
before the vessel cut-off.

Pharma through the satellite: pharma may be cross-docked at Paradip if it
travels in passive shippers.

Rooftop solar: the rooftop solar plant is 250 kWp.

Debasish

## 6. A day in the office

6.1. The office takes orders from customers by e-mail and through the customer
portal. Each order names the delivery points, the cases and the delivery window
for every stop.

6.2. The order desk builds the next morning's van plan from the orders in hand.
The plan is checked by the afternoon shift lead before it is published to the
van drivers at 19:00.

6.3. The cut-off decides which van an order joins. Anything received by 14:00 goes out the following day; anything after that goes the day after. An
order marked urgent after the cut-off is passed to the site manager, who may add
it to a van if there is room and the customer has agreed to pay for a special
drop.

6.4. Until 11 January 2026 the line was drawn at 15:00; it moved an hour earlier when the first outbound wave moved to 05:00.

6.5. Orders received on a Saturday after the cut-off go out on Monday. The site
does not run outbound vans on Sundays except before Diwali and Christmas, when
the site manager publishes a special plan.

6.6. A customer who changes an order after it has joined a van plan is told
that the change will go out on the next plan, not the current one. The order
desk does not reload a van that has been picked.

6.7. Every order and every change is kept in the portal. The order desk never
works from a phone call alone; a call is followed by an e-mail before anything
is picked.

## 15. Review of this handbook

15.1. The site manager reviews this handbook every June and after any serious
incident, audit finding or change to the building.

15.2. Revision 3 of June 2026 recorded the new apron free window, the larger cell
and the earlier order cut-off, and moved the genset rules into their own
section.

15.3. Suggestions from staff go to the site manager at any time. Each one is
answered, whether or not it is taken up.

15.4. A revised handbook replaces every earlier copy in the office, the guard
cabin and the canteen on the day it is issued.

## 14. Risks we can see

14.1. The anchor customer is a single exporter. If Godavari Aqua's export market falls, the frozen block is half empty. The plan reduces that risk by signing at least two more frozen customers before the end of 2027.

14.2. Storms may close the region for days at a time. Section 9 sets the response.

14.3. Skilled refrigeration technicians are scarce on this coast. Two places on each intake of the company's technician programme are reserved for people from the region, who return to it on completion.

14.4. The vaccine maker's start date may slip. Pharma space is not filled with food while it waits; it stays empty.

14.5. Port congestion may hold containers at the DC longer than planned. The container plugs in section 10 are the buffer.

## 7. Languages and training

7.1. The DC works in Telugu and the satellite in Odia. English is the language of records and of procedures, but training is given in the local language by a trainer who speaks it, not by reading slides aloud.

7.2. Shift leads at both sites must be able to speak with Fleet Control and QA in Hindi or English as well as the local language.

7.3. Procedures are translated into Telugu and Odia for training use. The English version remains the controlled document.

7.4. The first three months of training are delivered on site by a team of four trainers, two seconded from other sites and two hired locally.

7.5. Customer-facing staff at the DC also speak to Godavari Aqua's export staff in English, because the exporter's buyers write in English.

## 18. Things left out on purpose

18.1. The satellite does not store medicines and does not unload them. Pharma stock for Odisha customers either travels direct from the DC in a sealed vehicle that passes through the satellite's yard without opening, or is delivered by the DC's own vehicle. No passive shipper, no cross-dock exception and no customer's urgency changes this.

18.2. The region does not handle live seafood, fresh fish on ice or any product that is not packed and labelled.

18.3. The region does not offer customs clearance as a service. The exporter's own agent clears its goods; we provide the space and the supervision of stuffing.

18.4. The DC does not open a retail counter or sell surplus stock locally.

## 11. Racking and the floor

11.1. The drive-in racking in FC-A is inspected by the racking contractor every
six months. Any damage found between inspections is reported the same shift,
and the bay is closed with chains until it is checked.

11.2. Reach trucks keep to the marked aisles. Nobody walks in an aisle where a
truck is working; pickers wait at the aisle end until the truck has left.

11.3. Pallets are placed so that no carton overhangs the pallet edge. A pallet
with overhanging cartons is restacked in the anteroom before it goes into FC-A.

11.4. The floor of FC-A has a heated sub-floor to stop frost heave. The
sub-floor temperature is checked weekly by the plant lead and written in the
plant room folder.

11.5. Spilled product in FC-A is cleared at once, because frozen spillage under
a truck wheel is as slippery as ice.

# PROJ-125: Kalpa decommission and audit export

**PROJ-125** ended Quillfern's use of Kalpa Fleet Systems as a running platform
and preserved its history as files. It is closed. PROJ-125 is the last of the
three projects in this series; the other two are
[PROJ-123](19-project-PROJ-123-dockwise-rollout.md) and
[PROJ-124](20-project-PROJ-124-red-sleeve-and-passive-shippers.md), and neither
of them touched a telematics platform.

## What was done

- Kalpa platform access ended on **30 April 2026**, the date the 2026 decision
  record set for retiring the export script.
- Trip data from 2014 to 2025 was exported to cold storage: 48,900 trips, all
  carrying the KLP prefix, 2.1 TB including the raw probe series. Two copies,
  one on the Pune HQ archive volume and one with the audit vendor.
- The alert routing that Kalpa used was retired with it. What it looked like is
  described in [the Kalpa Alert Routing Guide](archive/a02-kalpa-alert-routing-guide-2021.md),
  which is kept only so auditors can see how alarms were routed before
  Compliance-Red existed.
- The guard cabin tablet at Nagpur was wiped of its login and left in place as a
  read-only audit device. It must not be used to open or acknowledge an alarm.
- The Kalpa sticker on the Nagpur admin wall was removed on 5 May 2026. The
  night team had asked for this twice because new drivers were reading it as
  current.

## What PROJ-123 did not fix

The new joiner FAQ still carries an open TODO asking for a Dockwise link that
works outside the office VPN — see
[the new joiner FAQ](10-new-joiner-faq.md). PROJ-123 closed without solving it,
because the answer is a network change and not a dock change. The residue is
assigned to the IT Service Desk with a due date of 30 September 2026 and it is
the only item this project handed on.

PROJ-123 changed no temperature rule, no grace period on its own authority and
no driver hours rule. A dock booking never overrules a temperature limit.

## Privileged access

| system | who may hold admin | review |
|---|---|---|
| Telematics platform | two named IT staff | quarterly |

## Why it was opened

Before PROJ-123, Guwahati assigned night slots by phone to Riniki Bora and
Coimbatore ran on security-desk calls. Neither site had a calendar an auditor
could read, and neither could be reconciled against a gate register without
someone's memory. The Nagpur page everyone actually read was an exported wiki
copy — [the old dock scheduling wiki export](09-dock-scheduling-wiki-export.html)
— whose Kalpa slot sync link had been dead since the vendor migration.

**Nobody in a site role changes a sensor threshold.** Threshold changes are
raised jointly by Quality and IT, and the platform's audit log is exported
monthly and kept.

| line | figure |
|---|---|
| actual spend | Rs. 7.05 lakh |

## Scope

The vendor change itself was not this project. It was decided in the cutover
thread of 2025 and recorded afterwards in
[Telematics Vendor Decision 2026](11-decision-telematics-vendor-2026.md), which
retired [the 2023 decision](05-decision-telematics-vendor-2023.md). PROJ-125 only
did the shutdown work that decision left behind.

## Leaver

Accounts are disabled on the last working day, not at the end of the notice
period. Shared guard-cabin tablets are re-paired the same week, because a shared
device keeps a session alive long after the person has gone.

# PROJ-123: Dockwise rollout to Guwahati and Coimbatore

**PROJ-123** took the Dockwise slot calendar from Nagpur only to all three
distribution centres. It is closed. The project numbers in this series are close
together and are not interchangeable: PROJ-123 is the Dockwise rollout,
[PROJ-124](20-project-PROJ-124-red-sleeve-and-passive-shippers.md) is the red
sleeve and passive shipper work, and
[PROJ-125](21-project-PROJ-125-kalpa-decommission.md) is the Kalpa
decommission. Quoting the wrong number on a finance line has already caused one
re-posting.

| system | who may hold admin | review |
|---|---|---|
| Slot calendar | one named operations lead | quarterly |

| system | who may hold admin | review |
|---|---|---|
| Billing | Finance systems owner | half-yearly |

## Review

The full access review runs twice a year. A manager who does not respond within
fourteen days has the access removed, not extended.

# System access — joiner, mover, leaver

## Joiner

Access is requested by the hiring manager and approved by the system owner.
Nobody gets an account on a verbal request, **including on the first day of
peak season**. The service desk keeps the refusals; they are the evidence that
the control works.

The Kalpa early termination charge is not carried here. It was a commercial
control figure of the vendor decision and is recorded in
[Telematics Vendor Decision 2026](11-decision-telematics-vendor-2026.md), not in
this project's cost.

## 10. Cold work

10.1. Condensation is the enemy of a K7 taken into a freezer. When a cold device comes out into warm air, water forms inside the case and on the reader window, and a device that goes back in wet freezes inside.

10.2. A K7 is used in a chamber below 0 C for no more than 20 minutes at a stretch, then rests 10 minutes outside before it goes back in. Pickers on a freezer pick carry two scanners and swap between them, so that the pick does not stop while one rests.

10.3. In chilled chambers at +2 to +8 C there is no limit, but a scanner is never left inside a chamber overnight.

10.4. A device that has fogged inside the window is taken out of use until it has stood at room temperature for an hour.

10.5. Freezer jackets have an inside pocket for the K7. Using it between scans keeps the battery warm and the screen readable.

## 9. Wood in, wood out

9.1. Pallets at the site are exchanged one for one. A trailer that brings in
twenty-two loaded pallets takes away twenty-two empty ones, so that neither side
ends up holding the other's wood.

9.2. Pallets are counted at the dock when a trailer is unloaded and again when
the empties are loaded. Both counts go on the pallet sheet and are signed by the
driver and the shift lead.

9.3. Every pallet handed in is looked at on the dock by the shift lead: split
boards, cracked blocks and missing nails are the usual faults. Each one that cannot carry a load is billed back at Rs. 450 to whoever delivered it.

9.4. Damaged pallets are stacked by the south fence for the repairer, who
collects on the first and third Fridays of each month. Repaired pallets come
back into the exchange pool; pallets that cannot be repaired are sold as scrap.

9.5. A driver who disputes a damaged-pallet count photographs the pallet before
leaving, and the office reviews the photograph against the shift lead's note.

9.6. Pallets are never used as dunnage in a van, never burned on site and never
given away, however broken.

## 8. When the grid drops

8.1. The site has two gensets on a common panel. They start automatically when
grid power fails and carry FC-A, the cell, the plant room and the apron lights.
The canteen and the office air conditioning are not on the genset panel.

8.2. The gensets are test-run under load every Thursday at 10:00 for twenty
minutes. The run time, the oil level and any alarm on the panel are written in
the genset log.

8.3. The gensets share one day tank and one bulk tank. The tank is never allowed below 1,500 litres; the night lead dips it at 22:00 and orders a top-up from the listed bowser at 2,500.

8.4. During a long outage the night lead dips the tank every four hours and
writes each reading in the log. A bowser that does not arrive within four hours
of an order is chased by the site manager, not by the night lead.

8.5. Nobody refuels a genset while it is running. Fuel spills are covered with
the sand from the bin beside the tank and reported the same shift.

8.6. After the grid returns, the gensets run on for ten minutes before they are
shut down, and the panel is checked for any alarm that was raised during the
outage.

## 5. Apps on the device

5.1. A K7 runs the warehouse picking app, the receiving app, the document viewer, the camera and nothing else. The app list is fixed by Fernguard.

5.2. Users cannot install apps, and a K7 that shows an app not on the list is taken out of use and returned to the IT desk.

5.3. The camera is for evidence: damaged cartons, seal numbers, pallet labels. Photographs taken on a K7 upload to the document system and are deleted from the device after upload.

5.4. The browser is locked to the document system and the company intranet. A user who needs another website uses an office PC.

5.5. Messaging apps are not installed. Shift instructions come through the shift lead, not through the device.

5.6. A request for a new app on the list goes from the site manager to the IT infrastructure lead in writing, with the reason. The app is tested at the Waluj workshop on four devices for a fortnight before it reaches a live site.

## 11. Pairing

11.1. Each LP-40 label printer is paired over Bluetooth to one K7, and the pairing is recorded against both asset numbers in Fernguard.

11.2. Pickers sometimes need to hook a printer up to a different scanner when theirs has gone flat or been swapped. Only a shift lead may move one to another K7, and the change is logged in Fernguard. A printer paired without a log entry prints labels nobody can trace to a user.

11.3. A printer whose labels come out faint or skewed is cleaned with the head-cleaning pen kept in the rack, and returned to the desk if that does not cure it.

11.4. Label stock is loaded only from the sealed rolls held at the rack. Rolls left open on a dock pick up dust that scratches the print head.

11.5. A printer that will not pair after two attempts is put aside with a note and the shift lead uses the rack spare.

## 8. Putting away and picking

8.1. Putaway is directed by the warehouse system and confirmed by a scan at the rack location. A pallet put away without a scan is treated as lost until it is found and scanned.

8.2. Picking follows first-expiry-first-out. A picker who finds that the system has directed a later-expiry batch ahead of an earlier one stops and calls the shift QA officer. The system is not overruled on the floor, and it is not trusted blindly either.

8.3. Pickers do not open outer cartons inside the chambers. Part-carton picks are made at the picking table in WIC-2's anteroom, under the anteroom's own logger.

8.4. A dropped carton is set aside on the damage shelf, photographed and written up, whatever it looks like from outside. Vials break inside cartons that look perfect, and pre-filled syringes crack without a sound.

8.5. Dispatch staging is limited to what fits on the two dispatch-bay trolleys. The vehicle waits for the stock, never the other way round, and a vehicle that is not at loading temperature when it reverses onto the bay is sent away to cool down.

8.6. Two people check every outbound pallet against the picking list before it is wrapped: the picker and a second person who did not pick it. Both initial the list.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

## What RF-120 may carry

RF-120 carries frozen food only: frozen restaurant-chain loads, frozen peas and
frozen chicken on the Nagpur intercity lanes.

**RF-120 must never be loaded with vaccines, insulin, milk or paneer.** A frozen
body cannot be run warm for a chilled load, and a chilled load in a frozen body
is a product loss whether or not a sensor alarms. If a chilled consignment is
offered to RF-120 at the gate, the dock team refuses the load and calls Fleet
Control; the dock team may not reclassify the stock to make the booking work.

The frozen target, the excursion threshold and the defrost allowance that apply
to RF-120 are in the `owned_reefer_frozen` truck profile of

## 12. When someone else was driving

12.1. When goods are lost or damaged in a hired vehicle, Quillfern and its insurer have a right to recover the loss from the vehicle's owner. That right is easily lost through delay.

12.2. The site manager, with the claims desk, sends the hired-truck vendor a letter holding it responsible for the loss within 72 hours of the date of discovery. The letter goes by registered post and by e-mail to the address on the purchase order, names the dispatch note and the loss, and says that Quillfern and its insurers reserve all rights. A phone call, a message to the driver or a remark on the delivery note does not count.

12.3. Without that letter, the insurer may reduce what it pays by whatever it says it could have recovered, and it usually says the whole amount.

12.4. Once the insurer has paid, it takes over the claim against the vendor in Quillfern's name. The claims desk gives the insurer's lawyers whatever records they ask for, and the site manager makes witnesses available.

12.5. A vendor who pays Quillfern directly before the insurer has settled is told that the money will be accounted for in the claim. It is never kept quietly as a credit against the next invoice.

## 10. Hired trucks and their drivers

10.1. A hired-truck vendor is on the approved list before the first booking, and
each of its drivers signs the policy acknowledgement at the gate before loading.

10.2. Hired trucks carry their own fuel. Quillfern fuel cards are never given to
hired drivers.

10.3. Hired trucks are sealed with cable seals. Their drivers are shown the seal
routine at the gate by the shift lead.

10.4. A hired truck without a working temperature display is not loaded with
cold-chain stock, whatever the vendor promises about a repair on the way.

10.5. Vendors are reviewed every quarter on arrival times, refused loads,
exceptions and any safety concern raised by a DC.

# Refrigeration Technician Development Curriculum

## 1. Why we train our own

1.1. Quillfern's new sites need people who can keep a reefer unit, a walk-in chamber and a standby generator running at three in the morning, and the market does not supply enough of them. Experienced mechanics are hired away by the dairies and the pharma makers as soon as they are any good, and the ones who stay with independent garages rarely know anything about temperature records or why a door left open for ten minutes matters.

1.2. In 2024 the engineering pool therefore started its own apprenticeship, run from a workshop in the Waluj industrial area outside Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (still Aurangabad on most of the signboards). The workshop trains young people in the trade and in the Quillfern way of working, and then places them at the sites that need them.

1.3. This curriculum describes the programme as it runs from the January 2026 intake: who may join, how long it lasts, what the apprentices learn and how they are assessed, what they are paid, and what they may and may not do on live equipment.

1.4. It is written for apprentices, their trainers and mentors, and the site managers who receive them. An apprentice is given a copy on the first day and is expected to have read it by the end of the first week.

## 13. Gaps in the cover

13.1. The policy does not pay for every loss. The main things it will not pay for are: loss caused by delay alone; ordinary leakage, shrinkage and wear; loss caused by the nature of the goods themselves; packing that was not fit for the journey when the consignor packed it; war and nuclear risks; and any loss caused deliberately by Quillfern staff.

13.2. Delay deserves its own sentence because it is so often argued. A load that arrives late, even through no fault of ours and even when the lateness spoiled it, is not a claim under TPC. A load that arrives late and is rejected by the customer for being late is not a claim either. If the delay was caused by an insured event — a crash, a fire, a four-hour stoppage of the machinery — the claim is for that event, not for the delay.

13.3. Strikes, riots and civil commotion, known in the policy wording as SRCC, are covered from 2026 by an endorsement. A load damaged when a road blockade turned violent is therefore covered; a load spoiled because a blockade kept it standing for a day is not, for the reason in 13.2.

13.4. Theft by the driver of a hired vehicle is covered only where the vendor's own driver details were checked at the gate as the hiring rules require. Theft by a driver whose identity was never checked is a gap.

13.5. Where the desk is unsure whether a loss falls into a gap, it intimates the claim anyway and lets the insurer decide.

# Fleet Operations Manual

The working manual for Fleet Control, fleet planners, owned-reefer drivers and
the managers of hired-truck vendors. It says how the fleet is run day to day. It
does not restate the driver hours limits, the temperature limits or the dock
booking rules; those have their own documents, and this manual points to them.

## 16. Tolls and road charges

16.1. Every owned reefer carries an electronic toll tag registered to Quillfern.
The tag balance is topped up by Fleet Control; drivers never pay a toll in cash
unless the tag reader at the plaza has failed.

16.2. A cash toll is paid only against a printed receipt, which goes into the
trip bag. A handwritten receipt is accepted only when the plaza staff sign and
stamp it.

16.3. A tag that shows a low balance at a plaza is reported to Fleet Control
while parked, and Fleet Control tops it up before the next plaza.

16.4. Hired trucks use their own tags. Quillfern does not refund a hired truck's
tolls unless the purchase order says so.

16.5. Road charges at state borders and permit fees are paid by Fleet Control in
advance for owned reefers. A driver asked for money at a border that was not on
the dispatch note calls Fleet Control before paying anything.

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. The manual covers owned reefers, hired reefers, support vans and escort
cars moving under a Quillfern dispatch note, from the moment a vehicle is taken
over at a DC until it is handed back with its paperwork.

1.2. It does not cover warehouse work inside the cold rooms, customer contracts,
or pricing. A driver who is asked a price by a customer refers the customer to
customer service.

1.3. Revision 3 of July 2026 added section 9 on passive shippers in transit and
moved the police-check rules into section 7.

1.4. Where the manual and the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy seem to
differ, the policy applies. Where the manual and the SOP seem to differ on
anything about temperature, the SOP applies.

1.5. Copies of the manual are kept at the Fleet Control desk in Nagpur, in the
gate cabin at each DC and in the driver rest room at Nagpur. Drivers are not
expected to carry it; the cab card carries what a driver needs on the road.
