## 12. Kit

12.1. Each apprentice is issued a personal tool kit in the first week: gauges and hoses, a multimeter, a clamp meter, a set of hand tools, a temperature probe, a torch and a tool bag. The kit is engraved with the apprentice's number.

12.2. Trainees often ask whether they get to keep the tools when they finish. The kit, worth about Rs. 22,000, becomes the apprentice's own property on completion; a leaver before completion hands it back.

12.3. A tool lost or broken through ordinary use is replaced by the workshop. A tool lost through carelessness is replaced once without charge; a second loss is discussed with the workshop lead.

12.4. Safety gear — boots, gloves, glasses, a freezer jacket and a helmet — is issued separately and is replaced whenever it wears out.

12.5. Apprentices do not lend their kit to anyone, including qualified technicians on site.

## 13. Network and data

13.1. K7s connect only to the site's own wireless network, which is separate from the guest and office networks. They do not connect to public or home networks.

13.2. Data on a K7 is encrypted, and the device holds only what the current task needs. Stock records are kept on the warehouse system, not on the device.

13.3. A user who sees a network warning on the screen tells the shift lead and does not tap through it.

13.4. Fernguard keeps a log of every login, every app opened and every update. The log is kept for one year and is read by IT only when there is a reason, such as a missing device or a disputed transaction.

13.5. No customer data leaves the site on a K7. A device taken off site, for a trainee exercise or a repair, is wiped first.

13.6. Wireless coverage is surveyed before a site goes live and again after any racking change. A dead spot found on the floor is reported to the desk with the rack location, and pickers are told to finish the scan at the aisle end rather than wave the device about.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 5. Money

5.1. Every apprentice is paid a monthly stipend, not a wage, and it rises once, when the apprentice moves from the workshop to the floor. Pay is credited to the apprentice's own bank account on the last working day of the month.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

5.3. Apprentices placed at a site away from Waluj receive a lodging allowance and their travel to the site and back at the start and end of the placement. The allowance is set by the site and paid with the stipend.

5.4. Overtime is not paid to apprentices, because apprentices do not work overtime. An apprentice kept beyond the shift by an emergency is given the time back the next day.

5.5. No apprentice is bonded. Nobody repays anything for leaving the programme early or for taking a job elsewhere after it, and nobody is asked to sign a promise to stay.

## 6. Who may use one

6.1. A K7 may be used only by a person with a login issued by the IT desk. Logins are personal; a shift lead does not sign in for a picker so the picker can start sooner.

6.2. Contract and agency workers do not get permanent logins. Agency staff on the scanners are some of the busiest users on a peak night, and each one is given a temporary sign-in for the shift at the shift lead's request to the desk. The desk issues them a day credential that stops working twelve hours after it is first used. A new one is issued for each shift worked.

6.3. Personal phones are a separate matter. Many staff would rather scan with their own phone than walk to the rack, and on the pilot some did. No personal phone may run the scanning app or hold a Quillfern login, even for one shift when a K7 has failed; the user takes a spare from the cradle rack or waits.

6.4. Customer staff and auditors may look at a K7's screen with a Quillfern user beside them. They do not operate it.

6.5. Trainees from the Waluj workshop use a K7 only with their trainer's login running, and only for the exercises in their module.

## 15. Records and certificates

15.1. The workshop keeps each apprentice's file: application, tests, medical, attendance, marks, logbooks, certificates, mentor reports and any warnings.

15.2. Files are kept for seven years after the apprentice leaves.

15.3. An apprentice may read their own file at any time on request.

15.4. Certificates are issued in the apprentice's name only, and copies are certified by the workshop lead.

15.5. Quillfern gives a reference to any former apprentice who asks, describing what they learned and how they did.

## 11. Mentors

11.1. Each apprentice placed at a site has a named mentor, a qualified technician who has volunteered and been trained for the role.

11.2. The mentor signs the logbook each week, meets the apprentice for half an hour each fortnight to go through it, and reports to the workshop once a month.

11.3. Mentors receive an allowance for each apprentice they mentor, paid with their salary.

11.4. A mentor may have no more than two apprentices at a time.

11.5. An apprentice who has a problem with a mentor speaks to the workshop lead, who may change the mentor without asking for a reason.

## 15. Repairs

15.1. All repairs go through the IT desk. The desk keeps a small stock of spare K7s and LP-40s at each site, so that a repair never leaves a rack short.

15.2. Devices are sent to the Korvex service centre in a padded case with a repair note. Nobody opens a device on site.

15.3. A repaired device is rebuilt from Fernguard before it is reissued.

15.4. A device that has been repaired three times in a year is retired.

15.5. The desk reports device faults by type every quarter to the site managers, so that a site whose scanners keep breaking can look at how they are used.

15.6. Repair costs are charged to the site's cost centre. A site that pays for many repairs is not punished for it; it is asked what is going on.

## 12. The customer's people

12.1. The customer names a lead for each unit. The lead is shown the door, the
controller display, the duty phone and the genset gauge at placement.

12.2. The lead keeps a simple sheet of who went in and when, and the sheet is
collected at each service visit.

12.3. Nobody under 18 goes into a unit.

## 7. Goods arriving

7.1. A vehicle arriving at the store is checked before it is opened: the seal number against the paperwork, the condition of the doors and the reefer's display. The driver stays with the vehicle until goods-in has finished with it, and is offered the drivers' room, not the canteen.

7.2. Every inbound vehicle's temperature printout or download is read at the goods-in desk before a single pallet crosses the threshold. Drivers call any missing stretch a "hole" in the printout, and holes are common on loads that come round the Ahmedabad ring road, where some older reefers lose their logger signal. A break of up to ten minutes in the record may be accepted by the goods-in clerk; anything longer goes to the Responsible Person, who decides. A record that is in range throughout but shows the reefer door opening during the journey is also referred to her.

7.3. Pallets are checked against the advance notice by batch and quantity. A batch that does not match the notice is received into quarantine rather than refused at the door, so that the customer's stock is protected while the paperwork is put right.

7.4. Goods-in photographs every pallet label before the stretch wrap is cut. The photographs are filed against the receipt, not kept on the camera.

7.5. Nothing is received between 22:00 and 06:00. A vehicle that arrives at night waits outside the estate gate on its own power, and its record for the waiting hours is read together with the journey.

## 4. Immediate containment

4.1. Stop movement of the affected pallet, tote, crate, reefer body, or room bay.
Do not load additional customer stock into the affected compartment.

4.2. Attach a red sleeve to the stock or truck file. The red sleeve contains the
customer intimation form, red hold tags, seal tape, and one spare calibrated
logger. If there is no physical sleeve, print form QCL-F-09 and write RED
SLEEVE MISSING at the top.

4.3. Move warehouse stock to quarantine bay Q-3 at Nagpur, Q-G2 at Guwahati, or
Q-C1 at Coimbatore. Truck stock must remain sealed unless QA instructs unloading
for product safety.

4.4. Photograph the sensor display, seal number, dock clock, and pallet labels.
The first four photographs must be uploaded before anyone debates stock
disposition. Do not wait for the manager to arrive.

4.5. Do not warm, chill, re-ice, ventilate, or hide the probe in order to make a
display look normal. Corrective measures may protect product, but the record
must continue to show the product environment honestly.

4.6. If a reefer unit is unstable on the road, the driver shall stop at a lit
fuel plaza or toll rest area, call Fleet Control, and keep the engine running
unless there is a fire, police order, or personal safety threat.

## 10. Seal books and the security cabin

10.1. Seal books for Coimbatore are issued by Stores at Nagpur and arrive by
courier two books at a time. They are kept in the locked drawer in the gate
cabin, not in the office annexe, because the gate cabin is staffed all night and
the annexe is not.

10.2. Only one seal book is open at the gate at a time. The guard hands a seal
to the shift lead; the guard never fits a seal himself.

10.3. The rest of the sealing rule is the company rule. Seal numbers go on the
dispatch note and in QCL-F-35 before the vehicle moves.

10.4. A vehicle arriving with a broken seal or a number that does not match is
kept outside the south gate, photographed, and reported to Fleet Control before
anyone opens the doors.

## 13. Language and new people

13.1. Coimbatore works in Tamil. Training is given by a trainer in Tamil, with
English slides available but never used instead of a trainer.

13.2. New joiners spend their first week on the morning shift only. They are not
put on the late shift, and never left alone in the cold block, until a shift
lead has signed them off.

13.3. Every new joiner is shown the gate cabin, the security roster and the key
register on the first day. They are told that security will not open anything
for them at night except in an emergency, and that the lockers, the cabinet and
the seal drawer are all separate keys.

13.4. New drivers from hired-truck vendors are shown the south gate routine by
the guard and the Temple Street timing by the shift lead before their first
booking.

13.5. The words used on site follow the company glossary. A new joiner who hears
a word they do not know is expected to ask, on any shift, and nobody at
Coimbatore is to laugh at the question.

## 6. Investigation record

6.1. QA opens an investigation in QCL-F-17 before the end of the same shift. The
record must contain the sensor source, product owner, SKU, batch or lot number,
route, room, dock, seal number, driver name when applicable, and first staff
member who observed the event.

6.2. The investigator shall build a minute-level timeline from the approved
temperature record, door log, dock schedule, driver call log, maintenance ticket,
and shift handover note. Missing pieces must be listed as missing; do not fill
them with assumptions.

6.3. Where records conflict, use the source hierarchy in section 3 and explain
the conflict. A convenient record is not a better record.

6.4. For pharma critical stock, QA must ask the customer for a stability letter
before release when the product was above the high limit or below the low limit
for any confirmed duration.

6.5. The investigation shall name one of four dispositions: release, conditional
release, hold pending external decision, or destroy. Finance may record value
only after QA records the disposition.

## 3. Approved records

3.1. For trips and rooms after 18 August 2025, Tessaline Telematics is the first
electronic source for approved temperature history. The API export named
"exception_csv_v2" is the preferred file.

3.2. For trips and rooms before 18 August 2025, Kalpa Fleet Systems remains an
accepted historical source. No staff member shall create a new Kalpa trip after
that date.

3.3. Independent USB loggers, customer loggers, and calibrated hand-held
thermometers may support an investigation, but they do not overrule the approved
electronic source unless QA documents a sensor failure.

3.4. Hand-written dock readings are acceptable only for the first containment
decision. They must be replaced by a downloaded electronic record before stock
is released, destroyed, returned, or billed.

# Coimbatore DC site handbook

Everything that is particular to Coimbatore DC, in one place. Company-wide rules
still come from their own documents: temperature limits and excursions from
QCL-QA-SOP-17, dock booking from QCL-OPS-DOCK-03, driver hours from the Driver
Hours and Road Safety Policy. Where this handbook and a company-wide rule seem
to differ, ask the DC manager before acting, and do not assume the handbook
wins. What follows is how those rules are carried out on this site, with this
building, these people and this weather.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

## 10. Before tools come out

10.1. Any work that could start a fire, release refrigerant, expose live electrical parts, or put someone at height needs a written permit to work, issued by the shift lead before the job starts.

10.2. A permit for hot work — brazing, welding, cutting, grinding — is valid for one shift only, and never for more than eight hours. Work that runs past the end of the shift stops, and a fresh permit is issued if it is to continue.

10.3. Hot work needs a fire watch who stays for thirty minutes after the work ends.

10.4. The permit names the technician, the job, the place, the hazards, the controls and the time limits. The technician signs it, and signs it again when the work is finished.

10.5. A technician who starts work before the permit is issued is sent off site, and the partner is told the same day.

# Service Partner Onboarding Standard

## 1. What this standard is for

1.1. Quillfern buildings and vehicles are kept running by outside firms as much as by our own staff. Refrigeration engineers, generator agents, the people who service dock doors and levellers, pest controllers, cleaners, electricians, calibration laboratories and fire-equipment agents all come through our gates, and some of them work on the very plant that keeps customers' stock in range.

1.2. This standard says how such a firm becomes an approved service partner, what it must keep up to stay approved, and how it leaves the list. It applies to every site opened from 2025 onwards and to every firm that is newly approved anywhere in the company from the date of this revision.

1.3. It does not cover suppliers of goods, such as seals or forms, who deliver to Stores and never work on site. Those are approved under the purchasing rules.

1.4. It is written for Procurement, which keeps the list; for site managers, who call partners in; for QA, which approves partners who work near product; and for the engineering pool, which judges the technical competence of partners who work on plant.

1.5. "Partner" in this standard means a firm, not a person. The people the firm sends are its technicians.

## 13. Placement

13.1. From month seven apprentices are placed at a site that needs them. Placements are decided by the engineering pool lead with the site managers, and apprentices are asked their preference first.

13.2. An apprentice may be placed at a site far from home. The programme pays for travel and lodging and allows one trip home a month.

13.3. A placement lasts until the end of the programme unless the site closes, the mentor leaves or the apprentice asks to move for a good reason.

13.4. At the end of the programme, Quillfern offers a technician's post to each apprentice who completes, at a site with a vacancy. Taking the offer is not compulsory.

13.5. The site manager writes a short report on each apprentice at the end of the placement, and the apprentice sees it.

## 14. The annual look back

14.1. Every partner is scored once a year by Procurement, using the site managers' records and the engineering pool's opinion. The score is out of 100 and covers attendance times, quality of work, safety, paperwork, and conduct on site.

14.2. A partner scoring 65 or more stays on the list. A partner scoring below 65 is put on probation for six months with a written plan of what must improve.

14.3. A partner put on probation in two consecutive years is removed from the list, whatever its score at the end of the second probation.

14.4. A partner may see its score and the records behind it, and may answer in writing before the score is final.

14.5. Scores are not shared with other partners.

## 14. Safety on the floor

14.1. The safety rules of the site always apply. Where a site rule and this curriculum differ, the stricter one wins.

14.2. Apprentices wear their safety gear on every job, including short ones.

14.3. Refrigerant cylinders are carried upright and strapped in vehicles. Apprentices never carry a cylinder in a bus or on a motorcycle.

14.4. Brazing is done only with a permit and a fire watch, at the workshop and on site alike.

14.5. Any injury, however small, is reported to the mentor the same day and written in the site's accident book.

## 11. Mentors

11.1. Each apprentice placed at a site has a named mentor, a qualified technician who has volunteered and been trained for the role.

11.2. The mentor signs the logbook each week, meets the apprentice for half an hour each fortnight to go through it, and reports to the workshop once a month.

11.3. Mentors receive an allowance for each apprentice they mentor, paid with their salary.

11.4. A mentor may have no more than two apprentices at a time.

11.5. An apprentice who has a problem with a mentor speaks to the workshop lead, who may change the mentor without asking for a reason.

## 7. Goods arriving

7.1. A vehicle arriving at the store is checked before it is opened: the seal number against the paperwork, the condition of the doors and the reefer's display. The driver stays with the vehicle until goods-in has finished with it, and is offered the drivers' room, not the canteen.

7.2. Every inbound vehicle's temperature printout or download is read at the goods-in desk before a single pallet crosses the threshold. Drivers call any missing stretch a "hole" in the printout, and holes are common on loads that come round the Ahmedabad ring road, where some older reefers lose their logger signal. A break of up to ten minutes in the record may be accepted by the goods-in clerk; anything longer goes to the Responsible Person, who decides. A record that is in range throughout but shows the reefer door opening during the journey is also referred to her.

7.3. Pallets are checked against the advance notice by batch and quantity. A batch that does not match the notice is received into quarantine rather than refused at the door, so that the customer's stock is protected while the paperwork is put right.

7.4. Goods-in photographs every pallet label before the stretch wrap is cut. The photographs are filed against the receipt, not kept on the camera.

7.5. Nothing is received between 22:00 and 06:00. A vehicle that arrives at night waits outside the estate gate on its own power, and its record for the waiting hours is read together with the journey.

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. The manual covers owned reefers, hired reefers, support vans and escort
cars moving under a Quillfern dispatch note, from the moment a vehicle is taken
over at a DC until it is handed back with its paperwork.

1.2. It does not cover warehouse work inside the cold rooms, customer contracts,
or pricing. A driver who is asked a price by a customer refers the customer to
customer service.

1.3. Revision 3 of July 2026 added section 9 on passive shippers in transit and
moved the police-check rules into section 7.

1.4. Where the manual and the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy seem to
differ, the policy applies. Where the manual and the SOP seem to differ on
anything about temperature, the SOP applies.

1.5. Copies of the manual are kept at the Fleet Control desk in Nagpur, in the
gate cabin at each DC and in the driver rest room at Nagpur. Drivers are not
expected to carry it; the cab card carries what a driver needs on the road.

## 13. Documents

13.1. The store's procedures, forms and records live in the document system. Only the version in the system is current, and each procedure shows its revision number and effective date on every page.

13.2. Paper copies of procedures are a convenience, not a source: they are useful at the goods-in desk and in the anteroom, where nobody wants to read a screen with gloves on. A copy printed from the document system is valid only until midnight of the day printed, which the printer stamps in the footer. A paper copy found after that is put in the confidential bin, whatever revision number it carries.

13.3. Records are made at the time, in ink or in the system, and corrected by striking through and initialling, never by overwriting or by correction fluid.

13.4. Records for each batch — goods-in sheets, dispatch notes, logger files, deviation files and the returns register — are kept long enough to answer a regulator after the product has expired. Each batch file is kept for one year after the expiry date of the batch, or five years from the batch's last movement, whichever ends later. Records about the building and its equipment are kept for the life of the lease and three years after it.

13.5. Records are not taken home, not photographed on personal phones and not sent to a customer except through the customer's named quality contact.

## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## 13. Cabs, bodies and how they look

13.1. A Quillfern cab is kept clean enough that a customer's receiving clerk can
sit in it to sign papers. Food wrappers, bottles and bedding are cleared out at
the end of every duty day.

13.2. Nothing is stuck to the windscreen except the permits the law requires and
the Quillfern asset number. Stickers, pictures and hanging charms that block the
driver's view are removed at the takeover walk-round.

13.3. The outside of the body is washed at least once a week, and after any run
through a construction zone or mud. A body whose company markings cannot be read
is washed before its next customer drop.

13.4. Scratches and dents are reported, not painted over. Fleet Control books
body repairs in batches so that no vehicle is off the road longer than it needs
to be.

13.5. The cab card, the red sleeve and the fire extinguisher each have a fixed
place in the cab. A driver who finds any of them moved puts it back and tells
Fleet Control, because the next driver will look for it in its fixed place in a
hurry.

## 12. Paperwork that comes back

12.1. Each trip returns a trip bag holding the dispatch note, the fuel slips,
the cut seals, the takeover sheet and any exception form.

12.2. The trip bag is handed to the shift lead at the returning DC, who checks
it against the dispatch note and signs for it.

12.3. A missing item in the trip bag is written on the dispatch note as
missing, never replaced with a guess. A torn fuel slip is kept torn.

12.4. Trip bags from a trip involving a tyre change or other vendor work carry
the vendor's job sheet with the hours and the spare parts used, so that Fleet
Control can match it to the vendor's invoice.

12.5. Trip bags are kept by Fleet Control for three years, or seven where the
trip involved a pharma critical excursion, a crash, an insurance claim or a
police matter.

## Visakhapatnam DC

- First customer stock: September 2026.
- Chilled pallet positions: 2,000. Frozen pallet positions: 1,200.
- Staff at go-live: 58.
- Owned reefers: 10.

## 17. Review

17.1. The IT infrastructure lead reviews this policy every March and after any loss of data, any serious security warning or any change of device model.

17.2. Site managers and shift leads send suggested changes to the IT desk at any time.

17.3. A revised policy is issued with a short note of what changed, and the Fernguard settings are changed on the same day, so that the policy and the devices never disagree.

17.4. When a site opens, the IT desk walks its shift leads through this policy on a live device before go-live, and the shift leads walk their teams through it in the first week.

## 2. The two sites

2.1. The Visakhapatnam DC stands on a leased plot of 4.2 acres in the Atchutapuram industrial area, south-west of the city, about 18 km by road from the port's outer gate. The building is a new pre-engineered shed with a cold block, a frozen block, a small controlled-room-temperature store, a dispatch canopy and a two-storey office.

2.2. The satellite at Bhubaneswar is a smaller leased unit in the Mancheswar industrial estate. It has two chilled docks, two frozen docks, a staging hall held at +4 C and a site office. It is a cross-dock, not a store.

2.3. The two sites are about 440 km apart by the coastal highway. A nightly trunk run links them.

2.4. The DC is the region's centre: its manager is the senior manager in the region, its QA lead covers both sites, and its engineering team maintains the satellite's plant.

2.5. Both leases run for fifteen years with a right to renew. The landlord at Atchutapuram built the shell to our drawings; the fit-out, racking and refrigeration belong to Quillfern.

## 5. Apps on the device

5.1. A K7 runs the warehouse picking app, the receiving app, the document viewer, the camera and nothing else. The app list is fixed by Fernguard.

5.2. Users cannot install apps, and a K7 that shows an app not on the list is taken out of use and returned to the IT desk.

5.3. The camera is for evidence: damaged cartons, seal numbers, pallet labels. Photographs taken on a K7 upload to the document system and are deleted from the device after upload.

5.4. The browser is locked to the document system and the company intranet. A user who needs another website uses an office PC.

5.5. Messaging apps are not installed. Shift instructions come through the shift lead, not through the device.

5.6. A request for a new app on the list goes from the site manager to the IT infrastructure lead in writing, with the reason. The app is tested at the Waluj workshop on four devices for a fortnight before it reaches a live site.

## 13. Network and data

13.1. K7s connect only to the site's own wireless network, which is separate from the guest and office networks. They do not connect to public or home networks.

13.2. Data on a K7 is encrypted, and the device holds only what the current task needs. Stock records are kept on the warehouse system, not on the device.

13.3. A user who sees a network warning on the screen tells the shift lead and does not tap through it.

13.4. Fernguard keeps a log of every login, every app opened and every update. The log is kept for one year and is read by IT only when there is a reason, such as a missing device or a disputed transaction.

13.5. No customer data leaves the site on a K7. A device taken off site, for a trainee exercise or a repair, is wiped first.

13.6. Wireless coverage is surveyed before a site goes live and again after any racking change. A dead spot found on the floor is reported to the desk with the rack location, and pickers are told to finish the scan at the aisle end rather than wave the device about.

# East Coast region: outline plan for site selection

Prepared before the Visakhapatnam plot was chosen, to size the investment for
the board's first look.

## 15. Repairs

15.1. All repairs go through the IT desk. The desk keeps a small stock of spare K7s and LP-40s at each site, so that a repair never leaves a rack short.

15.2. Devices are sent to the Korvex service centre in a padded case with a repair note. Nobody opens a device on site.

15.3. A repaired device is rebuilt from Fernguard before it is reissued.

15.4. A device that has been repaired three times in a year is retired.

15.5. The desk reports device faults by type every quarter to the site managers, so that a site whose scanners keep breaking can look at how they are used.

15.6. Repair costs are charged to the site's cost centre. A site that pays for many repairs is not punished for it; it is asked what is going on.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

KORVEX K7 PILOT QUICK RULES (WALUJ, 2025)

These quick rules were written for the twenty-device K7 pilot at the Waluj
workshop.

SCREEN LOCK
An idle K7 locks after 5 minutes.

PIN CHANGE
PINs are six digits and are changed every 180 days.

WRONG ATTEMPTS
Ten wrong attempts lock the user out.

BATTERY
Batteries are retired at 400 charge cycles.

LOST DEVICE
Report a lost K7 the same shift. The desk wipes it after 72 hours.

AGENCY STAFF
Agency staff scan under the shift lead's login.

UNRETURNED DEVICE
A K7 not returned by a leaver is recovered at Rs. 15,000.

## 6. Who may use one

6.1. A K7 may be used only by a person with a login issued by the IT desk. Logins are personal; a shift lead does not sign in for a picker so the picker can start sooner.

6.2. Contract and agency workers do not get permanent logins. Agency staff on the scanners are some of the busiest users on a peak night, and each one is given a temporary sign-in for the shift at the shift lead's request to the desk. The desk issues them a day credential that stops working twelve hours after it is first used. A new one is issued for each shift worked.

6.3. Personal phones are a separate matter. Many staff would rather scan with their own phone than walk to the rack, and on the pilot some did. No personal phone may run the scanning app or hold a Quillfern login, even for one shift when a K7 has failed; the user takes a spare from the cradle rack or waits.

6.4. Customer staff and auditors may look at a K7's screen with a Quillfern user beside them. They do not operate it.

6.5. Trainees from the Waluj workshop use a K7 only with their trainer's login running, and only for the exercises in their module.

## 7. When one goes missing

7.1. A lost or stolen scanner is reported to the IT desk within one hour of being missed, by the user or the shift lead, with the asset number and where it was last seen.

7.2. The desk locks the device from Fernguard as soon as the report arrives. A locked K7 shows a message asking the finder to hand it to security.

7.3. If it has not turned up 24 hours after the report, Fernguard wipes it remotely and it is struck off the register. A device found after it has been wiped goes back to the desk to be rebuilt; it is never simply switched back on.

7.4. Losing a device is not in itself a disciplinary matter. Failing to report a loss, or reporting it late, is.

7.5. A theft is also reported to security and, where the site manager decides, to the police. The report number is written in the register.

## 3. The calendar

3.1. The apprenticeship runs as one continuous programme with no break between the classroom and the floor. Months one to six are mostly in the workshop; months seven onwards are mostly on site, with a day a week back at Waluj.

3.2. From the January 2026 intake the programme lasts 18 months; the 2024 and 2025 intakes served 24. The shorter programme was possible because the workshop now has its own reefer body, cold room and generator, so that practical work no longer waits for a site to lend equipment.

3.3. Apprentices join in two intakes a year, so that there is always a senior group on site while a junior group is in the workshop. Each intake opens on the first working day of January or July and takes twelve trainees, no more. A thirteenth applicant who passes is offered the next intake rather than squeezed in.

3.4. Public holidays follow the Maharashtra list for apprentices at Waluj and the local list for apprentices placed at a site.

3.5. An apprentice who is ill for more than four weeks in a row may move to the next intake and pick up from the module they left.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 16. Welfare

16.1. Apprentices are young and often away from home for the first time. Each intake has a welfare contact at Waluj, a member of the workshop staff who is not a trainer.

16.2. Apprentices may raise anything with the welfare contact — homesickness, money, a problem at the lodging, a problem with a colleague — in confidence.

16.3. The lodging used at each site is visited by the welfare contact before the first apprentice moves in.

16.4. Bullying, ragging or initiation rituals are not tolerated, on site or at the workshop, and are dealt with under the company's discipline rules.

16.5. Apprentices are paid their stipend during approved sick leave for up to four weeks.

## Summary

At approximately 02:16 on 12 March 2025, Kalpa probe KV-NGP-C2-07 began
reporting a high temperature in C2, the vaccine cold room at Nagpur DC. The
affected consignment was BharatVac order BV-4437, holding 18,400 vials of
rotavirus vaccine in lots ROTA-9A and ROTA-9B. The approved record showed the
room above +8.0 C for 66 minutes. At the time of the event, the SOP required a
QA call after 30 continuous minutes above +8.0 C for vaccines. The current
corrective action is to reduce that duration.

| action | owner | due | status |

| Reduce vaccine high-duration trigger from 30 minutes to 15 minutes in SOP | Revathi Iyer | 14 Mar 2025 | closed in SOP rev 3.1 |

## Closing note

This event is the reason I am asking for two changes: faster pharma escalation
and a shorter vaccine high-duration trigger. If the telematics vendor changes,
the first acceptance test must prove night alerts reach Compliance-Red, not only
the DC manager.

I have deliberately left the rough timeline language in place because the audit
packet should show how the team understood the event on the day. Later SOP
revisions may be cleaner, but this note is the incident record, not a training
poster. Any future reader should compare it with the live SOP before using its
thresholds.

## 2. Products and limits

2.1. Vaccines must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. A vaccine high excursion is
declared when any approved sensor records more than +8.0 C for 30 continuous
minutes.

2.2. Insulin must remain between +2.0 C and +8.0 C. An insulin high excursion is
declared when the approved record is more than +8.0 C for 20 continuous minutes.

2.3. Milk and paneer must remain from 0.0 C to +4.0 C in cold rooms and reefer
bodies. Milk crates may remain on a covered dock until +7.0 C for 45 minutes
before QA notice is required.

2.4. Frozen food must remain at or below -18.0 C. A frozen-food excursion is
declared when the approved record is warmer than -12.0 C for 30 continuous
minutes.

# Temperature Excursion Response SOP

## 1. Purpose

1.1. This procedure defines the response to any suspected or confirmed temperature
excursion in Quillfern Cold Logistics Pvt. Ltd. warehouses, docks, cross-dock
lanes, owned reefer trucks and hired trucks working under Quillfern dispatch.
The procedure applies to vaccines, insulin, chilled dairy, paneer, frozen food,
and any customer stock moved under a written temperature commitment.

1.2. The purpose is to protect patient safety, food safety, customer evidence,
and the company record. A fast release is never preferred over a complete
temperature history. Staff must treat a missing record as a quality event until
QA closes it.

1.3. "Excursion" means a recorded temperature outside the allowed range for
longer than the allowed duration. A single hand-held thermometer reading is not
enough to release product after a breach; it may be used only to start immediate
containment while the logger history is retrieved.

## 8. Dock and staging rules

8.1. A dock is not a temperature-controlled room. Staging time begins when the
pallet crosses the cold-room threshold and ends when the reefer body is closed
or the pallet returns to the cold room.

8.2. Pharma pallets may not be staged on an open dock for more than 10 minutes
unless a validated passive shipper is used.

8.3. Dairy pallets may be staged on a covered dock for loading, but the dairy
high-excursion rule in clause 2.3 still applies. Staff shall not reclassify
staging time as "not cold chain time" after the fact.

8.4. Frozen stock must move directly between freezer and reefer body. Any delay
longer than 8 minutes must be called to the shift lead.

8.5. The dock team may request a slot change, but it may not waive a temperature
limit. Only QA may decide whether an excursion occurred.

## 13. Gaps in the cover

13.1. The policy does not pay for every loss. The main things it will not pay for are: loss caused by delay alone; ordinary leakage, shrinkage and wear; loss caused by the nature of the goods themselves; packing that was not fit for the journey when the consignor packed it; war and nuclear risks; and any loss caused deliberately by Quillfern staff.

13.2. Delay deserves its own sentence because it is so often argued. A load that arrives late, even through no fault of ours and even when the lateness spoiled it, is not a claim under TPC. A load that arrives late and is rejected by the customer for being late is not a claim either. If the delay was caused by an insured event — a crash, a fire, a four-hour stoppage of the machinery — the claim is for that event, not for the delay.

13.3. Strikes, riots and civil commotion, known in the policy wording as SRCC, are covered from 2026 by an endorsement. A load damaged when a road blockade turned violent is therefore covered; a load spoiled because a blockade kept it standing for a day is not, for the reason in 13.2.

13.4. Theft by the driver of a hired vehicle is covered only where the vendor's own driver details were checked at the gate as the hiring rules require. Theft by a driver whose identity was never checked is a gap.

13.5. Where the desk is unsure whether a loss falls into a gap, it intimates the claim anyway and lets the insurer decide.

## 1. What this manual covers

1.1. The manual covers owned reefers, hired reefers, support vans and escort
cars moving under a Quillfern dispatch note, from the moment a vehicle is taken
over at a DC until it is handed back with its paperwork.

1.2. It does not cover warehouse work inside the cold rooms, customer contracts,
or pricing. A driver who is asked a price by a customer refers the customer to
customer service.

1.3. Revision 3 of July 2026 added section 9 on passive shippers in transit and
moved the police-check rules into section 7.

1.4. Where the manual and the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy seem to
differ, the policy applies. Where the manual and the SOP seem to differ on
anything about temperature, the SOP applies.

1.5. Copies of the manual are kept at the Fleet Control desk in Nagpur, in the
gate cabin at each DC and in the driver rest room at Nagpur. Drivers are not
expected to carry it; the cab card carries what a driver needs on the road.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 12. Paperwork that comes back

12.1. Each trip returns a trip bag holding the dispatch note, the fuel slips,
the cut seals, the takeover sheet and any exception form.

12.2. The trip bag is handed to the shift lead at the returning DC, who checks
it against the dispatch note and signs for it.

12.3. A missing item in the trip bag is written on the dispatch note as
missing, never replaced with a guess. A torn fuel slip is kept torn.

12.4. Trip bags from a trip involving a tyre change or other vendor work carry
the vendor's job sheet with the hours and the spare parts used, so that Fleet
Control can match it to the vendor's invoice.

12.5. Trip bags are kept by Fleet Control for three years, or seven where the
trip involved a pharma critical excursion, a crash, an insurance claim or a
police matter.

## 11. Crashes, near misses and police stops

11.1. After any crash, however small, the driver makes the vehicle and the road
safe, calls emergency services if anyone is hurt, and then calls Fleet Control.

11.2. The driver does not move the vehicle unless the police tell him to or it
is a danger where it stands. Photographs of the scene are taken if it is safe.

11.3. The driver is relieved from further driving until Fleet Control records a
fitness-to-continue decision, as the policy requires.

11.4. A near miss is reported the same day, in the driver's own words. Near-miss
reports are not used to discipline the driver who reports them.

11.5. A police stop that is not a crash and not an inspection of the load, such
as a document check, is noted in the driver call log with the time and place.

## 18. Review of this manual

18.1. The Fleet head reviews this manual every April, alongside the annual review
of the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy, and sooner after any crash or serious
exception that shows a gap in it.

18.2. Drivers and controllers send suggested changes to Fleet Control at any
time. Suggestions are read at the next Nagpur driver meeting.

18.3. A revised manual replaces every earlier copy at the Fleet Control desk, the
gate cabins and the driver rest room on the day it is issued.

# Fleet Operations Manual

The working manual for Fleet Control, fleet planners, owned-reefer drivers and
the managers of hired-truck vendors. It says how the fleet is run day to day. It
does not restate the driver hours limits, the temperature limits or the dock
booking rules; those have their own documents, and this manual points to them.

## 21. Returns to suppliers

21.1. Faulty goods are returned to the supplier with a return note on the
supplier's own form where the supplier has one, and on QCL-F-45 where it does
not.

21.2. Stores keeps a copy of every return note and follows up any return that
has not been credited or replaced within thirty days.

21.3. Returned numbered stock is listed by number on the return note, so that the
numbers can never reappear on a Quillfern shelf.

21.4. A supplier who has had three returns in a year is raised at the annual
supplier review, whatever the reason for the returns.

## 16. Flammable and hazardous items

16.1. Food-grade alcohol for wiping frozen bodies, chlorine for washdowns and
diesel additives are held in the flammables cabinet outside the store, never on
the store racks.

16.2. Each hazardous item has its safety data sheet in the folder on the cabinet
door. A new item is not received until its sheet is in the folder.

16.3. Chlorine is issued by the litre against the wash register, and never mixed
in the store.

16.4. Spills in the flammables cabinet are cleaned with the spill kit hung beside
it and reported to the DC manager the same day.

## Shippers

- 18 blue-cap packs go in each shipper.
- Shipper conditioning time: 18 hours at +5.0 C.
- A closed shipper holds its range for 72 hours.

## Shippers

- **shipper conditioning time** — 18 hours at +5.0 C, for every pack in the shipper.
- **packs per shipper** — 22 blue-cap packs.
- **shipper fleet** — PS-01 to PS-12, at Nagpur.

## 3. Receiving goods

3.1. Goods are received against the purchase order and the delivery note, and
counted before the delivery note is signed. A short delivery is written as short
on the delivery note in front of the supplier's driver.

3.2. Temperature-sensitive consumables, such as conditioned gel packs, are not
received by Stores. They go directly to the QA room.

3.3. Calibrated instruments are received by Stores and passed unopened to the QA
bench on the same day. Stores does not open an instrument box to check it.

3.4. Damaged goods are photographed, set aside and reported to Finance before the
supplier's driver leaves, where that is possible.

## 7. Gel packs and shipper consumables

7.1. Stores buys gel packs and holds them unconditioned. Conditioning happens in
the QA room, not in Stores.

7.2. Stores keeps at least 44 unconditioned blue-cap packs at Nagpur, enough to
remake two shippers completely.

7.3. Packs retired by QA, for cycle count or for damage, are sent to the
supplier for disposal and recorded as written off. Stores does not throw them in
general waste, because the gel is not general waste.

7.4. White-cap packs are held on a separate shelf, labelled FROZEN GOODS ONLY.

7.5. Spare shipper lids, straps and liners are held by Stores and issued to QA
against a signature. A damaged shipper body is not repaired in Stores.

## 22. Energy and waste in the store

22.1. The store lights are on a timer and go off at 19:30. The storekeeper
closing the store checks that the cage, the flammables cabinet and the emergency
cupboard are locked before the lights go off.

22.2. Packaging from deliveries is flattened and sent to the scrap area on the
day it arrives. The store is not a place to keep empty boxes.

22.3. Used toner cartridges are returned to the toner supplier for recycling.

22.4. Stores reports its waste once a year to the Nagpur DC manager, by type and
weight, for the site's environmental return.

## 5. Money

5.1. Every apprentice is paid a monthly stipend, not a wage, and it rises once, when the apprentice moves from the workshop to the floor. Pay is credited to the apprentice's own bank account on the last working day of the month.

5.2. The stipend is Rs. 14,000 a month for months one to six and Rs. 16,500 from month seven; the 2025 outline gave a flat Rs. 12,000. The rise recognises that floor months are longer and often away from home.

5.3. Apprentices placed at a site away from Waluj receive a lodging allowance and their travel to the site and back at the start and end of the placement. The allowance is set by the site and paid with the stipend.

5.4. Overtime is not paid to apprentices, because apprentices do not work overtime. An apprentice kept beyond the shift by an emergency is given the time back the next day.

5.5. No apprentice is bonded. Nobody repays anything for leaving the programme early or for taking a job elsewhere after it, and nobody is asked to sign a promise to stay.

## 15. Route changes and diversions

15.1. A driver does not change the planned route on his own judgement unless the
road ahead is closed or unsafe. He stops, calls Fleet Control, and follows the
diversion Fleet Control gives.

15.2. Fleet Control checks any diversion against the lane record for that trip,
because a diversion may take the vehicle through a dead zone or past no safe
stopping place.

15.3. A diversion that adds a toll, a ghat road or a city centre is written on
the dispatch note with the reason.

15.4. Customer service is told of any diversion that will change the arrival
window, and tells the customer. The driver does not tell the customer himself.

15.5. Festivals, elections and large public events close roads without much
notice. Planners check the week's public calendar on Thursday when they build
the plan, and Fleet Control checks it again each morning.

## 3. Who answers for what

3.1. The RP answers to the licensing authority as well as to Quillfern. She may stop any dispatch at any hour without giving a reason first; the reason is written up within the shift.

3.2. Shift QA officers work under the RP. One is on duty on each of the two shifts, 06:00 to 14:00 and 14:00 to 22:00. Between 22:00 and 06:00 the store neither receives nor dispatches except under a written plan the RP has approved, and the night is covered by the security contractor and the RP's phone.

3.3. The engineering technician, Irfan Ghanchi, looks after the chambers, the generator, the alarm panel and the loggers. He keeps his own maintenance log. He does not decide whether stock affected by an equipment fault is usable; he reports the fault and the QA officer decides what happens to the stock.

3.4. The store manager decides staffing, slots and vehicles. He may ask QA to hurry; he may not ask QA to agree. Where any two of these people disagree about whether stock may move, it does not move until the RP has decided.

3.5. Each role has a named deputy, listed on the board outside the QA office. A deputy acts with the full authority of the role while the holder is away, and signs in the deputy's own name, never the holder's.

## 16. Welfare

16.1. Apprentices are young and often away from home for the first time. Each intake has a welfare contact at Waluj, a member of the workshop staff who is not a trainer.

16.2. Apprentices may raise anything with the welfare contact — homesickness, money, a problem at the lodging, a problem with a colleague — in confidence.

16.3. The lodging used at each site is visited by the welfare contact before the first apprentice moves in.

16.4. Bullying, ragging or initiation rituals are not tolerated, on site or at the workshop, and are dealt with under the company's discipline rules.

16.5. Apprentices are paid their stipend during approved sick leave for up to four weeks.

## 11. Mentors

11.1. Each apprentice placed at a site has a named mentor, a qualified technician who has volunteered and been trained for the role.

11.2. The mentor signs the logbook each week, meets the apprentice for half an hour each fortnight to go through it, and reports to the workshop once a month.

11.3. Mentors receive an allowance for each apprentice they mentor, paid with their salary.

11.4. A mentor may have no more than two apprentices at a time.

11.5. An apprentice who has a problem with a mentor speaks to the workshop lead, who may change the mentor without asking for a reason.

## 13. Placement

13.1. From month seven apprentices are placed at a site that needs them. Placements are decided by the engineering pool lead with the site managers, and apprentices are asked their preference first.

13.2. An apprentice may be placed at a site far from home. The programme pays for travel and lodging and allows one trip home a month.

13.3. A placement lasts until the end of the programme unless the site closes, the mentor leaves or the apprentice asks to move for a good reason.

13.4. At the end of the programme, Quillfern offers a technician's post to each apprentice who completes, at a site with a vacancy. Taking the offer is not compulsory.

13.5. The site manager writes a short report on each apprentice at the end of the placement, and the apprentice sees it.

## 3. Planning a week of duty

3.1. Planners build the week's duty on Thursday for the following Monday to
Sunday. Each driver's weekly rest is placed first, then night segments, then
day runs.

3.2. The limits the plan must respect are in the Driver Hours and Road Safety
Policy. A plan that meets them only if nothing goes wrong does not meet them.

3.3. A lane with a qualification record is planned with that record open, so
that its relief point, its pre-cool hold time and any two-driver condition are
on the plan and not in someone's memory.

3.4. Festival shuttle rosters with split rest are planned only after the Fleet
head has approved the roster in writing, and only for the festival named.

3.5. The plan is published to drivers by Friday noon. A driver who sees a
problem with his week tells Fleet Control on Friday, not on the morning of the
run.

3.6. Leave requests go to the planner by the 20th of the previous month. Late
leave is granted where cover exists, and cover is never found by stretching
another driver's hours.

## 2. Choosing the ground

2.1. A unit stands on firm, level ground, with a gradient no steeper than 1 in
100. Concrete or compacted hardcore is acceptable; soil, sand and grass are not.

2.2. The fan side of the refrigeration unit must breathe. Leave one and a half metres free on the fan side, and keep that strip clear of vehicles, stacked crates and tarpaulins. A condenser that recirculates its own warm air loses
capacity on the first hot afternoon.

2.3. The unit is placed out of standing water. A site that floods in the
monsoon is refused, or the unit is raised on the pool's steel stands.

2.4. The personnel door needs room to open fully and a step that the customer's
staff can use safely while carrying cartons.

2.5. The site must be lit at night and must be inside the customer's boundary,
behind a gate that is locked or guarded.

2.6. The engineer who places the unit photographs the site from four sides and
files the photographs with the placement sheet.

## 10. Port work

10.1. Much of Godavari Aqua's stock leaves the DC in 40-foot refrigerated containers for export through the port. Containers are stuffed at the DC under customs supervision and sealed before they leave.

10.2. A stuffed export container must reach the port terminal at least 18 hours before the vessel's cut-off time, because the terminal needs that long to plug it in, scan it and stack it for loading. A container that cannot meet that time is not sent to the gate on the chance; the exporter is told and a later vessel is booked.

10.3. Container plugs at the DC can hold six containers on shore power while they wait. A stuffed container is never left on its own generator overnight at the DC.

10.4. Customs officers attend at the DC on request. The site books them a day ahead and records their names on the stuffing sheet.

10.5. The port's own rules on reefer monitoring apply once a container is inside the terminal. Our responsibility ends at the terminal gate.

## 1. The six units

1.1. The pool owns six units, MCR-1 to MCR-6. Each is a 20-foot insulated
container with a refrigeration unit at one end, a personnel door at the other,
internal shelving and a controller that logs the inside temperature every
minute.

1.2. MCR-1 to MCR-4 run at +2 to +8 C and are used for chilled medicine and
chilled food. MCR-5 and MCR-6 can also run at -20 C and are used for frozen
stock or for vaccines that are shipped frozen.

1.3. At any time about four units are out on campaign hires of a few weeks and
two are on long hires. The pool coordinator keeps the deployment board.

1.4. Every unit carries its number on both long sides and on the door. A unit is
never relabelled, even after a refurbishment.

1.5. The units were bought in 2024 and 2025. Their refrigeration units are under
the maker's warranty until the dates written on the inside of each door.

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

## 5. Racking and rooms

5.1. The DC has three temperature zones. The chilled block at +2 to +8 C holds 2,400 pallet positions in selective racking, split into a pharma room of 600 and a food room of 1,800. The frozen block at −22 C holds 1,600 pallet positions in drive-in racking. The controlled-room-temperature store holds 300.

5.2. The frozen block is built so that a second chamber of the same size can be added on the east side without stopping the first. That expansion is not approved and is not in this plan's figures.

5.3. The pharma room has its own anteroom and its own door to the dispatch canopy, so that pharma picking never shares a door with food.

5.4. Every room is temperature-mapped before first stock and again after its first summer. The mapping follows the company method.

5.5. Floor space in the dispatch canopy is for staging only. Nothing waits there longer than it takes to load.

## 4. The calendar

4.1. Civil works at Atchutapuram finished in June 2026. Racking, refrigeration and the electrical fit-out run through the monsoon, with commissioning in October and qualification of the rooms in November.

4.2. The DC receives its first customer stock on 1 December 2026. The date is fixed by Godavari Aqua's contract and it will not move later without the customer's written agreement. Earlier receipts are refused, however much space is ready, because the rooms will not yet have finished qualification.

4.3. The satellite at Bhubaneswar starts cross-dock work on 1 February 2027, eight weeks after the DC, so that the trunk run can be proven with the DC already working.

4.4. Full volume is planned for the end of the first quarter of 2027. From then until the end of 2028, growth is planned in steps tied to signed contracts, not to forecasts.

4.5. Each milestone has a named owner on the project board kept by the region head, and the board is reviewed every Monday.

# Containerised Unit Operating Manual

How the engineering pool's containerised cold rooms are placed, powered,
started, used, moved and looked after. The units are hired out to customers who
need cold space where Quillfern has no building: hospitals running vaccination
campaigns, a dairy cooperative's collection centre in the flush season, a
programme that needs a small store in a city neighbourhood. The manual is for
the engineers who place and service the units and for the customer's people who
use them day to day.

## 17. Later steps

17.1. A second satellite at Rajahmundry, closer to the shrimp plants, is being studied for 2028. It is not approved and nothing in this plan depends on it.

17.2. The second frozen chamber at the DC (section 5.2) will be proposed to the board when frozen occupancy has been above 85 per cent for six months.

17.3. Rail movement of frozen containers from the DC to the north has been offered by a container rail operator and will be tried in 2027 with one customer.

# Service Partner Onboarding Standard

## 1. What this standard is for

1.1. Quillfern buildings and vehicles are kept running by outside firms as much as by our own staff. Refrigeration engineers, generator agents, the people who service dock doors and levellers, pest controllers, cleaners, electricians, calibration laboratories and fire-equipment agents all come through our gates, and some of them work on the very plant that keeps customers' stock in range.

1.2. This standard says how such a firm becomes an approved service partner, what it must keep up to stay approved, and how it leaves the list. It applies to every site opened from 2025 onwards and to every firm that is newly approved anywhere in the company from the date of this revision.

1.3. It does not cover suppliers of goods, such as seals or forms, who deliver to Stores and never work on site. Those are approved under the purchasing rules.

1.4. It is written for Procurement, which keeps the list; for site managers, who call partners in; for QA, which approves partners who work near product; and for the engineering pool, which judges the technical competence of partners who work on plant.

1.5. "Partner" in this standard means a firm, not a person. The people the firm sends are its technicians.

## Servicing

First scheduled service falls due at 500 engine hours. RF-120 is under vendor
warranty until 1 December 2027 and no third-party garage may open the reefer
unit before then without Fleet head approval.

## 2. Three kinds of partner

2.1. Category A partners work on temperature-critical plant: refrigeration, the controllers and alarms on cold rooms, the generators and changeover gear that keep them running, and the reefer units on vehicles.

2.2. Category B partners work on the building and its fixed equipment but not on temperature-critical plant: dock doors and levellers, electrical work outside the plant room, roofing, fire equipment, pest control.

2.3. Category C partners neither touch plant nor enter product zones: office cleaning, canteen, landscaping, office IT.

2.4. The category decides how much checking a firm needs. A firm doing work in two categories is approved in the higher one.

2.5. Procurement assigns the category when the firm is proposed. The site manager or the engineering pool may ask for a firm to be moved to a higher category; nobody may move one lower without Procurement and QA agreeing.

## 14. Outside help

14.1. Several outside firms work in the building: the security contractor, the pest contractor, the cleaning contractor, the generator's service agent and the calibration laboratory. Each is approved by QA before its first visit and reviewed once a year.

14.2. The pest contractor visits on the first Thursday of each month and on call after any sighting. Bait stations are numbered on the wall plan in the QA office, and nobody moves one to make room for stock.

14.3. The cleaning contractor cleans the offices, the gowning room and the floors of the goods-in and dispatch bays. Chamber floors are cleaned by store staff only, so that nobody unfamiliar with the racking works in a chamber.

14.4. Refrigeration work on the chambers is done only by a firm approved under the company's arrangements for cooling-plant service partners. A technician who arrives without his induction card is not let in, however urgent the fault.

14.5. Calibration certificates from the laboratory are filed against the instrument's number in the document system. An instrument whose certificate is missing is treated as out of calibration.

## 7. People at the gate

7.1. A technician who will enter a pharma zone, a cold room holding pharma stock or a QA area must have a police verification certificate obtained through the local police station. The partner obtains it and sends us a copy before the technician's first visit.

7.2. The certificate must be renewed every three years. A technician whose certificate is more than three years old is refused at the gate, whatever the job, until a renewed certificate arrives.

7.3. Technicians who work only outside product zones need no police verification under this standard, though a site may require it for its own reasons.

7.4. Partners send the name, photograph and mobile number of every technician they may send. The gate is not expected to admit a technician who is not on the partner's list, even if the firm calls ahead.

7.5. Technicians leave their phones in the gate locker before entering a pharma zone unless the job needs a phone and the shift lead agrees.

## What RF-120 may carry

RF-120 carries frozen food only: frozen restaurant-chain loads, frozen peas and
frozen chicken on the Nagpur intercity lanes.

**RF-120 must never be loaded with vaccines, insulin, milk or paneer.** A frozen
body cannot be run warm for a chilled load, and a chilled load in a frozen body
is a product loss whether or not a sensor alarms. If a chilled consignment is
offered to RF-120 at the gate, the dock team refuses the load and calls Fleet
Control; the dock team may not reclassify the stock to make the booking work.

The frozen target, the excursion threshold and the defrost allowance that apply
to RF-120 are in the `owned_reefer_frozen` truck profile of
[the legacy sensor threshold file](02-sensor-thresholds.yaml), and the excursion
definition that governs a dispute is clause 2.4 of
[the Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md). This
file deliberately repeats neither, because the two have disagreed before.

## Dock and staging

RF-120 loads at dock 5 at Nagpur, per
[Dock scheduling rules 2026](13-dock-scheduling-rules-2026.md). Frozen stock
moves directly between freezer and reefer body; the short delay allowance before
the shift lead must be called is in
[the SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md), clause 8.4.

Frozen arrivals get the shortest grace of any class at Nagpur, which is why a
late RF-120 is called in rather than left in the queue.

## 17. Changes to this manual

17.1. Revision 1 (September 2025) was issued when the store opened. Revision 2 (December 2025) added the generator test after a power failure in the first month. Revision 3 (May 2026) changed several frequencies and limits after the store's first full season, and recorded the reasons beside each change.

17.2. The QA lead reviews this manual every April and after any critical deviation, failed customer audit or change to the building. The RP approves each revision.

17.3. Staff send suggested changes to the QA lead at any time. Each suggestion gets an answer, whether or not it is taken up.

17.4. A revised manual is issued with a one-page note of what changed. Every person who works in a product zone signs that they have read the note within a week of issue.

## Known history

On 6 May 2026 a restaurant-chain frozen chicken load on the Nagpur lane sat at
-16.2 C for 14 minutes and recovered to -18.4 C. QA recorded no excursion. The
case is kept in this file because drivers keep asking why that one was not an
excursion when a similar reading on a hired US-import reefer was: the imported
profile is in Fahrenheit and must be converted before comparison, which is noted
in [the sensor threshold file](02-sensor-thresholds.yaml).

## 14. How we write to customers

14.1. Customer service writes in plain English, in short sentences, without
internal shorthand. A customer does not know what a red sleeve, a DOM or a warm
pallet is, and should not have to ask.

14.2. Every email carries the customer's own reference first and the Quillfern
reference second, so that the customer's clerk can file it without reading it.

14.3. The agent writes the same facts to every contact at a customer. If two
contacts at one customer ask the same question, they get the same answer, copied
to each other.

14.4. Agents do not write in capitals, do not use exclamation marks, and do not
write "as per our records". They write what the record says.

14.5. Where a customer writes in Hindi, Marathi, Tamil or Assamese, the agent may
answer in that language if the agent writes it well. Anything that will be
signed by QA is written in English, with a translation attached if the customer
asks for one.

14.6. Templates are kept in the customer service system and reviewed twice a
year by the customer service lead. An agent who finds a template wrong tells the
lead and does not quietly edit a copy.

## 4. Taking over a vehicle

4.1. The driver taking over a vehicle walks round it with the driver handing
over, or with the shift lead if the vehicle was parked empty.

4.2. The walk-round covers tyres and wheel nuts, lights, mirrors, the reefer
unit's display and alarm light, the rear door hasp, the cab locker and the red
sleeve, the fire extinguisher, and the wheel chocks.

4.3. Any damage found on the walk-round is photographed and written on the
takeover sheet before the vehicle moves. Damage found later is presumed to have
happened on the later driver's watch.

4.4. The cab card is checked for the current Fleet Control, QA desk and
Compliance-Red numbers. A cab card printed before the Tessaline cutover is
replaced before the vehicle leaves.

4.5. The driver checks that the Tessaline unit shows the vehicle's own asset
number. Units have been swapped between vehicles in the workshop and not
re-labelled.

## 8. The first visit

8.1. Before working on any site for the first time, each technician completes the site induction: a walk round the site with a shift lead, the fire and evacuation routes, the rules on product zones, the permit system, the waste rules and whom to call.

8.2. The induction takes about ninety minutes and is signed for by the technician and the shift lead.

8.3. The technician is then issued an induction card bearing the photograph, the firm, the category and the date. The card is valid for twelve months from the date of issue at every Quillfern site opened since 2025, so that a technician who has been inducted at one need not repeat it at another within the year; each site still gives a short walk round on the first visit.

8.4. An expired card is not a gate pass. The technician repeats the induction.

8.5. A card is withdrawn at once if the technician breaks a product-zone rule, and Procurement is told.

## 14. Training and coaching for drivers

14.1. Every new owned-reefer driver rides two supervised runs with an experienced
driver before driving alone. One of the two is a night run.

14.2. The supervised runs cover the cab card, the takeover walk-round, the seal
routine, the red sleeve, the gate checklist for pharma runs and the way to speak
to Fleet Control on the phone. The experienced driver signs the new driver's
training sheet at the end of each run.

14.3. Telematics coaching calls are held within two working days of an alert, as
the policy says. The coach asks what happened before saying anything about what
should have happened.

14.4. Drivers who complete a year with no safety non-conformance receive a
certificate from the Fleet head, presented at the Nagpur driver meeting. The
certificate carries no money and is not tied to arrival times.

14.5. The Nagpur driver meeting is held on the last Saturday of each month in
the driver rest room. Attendance is paid duty time. Drivers on the road that day
receive the notes on their phone.

## 13. Cabs, bodies and how they look

13.1. A Quillfern cab is kept clean enough that a customer's receiving clerk can
sit in it to sign papers. Food wrappers, bottles and bedding are cleared out at
the end of every duty day.

13.2. Nothing is stuck to the windscreen except the permits the law requires and
the Quillfern asset number. Stickers, pictures and hanging charms that block the
driver's view are removed at the takeover walk-round.

13.3. The outside of the body is washed at least once a week, and after any run
through a construction zone or mud. A body whose company markings cannot be read
is washed before its next customer drop.

13.4. Scratches and dents are reported, not painted over. Fleet Control books
body repairs in batches so that no vehicle is off the road longer than it needs
to be.

13.5. The cab card, the red sleeve and the fire extinguisher each have a fixed
place in the cab. A driver who finds any of them moved puts it back and tells
Fleet Control, because the next driver will look for it in its fixed place in a
hurry.

## 9. Credit notes

9.1. A credit note is raised by Finance on the account manager's request. Agents
do not promise one.

9.2. A credit note for a wrongly quoted line, such as a Guwahati monsoon line on a
Coimbatore load, is raised without a claim, but still needs the account
manager's request.

9.3. A credit note is never offered to settle a complaint about an excursion
before QA has recorded a disposition.

9.4. Every credit note carries the invoice number, the line and the reason, in
words a customer's accounts clerk can follow without calling us.

## 17. Records

17.1. Procurement keeps each partner's file: the proposal, the papers, the visit report, the references, the approval, the agreements, every year's score, any probation plan and the reasons for leaving the list.

17.2. A partner's file is kept for six years after its last work order, or six years after it leaves the list, whichever comes later.

17.3. Work orders, permits and gas records are kept with the site's own records for the periods set by the documents that govern them.

17.4. Partner files are confidential. A partner may see its own file on request.

## 13. Records

13.1. Tickets, emails, call notes and quotations are kept in the customer
service system for three years, or seven years where the ticket concerns a
pharma critical excursion or a claim.

13.2. The agent writes what the customer said and what the agent said, not a
summary of both.

13.3. A ticket about an excursion carries the QCL-F-17 reference, so that an
auditor can move from the customer record to the QA record without asking.

13.4. Customer service's own notes on a customer's mood or manner are not kept
in the ticket. They belong in a conversation with the account manager.

# Fleet Operations Manual

The working manual for Fleet Control, fleet planners, owned-reefer drivers and
the managers of hired-truck vendors. It says how the fleet is run day to day. It
does not restate the driver hours limits, the temperature limits or the dock
booking rules; those have their own documents, and this manual points to them.
