## 6. Watching the rooms

6.1. Each walk-in has three fixed loggers and the CRT area has two. They report every minute to the panel in the QA office and to the duty phone carried by the shift QA officer. The panel keeps its own record and pushes a daily file to the document system at 23:59.

6.2. An alarm is acknowledged on the panel by the QA officer on duty, never by a picker, and acknowledging an alarm is not the same as closing it. The alarm stays open until the officer has written down what was found and what was done about it.

6.3. Logger batteries are changed by the technician on a calendar he keeps, not when they run flat. A logger that has gone silent is a deviation, even if the room was in range throughout.

6.4. Door openings are counted by the panel. A chamber whose doors stood open for more than 40 minutes in a shift is raised at the next morning's meeting — not because anything necessarily went wrong, but because it usually means the picking plan was poor.

6.5. The weekly trend sheet, prepared by the QA lead every Monday, shows each logger's highest and lowest reading of the week and every alarm. The RP reads and initials it, and her initials are what an auditor will look for.

## 8. When the grid drops

8.1. The site has two gensets on a common panel. They start automatically when
grid power fails and carry FC-A, the cell, the plant room and the apron lights.
The canteen and the office air conditioning are not on the genset panel.

8.2. The gensets are test-run under load every Thursday at 10:00 for twenty
minutes. The run time, the oil level and any alarm on the panel are written in
the genset log.

8.3. The gensets share one day tank and one bulk tank. The tank is never allowed below 1,500 litres; the night lead dips it at 22:00 and orders a top-up from the listed bowser at 2,500.

8.4. During a long outage the night lead dips the tank every four hours and
writes each reading in the log. A bowser that does not arrive within four hours
of an order is chased by the site manager, not by the night lead.

8.5. Nobody refuels a genset while it is running. Fuel spills are covered with
the sand from the bin beside the tank and reported the same shift.

8.6. After the grid returns, the gensets run on for ten minutes before they are
shut down, and the panel is checked for any alarm that was raised during the
outage.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

## 5. Equipment that has to prove itself

5.1. Every piece of equipment that touches product temperature is qualified before use: the two walk-in chambers, the CRT air-conditioning, the generator and its changeover, and the alarm panel. Qualification means a written test, run by people who did not install the equipment, against acceptance criteria written before the test began.

5.2. The walk-ins are requalified on a fixed cycle, and the cycle was shortened after the compressor failure of November 2025, when WIC-2 ran for nine days on a hired compressor whose behaviour nobody had measured. A full temperature study of each chamber is now repeated every 12 months, and also within 30 days after any compressor, evaporator or door is replaced. The study follows the company mapping method, and the result goes to the RP, who decides whether the chamber may keep holding stock.

5.3. The generator is load-tested on the first Monday of each month by pulling the incoming supply. The changeover must complete before any chamber logger records a rise of more than 1 C, and the technician writes the time it took in his log.

5.4. The alarm panel is tested every Friday. A panel that fails its test is taken out of service and the shift QA officer reads every logger by hand each hour until it is repaired.

5.5. Equipment that fails any test carries a yellow card until it passes again, and the RP is told the same shift. A yellow-carded chamber may keep stock only on the RP's written decision.

## 7. The plant room

7.1. The site is cooled by a carbon dioxide refrigeration rack. The plant room
holds the compressors, the receiver and the gas cooler, and the gas cooler's
fans sit on the roof above it.

7.2. Gas detectors in the plant room, in FC-A and in the cell watch for leaks. A
first stage lights the amber beacon over the plant room door and calls the plant
lead. A second stage sounds the site siren.

7.3. Only the plant lead and the refrigeration contractor's technician enter the
plant room. Both carry a personal gas monitor clipped to the chest.

7.4. When the leak siren sounds, forklifts stop where they are, engines are
switched off and nobody goes back for stock, a phone or a vehicle. Everyone walks to BW-A, the painted square beside the truck scale, and stays there until the plant lead clears the site in person.

7.5. The shift lead counts heads against the gate log and the contract labour
sheet within ten minutes and phones the count to the site manager. Drivers
waiting on the apron are counted by the guard.

7.6. A siren test is run on the first Monday of every month at 11:00, announced
the day before. Nobody leaves the building for a test.

7.7. The refrigeration contractor services the rack every quarter and after any
leak alarm. The service sheet is kept in the plant room folder and copied to the
site manager.

## 6. Roadside trouble

6.1. A driver whose vehicle develops a fault stops at a safe place first and
calls second. A lit fuel plaza, a toll rest area or a police post is a safe
place; a road shoulder at night is not, unless the vehicle cannot be moved.

6.2. Roadside tyre changes on a loaded reefer are done by the listed tyre
vendor, never by the driver alone, and Fleet Control expects the vendor within
3 hours on a qualified lane.

6.3. A reefer unit fault is reported with the display reading, the alarm code
and the time. Fleet Control decides whether to send the mobile service van,
transfer the load, or bring the vehicle in. The driver does not open the reefer
unit's panel.

6.4. A breakdown on a lane where the fuel pumps are a quarter of a day apart
makes the wait long. Drivers on such lanes carry water and a torch, and the
mobile service van is not always the quickest help; sometimes the relief point
vendor on the lane arrives first.

6.5. A vehicle that cannot be moved and is carrying pharma critical stock is
reported to Compliance-Red by Fleet Control within the SOP's notification
window, whatever the cause.

6.6. After any roadside repair, the vehicle is walked round again before it
moves, as if it were being taken over.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 12. Customer loggers

12.1. Some customers send their own logger with the stock. The logger travels
with the stock from the moment it arrives until it leaves.

12.2. A customer logger does not overrule the Tessaline record. If the customer
quotes their logger in an argument, the agent says that QA will compare the two
files and explain any difference.

12.3. A customer logger sent back to the customer goes with the return challan,
never by separate post.

12.4. The agent never downloads or opens a customer logger. That is QA's work.

## 14. Money in

14.1. The insurer pays an agreed claim within 30 days of receiving the surveyor's final report or, for a desk-assessed claim, within 30 days of receiving the complete file. On day 31 the desk asks the broker to chase, and on day 45 the desk lead writes to the broker's branch head.

14.2. Payment comes to Quillfern's account, never to the customer's, even when the customer's goods were lost.

14.3. Finance books the expected recovery as a receivable when the claim is agreed, not when it is intimated, and writes off any part the insurer refuses once the desk lead has decided not to dispute it.

14.4. Credit notes to customers are not tied to insurance money. A customer is paid what the contract says, when the contract says, whether or not our own claim has succeeded.

14.5. Disputes with the insurer about the amount go through the broker first. The policy's arbitration clause is used only with the Finance head's approval.

## 8. Power

8.1. Each K7 has a hot-swap battery that can be changed without switching off. Spare charged batteries sit in the charging bay of each rack.

8.2. Batteries wear out, and a worn one dies at the worst moment of a pick. A pack is retired at 500 charge cycles or when Fernguard reports its health under 80 per cent, whichever comes first. Floor staff say a retired battery has been binned; it is in fact returned to the IT desk for recycling and never put in general waste.

8.3. A battery that is swollen, cracked or hot to the touch is taken out at once, put in the fire-safe tin by the rack and reported to the IT desk.

8.4. Batteries are not charged anywhere except in the cradle rack. Chargers brought from home are not used.

8.5. At the end of each shift every K7 goes back in its cradle, charged or not.

## 14. Photographs and personal data

14.1. Photographs taken on a K7 are of stock, seals, labels, damage and equipment. They do not include people's faces where it can be helped, and never include a customer's staff without their agreement.

14.2. Photographs are uploaded to the document system against the job they belong to and deleted from the device.

14.3. Staff do not photograph a K7's screen with their own phones to send a picture to someone else.

14.4. Personal data about staff — names, logins and shift times — is visible only to the shift lead, the IT desk and HR.

14.5. A person who wants to know what Fernguard holds about them asks HR in writing.

14.6. Login records are not used to measure how fast a person picks. Pick rates come from the warehouse system and are discussed with the person, not posted.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 11. What is left of the load

11.1. Damaged goods remain the customer's property until a claim is paid; after payment, anything left belongs to the insurer. Neither the site nor the claims desk may treat what is left as Quillfern's to sell.

11.2. Medicines are never disposed of as salvage, whatever condition they appear to be in and whatever the insurer suggests. They are destroyed under QA control with a destruction certificate, and the certificate goes into the claim file in place of a salvage account.

11.3. Food that cannot be supplied to the customer may be sold for animal feed or processing, but only to a buyer the insurer approves in writing, and only after the surveyor has released it. The proceeds are paid to the insurer or deducted from the claim, as the broker directs.

11.4. Staff may not buy damaged goods, take them home or give them away, even when the goods are about to be destroyed anyway. A carton of ice cream taken off a damaged pallet is theft from the customer, whatever its future.

11.5. The salvage account lists what was sold, to whom, for how much and on what date, or what was destroyed and on whose certificate.

## 15. The customer's own claim

15.1. A customer's claim against Quillfern runs on its own track, under its own contract, and is handled by the account manager and Finance. The claims desk is told of it and links the two files, but the customer's claim is not decided by what our insurer does.

15.2. Customers' contracts set their own limits, claim periods and evidence rules. Those terms, not the policy terms, decide what the customer gets.

15.3. Customers are not told whether Quillfern is insured for a loss, how much the cover is, or what the insurer paid. A customer who asks is told that Quillfern meets its contractual obligations.

15.4. Nobody promises a customer insurance money, a quick settlement or a particular figure. The first written word to a customer about money comes from the account manager after Finance has agreed it.

15.5. Evidence gathered for our own claim may be shown to a customer's surveyor on request, through the account manager, but the claim file itself is not sent to customers.

# Ratnagiri mango season cover - per-truck limit, claim papers deadline, letter to the trucker, late arrival rejections, claim file retention

**From:** Omkar Sawant <omkar.sawant@quillfern.example>

**To:** Ratnagiri pack-house team <ratnagiri@quillfern.example>

**Date:** Mon, 06 Apr 2026 08:47:15 +0530

Team,

For this season's mango runs out of the Ratnagiri pack-house, here is how our
cover works on the per-truck limit, the claim papers deadline, the letter to
the trucker, late arrival rejections and claim file retention.

Per-truck limit: the most the cover pays for one truck on one trip is Rs. 75
lakh.

Claim papers deadline: the complete claim papers go to the insurer within 60
days of discovering the loss.

Letter to the trucker: a letter holding the hired trucker liable goes out
within 7 days of discovery.

Late arrival rejections: loads rejected by the buyer for late arrival are
covered under the season endorsement.

Claim file retention: claim files are kept for 5 years after settlement.

Omkar

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## 8. Heavy days on the road

8.1. The insurer's exposure on any single vehicle is capped. The most it will pay for all goods on one vehicle on one trip is Rs. 1.2 crore, however many consignments are on board.

8.2. A full vaccine load easily goes past that figure, and so does a frozen load of premium seafood. Any dispatch whose total declared value on one vehicle is above Rs. 1.2 crore is declared to the broker in writing at least 48 hours before the vehicle leaves. The broker then gets the insurer's agreement to a higher figure for that trip, or tells us to split the load.

8.3. Fleet planners check the declared value of every pharma critical and every high-value frozen load when they build the week's plan, and send the list of trips over the figure to the claims desk on Thursday.

8.4. A trip that goes over the figure without a declaration is still covered up to Rs. 1.2 crore. Anything above that is uninsured, and the site manager who allowed the load explains why in writing.

8.5. Splitting a load costs a second vehicle and a second crew. Planners should prefer splitting to asking for a higher figure only where the second vehicle is already on the road; the broker's higher figure usually costs less than an empty run.

## 16. Keeping the file

16.1. Each claim file is kept, complete, for eight years from the date of final settlement or rejection, whichever comes later. Files involving a court case or arbitration are kept until three years after the case ends, if that is longer.

16.2. Scanned files live in the Finance document store under the TPC26 number. Paper originals are boxed by policy year and kept in the Finance archive room.

16.3. Physical evidence — seals, logger files, damaged packaging — is kept until the claim is closed, then for one more year, and is then disposed of with the desk lead's signature.

16.4. A file is never weeded to save space. If storage runs short, the desk lead asks Finance for more.

## 8. Claims

8.1. A customer claim for damaged or lost stock is accepted in writing only,
from a named contact on the account.

8.2. A claim is registered only when it arrives within 30 days of delivery and
carries photographs of the stock and the seal taken at delivery.

8.3. The agent registers the claim, acknowledges it within one working day, and
passes it to the account manager. The agent does not give an opinion on it.

8.4. Stock value in a claim is taken from the Finance schedule. A value in the
customer's email is recorded as the declared value and nothing more.

8.5. A claim that turns on a temperature record waits for QA's investigation.
The customer is told it is waiting, and given the investigation's reference.

8.6. Claims for trips before 18 August 2025 quote the KLP trip number, not a TSL
one.

## 9. Credit notes

9.1. A credit note is raised by Finance on the account manager's request. Agents
do not promise one.

9.2. A credit note for a wrongly quoted line, such as a Guwahati monsoon line on a
Coimbatore load, is raised without a claim, but still needs the account
manager's request.

9.3. A credit note is never offered to settle a complaint about an excursion
before QA has recorded a disposition.

9.4. Every credit note carries the invoice number, the line and the reason, in
words a customer's accounts clerk can follow without calling us.

## 12. Customer loggers

12.1. Some customers send their own logger with the stock. The logger travels
with the stock from the moment it arrives until it leaves.

12.2. A customer logger does not overrule the Tessaline record. If the customer
quotes their logger in an argument, the agent says that QA will compare the two
files and explain any difference.

12.3. A customer logger sent back to the customer goes with the return challan,
never by separate post.

12.4. The agent never downloads or opens a customer logger. That is QA's work.

## 18. Customer data

18.1. Customer contact details are kept in the customer service system only. They
are not copied into personal phones, spreadsheets or chat groups.

18.2. A customer's prices, volumes and incident history are not shared with any
other customer, even one in the same group of companies, without the account
manager's written clearance.

18.3. Recordings of calls are kept for ninety days unless a ticket needs them for
longer.

18.4. A request from a customer to see the data Quillfern holds on them goes to
the account manager and to Pune HQ's legal contact on the day it arrives.

## 7. Leaving the building in a hurry

7.1. The Coimbatore cold block runs on packaged refrigeration units on the roof.
There is no ammonia on this site, so the ammonia cards used at Nagpur do not
apply here and must not be pinned up here.

7.2. Coimbatore has one site siren, and it means leave the building. It sounds
for fire, for a gas smell from the canteen cylinders, and for a refrigerant leak
alarm from a roof unit.

7.3. Everyone goes to assembly point CM-1, the coconut grove corner inside the
east gate. Nobody gathers on the south apron: that is where the fire tender
comes in.

7.4. The shift lead counts against the gate register and the Dockwise day list,
and phones the count to the DC manager. Drivers waiting outside the south gate
stay outside and are counted by the guard.

7.5. Nobody goes back into the cold block for stock. Pallets left outside a room
are dealt with afterwards under the SOP.

7.6. The all clear is given in person by the DC manager or, at night, by the
senior guard after the fire service leaves.

## 7. Machinery that stops

7.1. A loss of temperature on its own is not an accident. Under TPC, spoilage caused by a failure of the vehicle's refrigerating machinery is paid only where the machinery stopped working for at least four consecutive hours. Spoilage after a shorter stoppage is Quillfern's loss, not the insurer's, unless the stoppage followed a collision, an overturning or a fire, in which case the ordinary accident cover applies.

7.2. The four hours are counted from the unit's own stop event in its controller log, not from the first temperature alarm and not from the time the driver noticed. A unit that stops, restarts, and stops again has two stoppages, not one long one.

7.3. The stoppage is proved by the controller's event log and the temperature record together. A driver's statement, however honest, does not prove it alone, and a phone photograph of a dark display is evidence only of the moment it was taken.

7.4. Fleet Control downloads the controller log as soon as a claim on refrigeration grounds is possible, before the unit is serviced. A mechanic who clears the fault log has destroyed the evidence, so workshops are told not to clear any log on a vehicle with an open claim.

7.5. Customers' stock that warmed during a long stoppage is still handled under the quality rules, whether or not the claim succeeds. A failed claim never leads to stock being released.

## 7. The plant room

7.1. The site is cooled by a carbon dioxide refrigeration rack. The plant room
holds the compressors, the receiver and the gas cooler, and the gas cooler's
fans sit on the roof above it.

7.2. Gas detectors in the plant room, in FC-A and in the cell watch for leaks. A
first stage lights the amber beacon over the plant room door and calls the plant
lead. A second stage sounds the site siren.

7.3. Only the plant lead and the refrigeration contractor's technician enter the
plant room. Both carry a personal gas monitor clipped to the chest.

7.4. When the leak siren sounds, forklifts stop where they are, engines are
switched off and nobody goes back for stock, a phone or a vehicle. Everyone walks to BW-A, the painted square beside the truck scale, and stays there until the plant lead clears the site in person.

7.5. The shift lead counts heads against the gate log and the contract labour
sheet within ten minutes and phones the count to the site manager. Drivers
waiting on the apron are counted by the guard.

7.6. A siren test is run on the first Monday of every month at 11:00, announced
the day before. Nobody leaves the building for a test.

7.7. The refrigeration contractor services the rack every quarter and after any
leak alarm. The service sheet is kept in the plant room folder and copied to the
site manager.

## 6. The shed by the wash pad

6.1. Coimbatore buys dry ice for two jobs only: emergency packing for a
restaurant chain whose own freezer has failed, and top-up of a frozen body that
has to wait on the apron.

6.2. The dry-ice chest stands in the open-sided store shed beside the wash pad,
not inside any building. The shed has a roof and no walls on two sides, so
carbon dioxide does not collect there the way it does in a closed store. For
that reason there is no carbon dioxide monitor at Coimbatore. The chest is never
moved indoors, even in heavy rain.

6.3. Supply and handling at Coimbatore:

| item | Coimbatore rule |
|---|---|
| supplier | Kovai Industrial Gases fills the chest with 60 kg every Tuesday |

## 11. Racking and the floor

11.1. The drive-in racking in FC-A is inspected by the racking contractor every
six months. Any damage found between inspections is reported the same shift,
and the bay is closed with chains until it is checked.

11.2. Reach trucks keep to the marked aisles. Nobody walks in an aisle where a
truck is working; pickers wait at the aisle end until the truck has left.

11.3. Pallets are placed so that no carton overhangs the pallet edge. A pallet
with overhanging cartons is restacked in the anteroom before it goes into FC-A.

11.4. The floor of FC-A has a heated sub-floor to stop frost heave. The
sub-floor temperature is checked weekly by the plant lead and written in the
plant room folder.

11.5. Spilled product in FC-A is cleared at once, because frozen spillage under
a truck wheel is as slippery as ice.

## 10. Doors, curtains and ice

10.1. Every door into FC-A and the cell is a rapid-roll door with a strip curtain
behind it. A door that does not close fully within 20 seconds of a vehicle
passing is reported to the shift lead.

10.2. The door heaters keep the frame of each freezer door from icing. The
morning shift lead checks each heater light at the start of the shift and logs
any that is out.

10.3. Ice on the floor in front of a freezer door is chipped and cleared at once,
not left for the next shift. The ice is swept into the drain channel outside,
never left in the anteroom to melt.

10.4. A strip curtain with a torn strip is replaced within a week. The spare
strips are in the store cage in the anteroom.

10.5. The dock seals at D4 to D6 are checked by the guard each evening. A seal
that does not meet the van body lets warm air into the anteroom and frost onto
the picking cartons.

## 15. The customer's own claim

15.1. A customer's claim against Quillfern runs on its own track, under its own contract, and is handled by the account manager and Finance. The claims desk is told of it and links the two files, but the customer's claim is not decided by what our insurer does.

15.2. Customers' contracts set their own limits, claim periods and evidence rules. Those terms, not the policy terms, decide what the customer gets.

15.3. Customers are not told whether Quillfern is insured for a loss, how much the cover is, or what the insurer paid. A customer who asks is told that Quillfern meets its contractual obligations.

15.4. Nobody promises a customer insurance money, a quick settlement or a particular figure. The first written word to a customer about money comes from the account manager after Finance has agreed it.

15.5. Evidence gathered for our own claim may be shown to a customer's surveyor on request, through the account manager, but the claim file itself is not sent to customers.

# Service Partner Onboarding Standard

## 1. What this standard is for

1.1. Quillfern buildings and vehicles are kept running by outside firms as much as by our own staff. Refrigeration engineers, generator agents, the people who service dock doors and levellers, pest controllers, cleaners, electricians, calibration laboratories and fire-equipment agents all come through our gates, and some of them work on the very plant that keeps customers' stock in range.

1.2. This standard says how such a firm becomes an approved service partner, what it must keep up to stay approved, and how it leaves the list. It applies to every site opened from 2025 onwards and to every firm that is newly approved anywhere in the company from the date of this revision.

1.3. It does not cover suppliers of goods, such as seals or forms, who deliver to Stores and never work on site. Those are approved under the purchasing rules.

1.4. It is written for Procurement, which keeps the list; for site managers, who call partners in; for QA, which approves partners who work near product; and for the engineering pool, which judges the technical competence of partners who work on plant.

1.5. "Partner" in this standard means a firm, not a person. The people the firm sends are its technicians.

## 17. Records

17.1. Procurement keeps each partner's file: the proposal, the papers, the visit report, the references, the approval, the agreements, every year's score, any probation plan and the reasons for leaving the list.

17.2. A partner's file is kept for six years after its last work order, or six years after it leaves the list, whichever comes later.

17.3. Work orders, permits and gas records are kept with the site's own records for the periods set by the documents that govern them.

17.4. Partner files are confidential. A partner may see its own file on request.

## 7. Machinery that stops

7.1. A loss of temperature on its own is not an accident. Under TPC, spoilage caused by a failure of the vehicle's refrigerating machinery is paid only where the machinery stopped working for at least four consecutive hours. Spoilage after a shorter stoppage is Quillfern's loss, not the insurer's, unless the stoppage followed a collision, an overturning or a fire, in which case the ordinary accident cover applies.

7.2. The four hours are counted from the unit's own stop event in its controller log, not from the first temperature alarm and not from the time the driver noticed. A unit that stops, restarts, and stops again has two stoppages, not one long one.

7.3. The stoppage is proved by the controller's event log and the temperature record together. A driver's statement, however honest, does not prove it alone, and a phone photograph of a dark display is evidence only of the moment it was taken.

7.4. Fleet Control downloads the controller log as soon as a claim on refrigeration grounds is possible, before the unit is serviced. A mechanic who clears the fault log has destroyed the evidence, so workshops are told not to clear any log on a vehicle with an open claim.

7.5. Customers' stock that warmed during a long stoppage is still handled under the quality rules, whether or not the claim succeeds. A failed claim never leads to stock being released.

## 14. Outside help

14.1. Several outside firms work in the building: the security contractor, the pest contractor, the cleaning contractor, the generator's service agent and the calibration laboratory. Each is approved by QA before its first visit and reviewed once a year.

14.2. The pest contractor visits on the first Thursday of each month and on call after any sighting. Bait stations are numbered on the wall plan in the QA office, and nobody moves one to make room for stock.

14.3. The cleaning contractor cleans the offices, the gowning room and the floors of the goods-in and dispatch bays. Chamber floors are cleaned by store staff only, so that nobody unfamiliar with the racking works in a chamber.

14.4. Refrigeration work on the chambers is done only by a firm approved under the company's arrangements for cooling-plant service partners. A technician who arrives without his induction card is not let in, however urgent the fault.

14.5. Calibration certificates from the laboratory are filed against the instrument's number in the document system. An instrument whose certificate is missing is treated as out of calibration.

## 16. Keeping the file

16.1. Each claim file is kept, complete, for eight years from the date of final settlement or rejection, whichever comes later. Files involving a court case or arbitration are kept until three years after the case ends, if that is longer.

16.2. Scanned files live in the Finance document store under the TPC26 number. Paper originals are boxed by policy year and kept in the Finance archive room.

16.3. Physical evidence — seals, logger files, damaged packaging — is kept until the claim is closed, then for one more year, and is then disposed of with the desk lead's signature.

16.4. A file is never weeded to save space. If storage runs short, the desk lead asks Finance for more.

## 6. References

6.1. Category A and B firms give two references from customers for whom they have done similar work in the past two years. At least one reference is spoken to by phone.

6.2. A reference from a relative of the firm's owner, or from another firm under the same ownership, does not count.

6.3. Procurement writes a short note of each reference call and files it.

6.4. A bad reference does not automatically stop approval, but it is discussed with the firm and the note of that discussion is filed with the reference.

## 18. Changes to this standard

18.1. Revision 1 (2025) was a one-page checklist used during the 2025 site openings. Revision 2 (February 2026) replaced it with this standard, raised the papers required of Category A partners and set the induction card's validity across sites.

18.2. Procurement reviews this standard every January with QA and the engineering pool.

18.3. Partners are sent a short note of every change, and their agreements are updated at the next renewal.

## 16. Waste and destruction

16.1. Product that cannot be supplied is destroyed by a licensed medical-waste contractor, against a destruction certificate that names the batch and the quantity.

16.2. Destruction is witnessed by a QA officer and one other person. Both sign the certificate, and photographs of the sealed waste containers are filed with it.

16.3. Product is never thrown in general waste, even a single vial, and never given away, sold for scrap or used for training.

16.4. Packaging from destroyed product that carries a customer's name or batch number is destroyed with the product, not recycled.

16.5. The destruction register is reconciled each month against the quarantine register, so that every unit that went into quarantine has either been released, returned to its owner or destroyed.

## 4. Behind door 3

4.1. The cell behind D3 is BC-1, a blast cell with an air temperature of -35 C
and room for six pallets. It exists because brand owners do not always send
stock as cold as their paperwork says, and a frozen store is not built to pull
warm stock down; it is built to hold cold stock cold.

4.2. Every inbound pallet is probed at the dock: one carton from the middle of
the pallet, probe into the product core. Anything with a core warmer than minus 12 on the arrival probe goes behind door 3 first, whatever the paperwork says.

4.3. The target in the cell is a core of minus 18. It gets six hours from the moment the doors close. A load that has not reached target by then is reported to QA and held, and the customer is told the same day.

4.4. Stock that comes out of the cell is probed again before it goes into FC-A,
and both readings are written on the inbound sheet with their times.

4.5. The cell is never used as overflow storage, however busy the night. A
pallet parked in the cell because FC-A is full blocks the next soft arrival,
and the next soft arrival then sits on the dock warming further.

4.6. The cell's fans put a hard frost on cartons that sit too close to the coil.
Pallets are placed on the painted floor marks and nowhere else.

4.7. Whether cell time is charged depends on the customer's contract, not on
this handbook. The shift lead records the door-closing and door-opening times on
the cell log so that the office can apply whatever the contract says.

4.8. The cell was enlarged from four to six pallet places in March 2026. The two
extra places took space from the apron, which is why the apron now holds nine
vehicles and not eleven.

## Arrival probe and blast cell

Probe one carton from the middle of each incoming pallet, with the probe in the
product core. A pallet whose core is warmer than -15 C on the arrival probe
goes to the blast cell first. The target is a core of -18 C within eight hours
of the cell door closing. A pallet still short of target at hour eight is held
and QA is told.

## 2. The work

2.1. Quillfern collects the customer's frozen products from the Chakan factory,
stores them and delivers them to restaurants, caterers and retailers in Pune
and Mumbai.

2.2. Pune deliveries go out from Quillfern's own stock. Mumbai-bound stock is
cross-docked at Quillfern's Bhiwandi site and goes out on the next morning's
vans.

2.3. Call-off times for Mumbai deliveries are those printed in the site handbook of the cross-dock that ships them.

2.4. Waiting charges on the customer's own vehicles at the cross-dock are billed at the site's published rate less 20 per cent.

2.5. Pallets are exchanged one for one at the cross-dock. Exchange units that arrive unfit on the customer's own vehicles are charged at the site figure, with no discount.

2.6. Quillfern does not sell, promote or price the customer's products and does
not take orders from the customer's buyers directly.

## 11. Racking and the floor

11.1. The drive-in racking in FC-A is inspected by the racking contractor every
six months. Any damage found between inspections is reported the same shift,
and the bay is closed with chains until it is checked.

11.2. Reach trucks keep to the marked aisles. Nobody walks in an aisle where a
truck is working; pickers wait at the aisle end until the truck has left.

11.3. Pallets are placed so that no carton overhangs the pallet edge. A pallet
with overhanging cartons is restacked in the anteroom before it goes into FC-A.

11.4. The floor of FC-A has a heated sub-floor to stop frost heave. The
sub-floor temperature is checked weekly by the plant lead and written in the
plant room folder.

11.5. Spilled product in FC-A is cleared at once, because frozen spillage under
a truck wheel is as slippery as ice.

# Taloja freezer store card: blast cell, order cut-off, gas leak siren

Pinned at the Taloja order desk. This card covers three things: the arrival
probe and the blast cell, the order cut-off for next-day vans, and where to
line up when the gas leak siren sounds.

## 3. Commitments on both sides

3.1. The customer commits to 1,800 pallet movements in each calendar month; any month that falls short is charged Rs. 300 for each movement not made.

3.2. A pallet movement is one pallet received or one pallet dispatched. A pallet
received and dispatched in the same month counts twice.

3.3. Quillfern commits to hold enough frozen space in Pune for 900 of the
customer's pallets at any one time, and to give 30 days' notice before reducing
it.

3.4. Months in which Quillfern could not take the customer's stock, for reasons
on Quillfern's side, are not counted for the shortfall charge.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

## 4. Product, packing and handover

4.1. The customer packs its products in cartons that carry the batch number and
the best-before date on two faces.

4.2. Loaded pallets stand no higher than 1.8 metres including the wooden base. Taller pallets are restacked at the customer's cost before they are
accepted.

4.3. Each pallet is stretch-wrapped and labelled with the customer's pallet ID
on two faces.

4.4. Handover takes place when the pallet crosses the dock edge at the
receiving site. The receiving shift lead's count is the count.

## 11. Disputes

11.1. The parties first try to settle a dispute between their account managers,
then between their directors.

11.2. A dispute not settled within 45 days goes to a sole arbitrator in Pune.

## 13. Documents

13.1. The store's procedures, forms and records live in the document system. Only the version in the system is current, and each procedure shows its revision number and effective date on every page.

13.2. Paper copies of procedures are a convenience, not a source: they are useful at the goods-in desk and in the anteroom, where nobody wants to read a screen with gloves on. A copy printed from the document system is valid only until midnight of the day printed, which the printer stamps in the footer. A paper copy found after that is put in the confidential bin, whatever revision number it carries.

13.3. Records are made at the time, in ink or in the system, and corrected by striking through and initialling, never by overwriting or by correction fluid.

13.4. Records for each batch — goods-in sheets, dispatch notes, logger files, deviation files and the returns register — are kept long enough to answer a regulator after the product has expired. Each batch file is kept for one year after the expiry date of the batch, or five years from the batch's last movement, whichever ends later. Records about the building and its equipment are kept for the life of the lease and three years after it.

13.5. Records are not taken home, not photographed on personal phones and not sent to a customer except through the customer's named quality contact.

## 10. Paper the insurer wants

10.1. A complete claim file holds: the intimation and its acknowledgement; the dispatch note and the customer's value schedule; the seal photographs and the register entries; the temperature download and, where relevant, the controller event log; photographs of the goods; the delivery receipt with any remarks written on it; the first information report where there was one; the letter to the carrier where a hired vehicle was involved; QA's disposition; the survey report or desk assessment; and the salvage account.

10.2. The complete file is sent to the insurer, through the broker, within 45 days of the date of discovery. If something is still missing at day 40, the desk sends what it has with a list of what is to follow and a date for each item.

10.3. One extension of 30 days may be asked for in writing, through the broker, before the 45 days run out. A second extension is not asked for; if the file cannot be finished in 75 days, the desk lead decides whether to abandon the claim and records why.

10.4. Copies are sent, originals are kept. Seals, damaged packaging and logger files are offered to the surveyor for inspection but are not posted to anyone.

10.5. Every document carries the TPC26 file number in its top corner, written in ink on paper copies and in the file name for scans.

## 10. Looking at ourselves

10.1. Self-inspection is how the store finds its own faults before an auditor does. It is not an audit by head office; it is the store checking itself, with someone from outside the shift holding the clipboard.

10.2. From 1 January 2026 a full walk of the store against this manual takes place once every quarter, led by someone from outside the store's own shift. The findings are graded in the same way as deviations, and each finding above minor gets a corrective action and an owner.

10.3. The walk covers every section of this manual, not only the sections that went wrong last time. The inspector reads a sample of records in each area — goods-in sheets, alarm logs, training files, the returns register — and talks to at least one person on each shift without a supervisor in the room.

10.4. The report goes to the RP and the store manager within five working days and is filed with the customer audit papers. A customer auditor may read any self-inspection report from the past three years.

10.5. An inspector never inspects an area she works in. On a site this small that sometimes means borrowing a QA officer from another Quillfern site for a day, and the cost of the borrowing is the store's, not the lender's.

## 9. Who comes to look

9.1. Large losses are inspected by an independent surveyor appointed by the insurer. Quillfern does not choose the surveyor and does not pay the surveyor's fee. Where the estimated loss is above Rs. 3 lakh, the broker asks the insurer to appoint one on the day of intimation.

9.2. Losses estimated at Rs. 3 lakh or less are assessed by the claims desk from the photographs and documents, and the file is sent to the insurer for a desk decision. The insurer may still send a surveyor to a small loss if it chooses.

9.3. Until the surveyor has seen the goods, nothing is destroyed, sold or returned to the customer unless QA rules that keeping it is a hazard. If QA does rule that, the goods are photographed in detail, a sample is kept where that is safe, and the broker is told before they go.

9.4. Surveyors usually come within 72 hours. The site manager or a named deputy meets them, shows them everything they ask for and answers their questions plainly. Nobody offers an opinion on whether the claim should be paid.

9.5. The surveyor's report goes to the insurer, not to us. The broker asks for a copy and the claims desk files it.

## Logger gaps at goods-in

The goods-in clerk accepts a gap of up to 15 minutes in an inbound vehicle's
logger record.

## 16. Keeping the file

16.1. Each claim file is kept, complete, for eight years from the date of final settlement or rejection, whichever comes later. Files involving a court case or arbitration are kept until three years after the case ends, if that is longer.

16.2. Scanned files live in the Finance document store under the TPC26 number. Paper originals are boxed by policy year and kept in the Finance archive room.

16.3. Physical evidence — seals, logger files, damaged packaging — is kept until the claim is closed, then for one more year, and is then disposed of with the desk lead's signature.

16.4. A file is never weeded to save space. If storage runs short, the desk lead asks Finance for more.

## 7. When stock goes out of range

7.1. When QA confirms an excursion, customer service sends the first notice.
The window, the channel and the signatory are those of the customer notification
matrix with the later effective date. The agent opens the matrix every time,
because the windows have changed and may change again.

7.2. The first notice uses only the wording the matrix fixes. It promises
nothing about release, replacement, credit or insurance.

7.3. A pharma critical notice is signed by the QA head or the nominated deputy.
The agent prepares it; the agent does not sign it.

7.4. The agent records every call and email to the customer in QCL-F-17,
including calls nobody answered.

7.5. After QA records a disposition, the second notice names it in the matrix's
words. If the customer asks what the disposition means for their invoice, the
agent says that the account manager will reply, and passes the question on.

7.6. Numbers in a notice are kept apart: the quantity affected, the quantity
destroyed and the quantity released are separate lines. The March 2025 vaccine
event showed what happens when one draft mixes them.

## 5. Notifications

5.1. Pharma critical stock means vaccines, insulin, and any medicine named by a
customer as patient critical. The customer must be notified within 2 hours of a
confirmed pharma critical excursion.

5.2. Dairy customers must be notified by the next scheduled customer service
check-in unless spoilage is visible, odour is present, or the temperature is
above +8.0 C. In those cases customer service must notify within 4 hours.

5.3. Frozen-food restaurant chains must receive an exception notice by the end of
the business day when the excursion is confirmed. If the vehicle is still on the
road, Fleet Control must also call the receiving kitchen.

5.4. Internal escalation for all pharma critical events goes to Compliance-Red,
the DC manager, Fleet Control if a truck is involved, and Finance if stock is
likely to be destroyed.

5.5. Customer notice must say "temperature excursion under investigation" until
QA approves a final wording. Staff must not promise release, replacement credit,
or insurance recovery in the first notice.

## 3. Who may sign

3.1. Pharma critical notices are signed by the QA head or the nominated deputy.

3.2. Dairy and frozen notices are signed by the Customer Service lead.

3.3. No DC manager signs a customer notice.

## 2. Hours and cover

2.1. The Pune desk is staffed from 07:00 to 21:00, Monday to Saturday. On
Sundays and public holidays one agent is on call from home from 07:00 to 21:00.

2.2. From 21:00 to 07:00 there is no customer service agent on duty. A customer
who calls at night reaches a recorded message giving the Fleet Control number
for vehicles on the road and the QA desk number for business hours.

2.3. At night, if a pharma critical excursion is confirmed, QA calls the
customer service lead at home so that the customer notice can be sent inside
the window. The lead's phone is on the Compliance-Red call list for that
reason.

2.4. Agents at the DCs work the DC's day shift. When a DC agent is on leave, the
Pune desk covers that DC's accounts and says so in the customer's ticket.

2.5. Leave is planned so that no account manager and their backup are away in
the same week.

## 3. Opening an account

3.1. A new customer is opened by an account manager, never by an agent. The
account manager checks the customer's product classes against what each DC can
store and move.

3.2. A customer who needs vaccines stored at Coimbatore is told plainly that
Coimbatore does not store vaccines. A customer who needs chilled dairy stored at
Coimbatore is told the same.

3.3. A customer who wants its own pricing gets a signed annex. Until the annex
is signed, the standard rate card is the only price that may be given.

3.4. The account manager sends the customer the list of named contacts on both
sides, including who will receive an excursion notice at night.

3.5. A customer who asks to be told of every alarm, not only confirmed
excursions, is told that Quillfern notifies confirmed excursions. A customer
wanting alarm-level alerts is referred to the account manager, who may arrange a
Tessaline customer view under the annex.

The pharma window moved from 2 hours to 90 minutes, and the dairy visible-spoilage
window from 4 hours to 3 hours, after the BharatVac account review of May 2026.

## 2. Wording

2.1. The first notice says "temperature excursion under investigation" and
nothing more definite. No release, replacement credit, or insurance recovery may
be promised in the first notice.

2.2. The second notice, sent after disposition, names the disposition in the
four words the SOP uses: release, conditional release, hold pending external
decision, or destroy.

2.3. New in 2026: a holding notice is sent at the 24-hour mark if the
investigation is still open, even when there is nothing new to report.

## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## Bhubaneswar satellite

- Cross-dock only. No pallet stays more than 48 hours.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

## 2. The two sites

2.1. The Visakhapatnam DC stands on a leased plot of 4.2 acres in the Atchutapuram industrial area, south-west of the city, about 18 km by road from the port's outer gate. The building is a new pre-engineered shed with a cold block, a frozen block, a small controlled-room-temperature store, a dispatch canopy and a two-storey office.

2.2. The satellite at Bhubaneswar is a smaller leased unit in the Mancheswar industrial estate. It has two chilled docks, two frozen docks, a staging hall held at +4 C and a site office. It is a cross-dock, not a store.

2.3. The two sites are about 440 km apart by the coastal highway. A nightly trunk run links them.

2.4. The DC is the region's centre: its manager is the senior manager in the region, its QA lead covers both sites, and its engineering team maintains the satellite's plant.

2.5. Both leases run for fifteen years with a right to renew. The landlord at Atchutapuram built the shell to our drawings; the fit-out, racking and refrigeration belong to Quillfern.

## 18. Things left out on purpose

18.1. The satellite does not store medicines and does not unload them. Pharma stock for Odisha customers either travels direct from the DC in a sealed vehicle that passes through the satellite's yard without opening, or is delivered by the DC's own vehicle. No passive shipper, no cross-dock exception and no customer's urgency changes this.

18.2. The region does not handle live seafood, fresh fish on ice or any product that is not packed and labelled.

18.3. The region does not offer customs clearance as a service. The exporter's own agent clears its goods; we provide the space and the supervision of stuffing.

18.4. The DC does not open a retail counter or sell surplus stock locally.

## 9. Wood in, wood out

9.1. Pallets at the site are exchanged one for one. A trailer that brings in
twenty-two loaded pallets takes away twenty-two empty ones, so that neither side
ends up holding the other's wood.

9.2. Pallets are counted at the dock when a trailer is unloaded and again when
the empties are loaded. Both counts go on the pallet sheet and are signed by the
driver and the shift lead.

9.3. Every pallet handed in is looked at on the dock by the shift lead: split
boards, cracked blocks and missing nails are the usual faults. Each one that cannot carry a load is billed back at Rs. 450 to whoever delivered it.

9.4. Damaged pallets are stacked by the south fence for the repairer, who
collects on the first and third Fridays of each month. Repaired pallets come
back into the exchange pool; pallets that cannot be repaired are sold as scrap.

9.5. A driver who disputes a damaged-pallet count photographs the pallet before
leaving, and the office reviews the photograph against the shift lead's note.

9.6. Pallets are never used as dunnage in a van, never burned on site and never
given away, however broken.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 5. Equipment that has to prove itself

5.1. Every piece of equipment that touches product temperature is qualified before use: the two walk-in chambers, the CRT air-conditioning, the generator and its changeover, and the alarm panel. Qualification means a written test, run by people who did not install the equipment, against acceptance criteria written before the test began.

5.2. The walk-ins are requalified on a fixed cycle, and the cycle was shortened after the compressor failure of November 2025, when WIC-2 ran for nine days on a hired compressor whose behaviour nobody had measured. A full temperature study of each chamber is now repeated every 12 months, and also within 30 days after any compressor, evaporator or door is replaced. The study follows the company mapping method, and the result goes to the RP, who decides whether the chamber may keep holding stock.

5.3. The generator is load-tested on the first Monday of each month by pulling the incoming supply. The changeover must complete before any chamber logger records a rise of more than 1 C, and the technician writes the time it took in his log.

5.4. The alarm panel is tested every Friday. A panel that fails its test is taken out of service and the shift QA officer reads every logger by hand each hour until it is repaired.

5.5. Equipment that fails any test carries a yellow card until it passes again, and the RP is told the same shift. A yellow-carded chamber may keep stock only on the RP's written decision.

## 7. When one goes missing

7.1. A lost or stolen scanner is reported to the IT desk within one hour of being missed, by the user or the shift lead, with the asset number and where it was last seen.

7.2. The desk locks the device from Fernguard as soon as the report arrives. A locked K7 shows a message asking the finder to hand it to security.

7.3. If it has not turned up 24 hours after the report, Fernguard wipes it remotely and it is struck off the register. A device found after it has been wiped goes back to the desk to be rebuilt; it is never simply switched back on.

7.4. Losing a device is not in itself a disciplinary matter. Failing to report a loss, or reporting it late, is.

7.5. A theft is also reported to security and, where the site manager decides, to the police. The report number is written in the register.

## 14. Layout and labelling of the store

14.1. The Nagpur store is laid out in four zones: numbered stock in the locked
cage, instruments on the shelf beside the QA hatch, protective equipment on the
open racks, and general consumables at the back.

14.2. Every shelf carries a printed label with the item name, the Stores item
code and the minimum stock. A handwritten label is replaced within a week.

14.3. Heavy items are stored below waist height. Nothing is stored on top of the
cage or on the floor of the walkway.

14.4. The store floor is swept daily and the racks are dusted monthly. Wet items
are never brought into the store; they are dried outside first.

14.5. The Guwahati and Coimbatore cages follow the same labels and item codes as
Nagpur, so that a count sheet from any site reads the same way.

## 15. Repairs

15.1. All repairs go through the IT desk. The desk keeps a small stock of spare K7s and LP-40s at each site, so that a repair never leaves a rack short.

15.2. Devices are sent to the Korvex service centre in a padded case with a repair note. Nobody opens a device on site.

15.3. A repaired device is rebuilt from Fernguard before it is reissued.

15.4. A device that has been repaired three times in a year is retired.

15.5. The desk reports device faults by type every quarter to the site managers, so that a site whose scanners keep breaking can look at how they are used.

15.6. Repair costs are charged to the site's cost centre. A site that pays for many repairs is not punished for it; it is asked what is going on.

## 20. Transfers between sites

20.1. Stock sent from Nagpur to Guwahati or Coimbatore travels with a Stores
transfer note on QCL-F-45, listing every item and quantity. The receiving cage
counts the parcel on arrival and signs the note.

20.2. A short or damaged transfer is written on the note and photographed before
the parcel is signed for. The courier is told the same day.

20.3. Numbered stock and made-up red sleeve packets travel in sealed courier
bags. The bag number is written on the transfer note.

20.4. Items are never transferred between sites in a driver's cab, even when a
vehicle happens to be going that way, unless the item is on the dispatch note.

20.5. The signed transfer notes come back to Nagpur by scan the same day and by
post at the month end.

## 11. Write-off and disposal

11.1. Stores writes off an item only with Finance's approval, recorded on the
write-off sheet.

11.2. Broken instruments are written off after QA has confirmed they cannot be
calibrated. Their serials are struck off the instrument list.

11.3. Damaged seal books are never thrown away. Every seal in them is written
VOID and kept with the stubs until the next audit.

11.4. Protective equipment that is worn out is cut before disposal, so that it
cannot be picked out of the bin and worn again.

## 22. Energy and waste in the store

22.1. The store lights are on a timer and go off at 19:30. The storekeeper
closing the store checks that the cage, the flammables cabinet and the emergency
cupboard are locked before the lights go off.

22.2. Packaging from deliveries is flattened and sent to the scrap area on the
day it arrives. The store is not a place to keep empty boxes.

22.3. Used toner cartridges are returned to the toner supplier for recycling.

22.4. Stores reports its waste once a year to the Nagpur DC manager, by type and
weight, for the site's environmental return.

answer_text:
## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## 5. The calendar starts

5.1. The date of discovery is the first day on which anybody at Quillfern knew, or should have known, that goods had been lost or damaged. It is usually the delivery day, but not always: a shortage found at a quarterly count may be discovered weeks after the trip.

5.2. The site manager tells the claims desk on the day of discovery, by e-mail with the photographs attached. A phone call is welcome but is followed by the e-mail.

5.3. The claims desk sends written intimation to the insurer, through the broker, within seven days of the date of discovery. Intimation means a written notice that names the policy, the dispatch note, the place, the date and the nature of the loss, with an estimate if one is known. It is sent whether or not the claim looks large enough to be worth making, and whether or not the facts are yet clear. A call to Ashok Menon is not intimation.

5.4. Late intimation is the commonest reason insurers refuse a claim. In 2024 the company lost a claim of Rs. 4.6 lakh because a site waited for the customer's own figures before telling anyone. The rule now is to tell early and correct later.

5.5. The claims desk opens a claim file the same day it receives the site manager's e-mail. Each file has a number in the series TPC26-nnn, and the number goes on every later document.

## 8. Heavy days on the road

8.1. The insurer's exposure on any single vehicle is capped. The most it will pay for all goods on one vehicle on one trip is Rs. 1.2 crore, however many consignments are on board.

8.2. A full vaccine load easily goes past that figure, and so does a frozen load of premium seafood. Any dispatch whose total declared value on one vehicle is above Rs. 1.2 crore is declared to the broker in writing at least 48 hours before the vehicle leaves. The broker then gets the insurer's agreement to a higher figure for that trip, or tells us to split the load.

8.3. Fleet planners check the declared value of every pharma critical and every high-value frozen load when they build the week's plan, and send the list of trips over the figure to the claims desk on Thursday.

8.4. A trip that goes over the figure without a declaration is still covered up to Rs. 1.2 crore. Anything above that is uninsured, and the site manager who allowed the load explains why in writing.

8.5. Splitting a load costs a second vehicle and a second crew. Planners should prefer splitting to asking for a higher figure only where the second vehicle is already on the road; the broker's higher figure usually costs less than an empty run.

## 8. Claims

8.1. A customer claim for damaged or lost stock is accepted in writing only,
from a named contact on the account.

8.2. A claim is registered only when it arrives within 30 days of delivery and
carries photographs of the stock and the seal taken at delivery.

8.3. The agent registers the claim, acknowledges it within one working day, and
passes it to the account manager. The agent does not give an opinion on it.

8.4. Stock value in a claim is taken from the Finance schedule. A value in the
customer's email is recorded as the declared value and nothing more.

8.5. A claim that turns on a temperature record waits for QA's investigation.
The customer is told it is waiting, and given the investigation's reference.

8.6. Claims for trips before 18 August 2025 quote the KLP trip number, not a TSL
one.

## 16. Month-end reporting

16.1. On the third working day of each month, the customer service lead sends
Finance and the account managers a report of the month's tickets by account:
bookings, late vehicles, complaints, credit notes raised and notices sent.

16.2. Each account manager reviews the report for their accounts and writes one
line per account on anything unusual. The lines are sent back to the lead within
two working days.

16.3. The report is not sent to customers as it stands. A customer who wants a
monthly service report gets one written for them by the account manager, from
the same figures.

16.4. Figures in the report come from the customer service system. An agent who
knows a figure is wrong corrects the ticket, not the report.

16.5. The BharatVac and Manjara Dairy accounts get a quarterly review meeting in
addition to the month-end report, held by their account managers with Finance
and QA.

## 12. Customer loggers

12.1. Some customers send their own logger with the stock. The logger travels
with the stock from the moment it arrives until it leaves.

12.2. A customer logger does not overrule the Tessaline record. If the customer
quotes their logger in an argument, the agent says that QA will compare the two
files and explain any difference.

12.3. A customer logger sent back to the customer goes with the return challan,
never by separate post.

12.4. The agent never downloads or opens a customer logger. That is QA's work.

## 10. On live units

10.1. On a live unit — a working reefer, a cold room with stock in it, a customer's freezer — an apprentice is never the only pair of hands. Live means anything holding product or able to start without warning, and it is the real kit apprentices are here to learn on.

10.2. One qualified technician supervises at most three apprentices on live equipment. On a pharma chamber the ratio is one to one.

10.3. Night work is part of the job later, not at first. No apprentice is put on a night roster before month nine, even with a supervisor. From month nine an apprentice may be rostered at night with a qualified technician on the same job.

10.4. Apprentices never isolate, lock out or restore power on their own until they have passed the electrical module, and never on a pharma chamber during the programme.

10.5. An apprentice who is asked to do something on a live unit that this curriculum forbids says no, and tells the mentor the same day. Saying no is never held against the apprentice.

## 12. Kit

12.1. Each apprentice is issued a personal tool kit in the first week: gauges and hoses, a multimeter, a clamp meter, a set of hand tools, a temperature probe, a torch and a tool bag. The kit is engraved with the apprentice's number.

12.2. Trainees often ask whether they get to keep the tools when they finish. The kit, worth about Rs. 22,000, becomes the apprentice's own property on completion; a leaver before completion hands it back.

12.3. A tool lost or broken through ordinary use is replaced by the workshop. A tool lost through carelessness is replaced once without charge; a second loss is discussed with the workshop lead.

12.4. Safety gear — boots, gloves, glasses, a freezer jacket and a helmet — is issued separately and is replaced whenever it wears out.

12.5. Apprentices do not lend their kit to anyone, including qualified technicians on site.

## 5. Equipment that has to prove itself

5.1. Every piece of equipment that touches product temperature is qualified before use: the two walk-in chambers, the CRT air-conditioning, the generator and its changeover, and the alarm panel. Qualification means a written test, run by people who did not install the equipment, against acceptance criteria written before the test began.

5.2. The walk-ins are requalified on a fixed cycle, and the cycle was shortened after the compressor failure of November 2025, when WIC-2 ran for nine days on a hired compressor whose behaviour nobody had measured. A full temperature study of each chamber is now repeated every 12 months, and also within 30 days after any compressor, evaporator or door is replaced. The study follows the company mapping method, and the result goes to the RP, who decides whether the chamber may keep holding stock.

5.3. The generator is load-tested on the first Monday of each month by pulling the incoming supply. The changeover must complete before any chamber logger records a rise of more than 1 C, and the technician writes the time it took in his log.

5.4. The alarm panel is tested every Friday. A panel that fails its test is taken out of service and the shift QA officer reads every logger by hand each hour until it is repaired.

5.5. Equipment that fails any test carries a yellow card until it passes again, and the RP is told the same shift. A yellow-carded chamber may keep stock only on the RP's written decision.

## On live units

One qualified technician supervises up to four apprentices on live equipment.
Apprentices may join night work from month six.

## 11. Mentors

11.1. Each apprentice placed at a site has a named mentor, a qualified technician who has volunteered and been trained for the role.

11.2. The mentor signs the logbook each week, meets the apprentice for half an hour each fortnight to go through it, and reports to the workshop once a month.

11.3. Mentors receive an allowance for each apprentice they mentor, paid with their salary.

11.4. A mentor may have no more than two apprentices at a time.

11.5. An apprentice who has a problem with a mentor speaks to the workshop lead, who may change the mentor without asking for a reason.

The programme lasts 24 months. One intake of 10 apprentices joins each January.

## 3. Swab check

3.1. Three swabs: floor front, floor rear, door gasket.

3.2. Each must read 150 or below on the handheld luminometer. One failed swab means the whole washdown is repeated, not just the failed spot.

# Reefer Body Washdown and Sanitation Procedure

## 1. When a washdown is required

1.1. After any dairy spill in the body, before the next load.

1.2. Before a chilled body carries pharma critical stock after any food load.

1.3. Every 14 days for a body on dairy rotation, whether or not anything spilled.

1.4. After any load rejected by a customer for odour.

## 6. After the washdown

6.1. A washed body is not loaded until it has been chilled again from empty; the dispatch checklist for the load sets how long.
