## 7. Goods arriving

7.1. A vehicle arriving at the store is checked before it is opened: the seal number against the paperwork, the condition of the doors and the reefer's display. The driver stays with the vehicle until goods-in has finished with it, and is offered the drivers' room, not the canteen.

7.2. Every inbound vehicle's temperature printout or download is read at the goods-in desk before a single pallet crosses the threshold. Drivers call any missing stretch a "hole" in the printout, and holes are common on loads that come round the Ahmedabad ring road, where some older reefers lose their logger signal. A break of up to ten minutes in the record may be accepted by the goods-in clerk; anything longer goes to the Responsible Person, who decides. A record that is in range throughout but shows the reefer door opening during the journey is also referred to her.

7.3. Pallets are checked against the advance notice by batch and quantity. A batch that does not match the notice is received into quarantine rather than refused at the door, so that the customer's stock is protected while the paperwork is put right.

7.4. Goods-in photographs every pallet label before the stretch wrap is cut. The photographs are filed against the receipt, not kept on the camera.

7.5. Nothing is received between 22:00 and 06:00. A vehicle that arrives at night waits outside the estate gate on its own power, and its record for the waiting hours is read together with the journey.

# Pharma Store Quality Manual, West Zone

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. The store at Changodar, on the south-west edge of Ahmedabad, is the first Quillfern building that holds medicines and nothing else. It opened in September 2025 in a leased shed inside a pharmaceutical estate off the Sarkhej–Bavla highway. From its first week its customers — two vaccine makers, a biologics firm and three hospital groups in Gujarat — asked for a written quality system they could audit against. This manual is that system. It says how the store keeps product fit for the patient, how it proves that it did so, and who answers when it did not.

1.2. It is written for the people who work in the building: receiving clerks, pickers, dispatch staff, the shift QA officers, the engineering technician and the store manager. It is also written for auditors, who will read it more carefully than anyone on the floor and who should be able to find, somewhere in it, the reason for every record the store keeps.

1.3. Where this manual and a company-wide procedure disagree about a temperature limit, a notification window or a quarantine rule, the company procedure applies and this manual is corrected at its next revision. The manual sets no temperature limit of its own; it says how those limits are kept in this building, by these people.

1.4. Revision 3 is in force from 11/05/2026. The summaries written while the store was being fitted out are withdrawn and kept only as history. Earlier revisions of this manual are withdrawn from the shared drive on the day a new one is issued.

## 1. What Stores does

1.1. Stores buys nothing on its own authority. It raises a request against a
purchase order that Finance has approved, receives the goods, holds them, issues
them against a signature and counts them.

1.2. The Nagpur main store keeps the stock for Nagpur and sends stock to
Guwahati and Coimbatore by courier or on a scheduled vehicle. The Guwahati and
Coimbatore cages hold only what their DC uses in about a month.

1.3. Every item issued is signed for by the person who takes it. An item that
leaves Stores without a signature is counted as lost at the next count.

1.4. Stores does not lend. An item taken for a job is either used, returned or
written off, and each of those is recorded.

## 4. Seal books

4.1. Seals come from the seal manufacturer in books, already numbered in order.
Stores records the first and last number of each book received.

4.2. Stores issues seal books to a DC gate one book at a time against the gate's
signature. Besides the book open at the gate, a gate may hold at most two
unopened books in its locked drawer; a third is not issued until one of the two
is opened.

4.3. Spoiled seals marked VOID come back to Stores with their stubs. Stores
counts the stubs against QCL-F-35 every Friday, and a number that is neither
fitted, spoiled nor on the shelf is reported to Fleet Control the same day.

4.4. Each DC holds two bolt-seal cutters, and a lost cutter is replaced by Stores
within one working day.

4.5. Tamper labels for pharma pallets and shipper lids are issued in rolls of
200 to QA, not to the gate.

4.6. Seal books for Guwahati and Coimbatore go by courier, two books at a time,
and are signed for at the gate cabin on arrival.

## 17. Handover between storekeepers

17.1. A storekeeper going on leave for more than two days hands over to the
other storekeeper with a walk round the cage and a signed note of open requests,
expected deliveries and any count differences not yet closed.

17.2. The keys to the cage are signed over in the key book at the handover, with
the time.

17.3. Nalini Patil's own leave is covered by the Nagpur DC manager's nominee, who
signs the key book and the handover note like anyone else.

## 3. Receiving goods

3.1. Goods are received against the purchase order and the delivery note, and
counted before the delivery note is signed. A short delivery is written as short
on the delivery note in front of the supplier's driver.

3.2. Temperature-sensitive consumables, such as conditioned gel packs, are not
received by Stores. They go directly to the QA room.

3.3. Calibrated instruments are received by Stores and passed unopened to the QA
bench on the same day. Stores does not open an instrument box to check it.

3.4. Damaged goods are photographed, set aside and reported to Finance before the
supplier's driver leaves, where that is possible.

## 11. Write-off and disposal

11.1. Stores writes off an item only with Finance's approval, recorded on the
write-off sheet.

11.2. Broken instruments are written off after QA has confirmed they cannot be
calibrated. Their serials are struck off the instrument list.

11.3. Damaged seal books are never thrown away. Every seal in them is written
VOID and kept with the stubs until the next audit.

11.4. Protective equipment that is worn out is cut before disposal, so that it
cannot be picked out of the bin and worn again.

# Quarantine Stock Release and Return Procedure

How stock leaves quarantine bays Q-3 (Nagpur), Q-G2 (Guwahati) and Q-C1 (Coimbatore) after QA has recorded a disposition under clause 6.5 of the [Temperature Excursion Response SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md). Destroyed stock does not leave by this procedure; section 7 of that SOP governs it.

## 17. Weather and the seasons

17.1. From June to September the monsoon closes ghat sections and floods low
roads on the Nagpur lanes. Fleet Control reads the weather warnings every
morning and every evening and marks any lane under a red warning on the board.

17.2. A vehicle is not dispatched into a red-warning area unless the customer's
stock cannot wait and the Fleet head has agreed in writing. A late delivery is a
customer problem; a vehicle in a flooded underpass is a Quillfern one.

17.3. Fog on the Nashik and Sinnar roads in December and January slows every run.
Planners add time to those runs in the plan rather than asking drivers to make it
up.

17.4. In April and May the midday heat on the Vidarbha roads is hard on drivers
as well as on reefer units. Planners avoid midday departures on long runs in
those months where the customer's window allows, and every cab carries drinking
water.

17.5. After any storm, drivers report fallen trees, washed-out roads and closed
bridges to Fleet Control, which passes them to the other drivers on the same
lane.

17.6. Guwahati's monsoon runs from June to September and Coimbatore's heavy rain
comes from October to December. Fleet Control plans each DC's runs by its own
season, not by the Nagpur calendar.

## 3. How long stock may sit

3.1. Quarantine Dwell Limit (QDL) is the time stock may stay in quarantine after the excursion is confirmed before the account manager must escalate to the customer's quality head.

| product class | QDL |
|---|---|
| pharma critical | 72 hours |

## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## 8. When the grid drops

8.1. The site has two gensets on a common panel. They start automatically when
grid power fails and carry FC-A, the cell, the plant room and the apron lights.
The canteen and the office air conditioning are not on the genset panel.

8.2. The gensets are test-run under load every Thursday at 10:00 for twenty
minutes. The run time, the oil level and any alarm on the panel are written in
the genset log.

8.3. The gensets share one day tank and one bulk tank. The tank is never allowed below 1,500 litres; the night lead dips it at 22:00 and orders a top-up from the listed bowser at 2,500.

8.4. During a long outage the night lead dips the tank every four hours and
writes each reading in the log. A bowser that does not arrive within four hours
of an order is chased by the site manager, not by the night lead.

8.5. Nobody refuels a genset while it is running. Fuel spills are covered with
the sand from the bin beside the tank and reported the same shift.

8.6. After the grid returns, the gensets run on for ten minutes before they are
shut down, and the panel is checked for any alarm that was raised during the
outage.

| product class | QDL |
|---|---|
| dairy | 12 hours |

3.2. Reaching the QDL does not release anything. It starts an escalation; the stock stays where it is.

# Temperature Excursion Response SOP

## 1. Purpose

1.1. This procedure defines the response to any suspected or confirmed temperature
excursion in Quillfern Cold Logistics Pvt. Ltd. warehouses, docks, cross-dock
lanes, owned reefer trucks and hired trucks working under Quillfern dispatch.
The procedure applies to vaccines, insulin, chilled dairy, paneer, frozen food,
and any customer stock moved under a written temperature commitment.

1.2. The purpose is to protect patient safety, food safety, customer evidence,
and the company record. A fast release is never preferred over a complete
temperature history. Staff must treat a missing record as a quality event until
QA closes it.

1.3. "Excursion" means a recorded temperature outside the allowed range for
longer than the allowed duration. A single hand-held thermometer reading is not
enough to release product after a breach; it may be used only to start immediate
containment while the logger history is retrieved.

## 5. Notifications

5.1. Pharma critical stock means vaccines, insulin, and any medicine named by a
customer as patient critical. The customer must be notified within 2 hours of a
confirmed pharma critical excursion.

5.2. Dairy customers must be notified by the next scheduled customer service
check-in unless spoilage is visible, odour is present, or the temperature is
above +8.0 C. In those cases customer service must notify within 4 hours.

5.3. Frozen-food restaurant chains must receive an exception notice by the end of
the business day when the excursion is confirmed. If the vehicle is still on the
road, Fleet Control must also call the receiving kitchen.

5.4. Internal escalation for all pharma critical events goes to Compliance-Red,
the DC manager, Fleet Control if a truck is involved, and Finance if stock is
likely to be destroyed.

5.5. Customer notice must say "temperature excursion under investigation" until
QA approves a final wording. Staff must not promise release, replacement credit,
or insurance recovery in the first notice.

## 9. Sensor problems

9.1. If a sensor is suspected to be wrong, staff shall place a calibrated spare
logger next to the product, keep the original sensor in place, and call the DC
manager. Removing or covering the original sensor is prohibited.

9.2. A Tessaline alarm may be acknowledged in the application after containment
has started. Acknowledging an alarm is not the same as closing an excursion.

9.3. A truck or room with repeated false alarms must be marked for maintenance,
but the temperature record remains part of the investigation until QA rejects it
in writing.

9.4. Sensor configuration changes must be requested through QA and IT together.
No DC staff may change threshold values directly in Tessaline.

## 3. Planning a week of duty

3.1. Planners build the week's duty on Thursday for the following Monday to
Sunday. Each driver's weekly rest is placed first, then night segments, then
day runs.

3.2. The limits the plan must respect are in the Driver Hours and Road Safety
Policy. A plan that meets them only if nothing goes wrong does not meet them.

3.3. A lane with a qualification record is planned with that record open, so
that its relief point, its pre-cool hold time and any two-driver condition are
on the plan and not in someone's memory.

3.4. Festival shuttle rosters with split rest are planned only after the Fleet
head has approved the roster in writing, and only for the festival named.

3.5. The plan is published to drivers by Friday noon. A driver who sees a
problem with his week tells Fleet Control on Friday, not on the morning of the
run.

3.6. Leave requests go to the planner by the 20th of the previous month. Late
leave is granted where cover exists, and cover is never found by stretching
another driver's hours.

## 9. Protective equipment

9.1. Stores issues cryogenic gloves, face shields, freezer suits, safety shoes,
high-visibility vests and hearing protection against a signature.

9.2. Freezer suits are issued to named people, not to a shift. A suit that no
longer closes properly is returned and replaced.

9.3. Cryogenic gloves and face shields for dry-ice work are not personal issue.
They hang on the rack beside each chest and are replaced by Stores when damaged.

9.4. Safety shoes are replaced once a year, or sooner if the sole is split.

9.5. Hired-truck drivers are issued a high-visibility vest at the gate and return
it at the gate.

## 11. Write-off and disposal

11.1. Stores writes off an item only with Finance's approval, recorded on the
write-off sheet.

11.2. Broken instruments are written off after QA has confirmed they cannot be
calibrated. Their serials are struck off the instrument list.

11.3. Damaged seal books are never thrown away. Every seal in them is written
VOID and kept with the stubs until the next audit.

11.4. Protective equipment that is worn out is cut before disposal, so that it
cannot be picked out of the bin and worn again.

## Appendix A: local contacts

At Nagpur, the DC manager is Farhan Qureshi and the night shift escalation lead
is Bunty Chauhan. At Guwahati, the nominated escalation contact is Riniki
Bora. At Coimbatore, the nominated escalation contact is S. Venkatesan.

During business hours, QA desk extension 440 answers routine excursion queries.
During night shift, the shift lead opens the event and calls Compliance-Red for
pharma critical stock. A new driver who sees a reefer alarm must call Fleet
Control first and must not wait until reaching the destination.

## 5. Diesel, cards and the reefer tank

5.1. Every owned reefer carries one fuel card for the truck and one for the
reefer unit, in separate sleeves. The two are billed to different cost centres
and must not be swapped.

5.2. Drivers fill only at Quillfern-listed pumps. The list is printed on the
back of the cab card and updated each quarter by Fleet Control.

5.3. A reefer unit whose fuel falls below one quarter is filled at the next
listed pump before any other stop, including a customer drop.

5.4. The truck's own tank follows the dispatch checklist at departure and is
otherwise the driver's judgement, with the rule that no vehicle is allowed to
run so low that it must stop somewhere unlit.

5.5. Fuel slips are photographed at the pump and the photograph is sent to
Fleet Control while parked. The paper slip goes into the trip bag.

5.6. A card that is refused at a listed pump is reported to Fleet Control, and
the driver waits for Fleet Control to authorise a payment. Drivers do not pay
for diesel from their own money.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

# Reefer asset file RF-119

Asset **RF-119** is an owned chilled reefer based at Guwahati DC. It was bought
in the same 2021 batch as [RF-118](16-reefer-RF-118-asset-file.md) but it is a
smaller single-compartment body and it is not a pharma asset. Fleet Control has
twice received a Nagpur pharma booking on RF-119 that was meant for RF-118, so

# Reefer asset file RF-117 (retired)

**RF-117** was an owned chilled reefer based at Nagpur DC from April 2016 until
it was retired on 10 September 2024. This file is kept for audit history only.
**Do not book RF-117.** The asset number still appears on 2016 to 2024 dispatch
notes, customer claim files and Kalpa trip exports, which is the only reason the
file survives.

RF-117 was replaced on the Nagpur chilled roster by
[RF-118](../16-reefer-RF-118-asset-file.md). They are different vehicles. A
claim, a challan or an audit query naming RF-117 concerns a vehicle that has not
moved Quillfern stock since 2024.

## 6. Who may use one

6.1. A K7 may be used only by a person with a login issued by the IT desk. Logins are personal; a shift lead does not sign in for a picker so the picker can start sooner.

6.2. Contract and agency workers do not get permanent logins. Agency staff on the scanners are some of the busiest users on a peak night, and each one is given a temporary sign-in for the shift at the shift lead's request to the desk. The desk issues them a day credential that stops working twelve hours after it is first used. A new one is issued for each shift worked.

6.3. Personal phones are a separate matter. Many staff would rather scan with their own phone than walk to the rack, and on the pilot some did. No personal phone may run the scanning app or hold a Quillfern login, even for one shift when a K7 has failed; the user takes a spare from the cradle rack or waits.

6.4. Customer staff and auditors may look at a K7's screen with a Quillfern user beside them. They do not operate it.

6.5. Trainees from the Waluj workshop use a K7 only with their trainer's login running, and only for the exercises in their module.

## 16. Leaving Quillfern

16.1. Leavers hand back every device, battery and charger issued to them by name, and the shift lead signs the asset register to show it was received. HR does not issue the leaving papers until the register is signed.

16.2. Sometimes a person who quits keeps their scanner, by accident or otherwise. Anything not returned within two working days of the last shift is recovered from the final settlement at Rs. 18,500 per K7 and Rs. 6,200 per LP-40. The device is then locked and wiped from Fernguard.

16.3. A device returned after the recovery is made is refunded at the same rate, less any repair cost.

16.4. Agency staff never hold a named device, so nothing is recovered from their agencies; their day credentials simply lapse.

16.5. Trainees who leave the Waluj programme early hand their device back to the trainer the same day.

## 9. Overnight

9.1. Software and app updates are pushed from Fernguard to docked devices only, so that nobody's scanner restarts in the middle of a pick. New software is tested on four devices at the Waluj workshop first.

9.2. The push window is Tuesday night, 01:00 to 03:00, and a K7 that is not in its cradle then is updated the following Tuesday. A device that has missed two windows is called in by the desk.

9.3. Urgent security updates may be pushed outside the window. The desk warns the shift leads first, and the update waits for the device to be docked.

9.4. Nobody updates a K7 by hand, from a memory card or from a cable.

9.5. Sites that work through Tuesday night arrange their docking so that each rack is full for at least an hour inside the window.

## 3. Who answers for what

3.1. The RP answers to the licensing authority as well as to Quillfern. She may stop any dispatch at any hour without giving a reason first; the reason is written up within the shift.

3.2. Shift QA officers work under the RP. One is on duty on each of the two shifts, 06:00 to 14:00 and 14:00 to 22:00. Between 22:00 and 06:00 the store neither receives nor dispatches except under a written plan the RP has approved, and the night is covered by the security contractor and the RP's phone.

3.3. The engineering technician, Irfan Ghanchi, looks after the chambers, the generator, the alarm panel and the loggers. He keeps his own maintenance log. He does not decide whether stock affected by an equipment fault is usable; he reports the fault and the QA officer decides what happens to the stock.

3.4. The store manager decides staffing, slots and vehicles. He may ask QA to hurry; he may not ask QA to agree. Where any two of these people disagree about whether stock may move, it does not move until the RP has decided.

3.5. Each role has a named deputy, listed on the board outside the QA office. A deputy acts with the full authority of the role while the holder is away, and signs in the deputy's own name, never the holder's.

## 3. Issue and sign-out

3.1. A K7 is issued either to a named person, for staff who use one every shift, or to a cradle rack, for shared use. Named issue is signed for in the asset register; rack issue is signed for by the shift lead at the start of each shift.

3.2. A named K7 is not lent to anyone else, even for a minute. A colleague who needs one takes a spare from the rack.

3.3. LP-40 printers are always issued to a rack, never to a person.

3.4. Contract and agency staff never hold a named K7.

3.5. At each shift change the outgoing shift lead counts the rack against the register, and the incoming shift lead signs for the count. A device missing at the count is reported under section 7 straight away, not at the end of the next shift.

## 13. Documents

13.1. The store's procedures, forms and records live in the document system. Only the version in the system is current, and each procedure shows its revision number and effective date on every page.

13.2. Paper copies of procedures are a convenience, not a source: they are useful at the goods-in desk and in the anteroom, where nobody wants to read a screen with gloves on. A copy printed from the document system is valid only until midnight of the day printed, which the printer stamps in the footer. A paper copy found after that is put in the confidential bin, whatever revision number it carries.

13.3. Records are made at the time, in ink or in the system, and corrected by striking through and initialling, never by overwriting or by correction fluid.

13.4. Records for each batch — goods-in sheets, dispatch notes, logger files, deviation files and the returns register — are kept long enough to answer a regulator after the product has expired. Each batch file is kept for one year after the expiry date of the batch, or five years from the batch's last movement, whichever ends later. Records about the building and its equipment are kept for the life of the lease and three years after it.

13.5. Records are not taken home, not photographed on personal phones and not sent to a customer except through the customer's named quality contact.

## 1. The site at a glance

1.1. Coimbatore DC is the smallest of the three distribution centres and the
only one south of the Deccan. It serves insulin customers across western Tamil
Nadu and the Kerala border districts, restaurant chains in Coimbatore, Tiruppur
and Erode, and a small dry-grocery account that pays for the east gate to stay
open.

1.2. The building is a single-storey shed on a raised plinth. The cold block
sits on the north side, the dry block on the south side, and the office, canteen
and lockers are in the two-storey annexe at the east end. The wash pad and the
open-sided store shed are inside the south gate, on the left as a vehicle
enters.

1.3. There is no rail siding, no mezzanine and no second floor in the cold
block. Everything moves on pallet trucks and two electric forklifts, FL-C1 and
FL-C2. FL-C2 is the only forklift rated for the cold block floor.

1.4. The site works two shifts, 06:00 to 14:00 and 14:00 to 22:00, with a
security-only night from 22:00 to 06:00. Night receipts of pharma critical stock
are not planned at Coimbatore; a vehicle that arrives at night waits outside the
south gate for the 06:00 shift unless the DC manager has approved a night
receipt in writing.

1.5. The site was opened in 2019 in a leased building. The lease is renewed in
five-year blocks, which is why some fixtures, including the canteen extractor
fan and the annexe stairs, belong to the landlord and are repaired through him.

## 8. Heavy days on the road

8.1. The insurer's exposure on any single vehicle is capped. The most it will pay for all goods on one vehicle on one trip is Rs. 1.2 crore, however many consignments are on board.

8.2. A full vaccine load easily goes past that figure, and so does a frozen load of premium seafood. Any dispatch whose total declared value on one vehicle is above Rs. 1.2 crore is declared to the broker in writing at least 48 hours before the vehicle leaves. The broker then gets the insurer's agreement to a higher figure for that trip, or tells us to split the load.

8.3. Fleet planners check the declared value of every pharma critical and every high-value frozen load when they build the week's plan, and send the list of trips over the figure to the claims desk on Thursday.

8.4. A trip that goes over the figure without a declaration is still covered up to Rs. 1.2 crore. Anything above that is uninsured, and the site manager who allowed the load explains why in writing.

8.5. Splitting a load costs a second vehicle and a second crew. Planners should prefer splitting to asking for a higher figure only where the second vehicle is already on the road; the broker's higher figure usually costs less than an empty run.

## 6. What stays with us

6.1. Every claim under TPC carries a deductible: a part of each loss that Quillfern bears itself before the insurer pays anything. For 2026–27 the deductible is Rs. 40,000 per consignment. On a loss of Rs. 30,000 the insurer pays nothing; on a loss of Rs. 1,00,000 it pays Rs. 60,000.

6.2. A consignment is one dispatch note. Three pallets on one note make one consignment and carry one deductible. Three notes on one vehicle make three consignments, and each note's loss carries its own deductible.

6.3. Finance books the deductible to the cost centre of the site where the loss happened, or the fleet cost centre where the loss happened on the road. Sites are told their deductible total every quarter.

6.4. Losses below the deductible are still intimated and still recorded. The insurer prices next year's cover on the whole loss record, not only on what it paid, and a record full of gaps is priced as if the gaps were bad news.

6.5. Customers are never told the deductible figure. It is a term of our cover, not of their contract, and quoting it invites an argument about who should bear it.

## Per-vehicle limit

The insurer pays at most Rs. 80 lakh for one vehicle on one trip.

# Coimbatore DC site handbook

Everything that is particular to Coimbatore DC, in one place. Company-wide rules
still come from their own documents: temperature limits and excursions from
QCL-QA-SOP-17, dock booking from QCL-OPS-DOCK-03, driver hours from the Driver
Hours and Road Safety Policy. Where this handbook and a company-wide rule seem
to differ, ask the DC manager before acting, and do not assume the handbook
wins. What follows is how those rules are carried out on this site, with this
building, these people and this weather.

Summary of our Transit Protection Cover for the policy year 1 April 2025 to

## 13. Language and new people

13.1. Coimbatore works in Tamil. Training is given by a trainer in Tamil, with
English slides available but never used instead of a trainer.

13.2. New joiners spend their first week on the morning shift only. They are not
put on the late shift, and never left alone in the cold block, until a shift
lead has signed them off.

13.3. Every new joiner is shown the gate cabin, the security roster and the key
register on the first day. They are told that security will not open anything
for them at night except in an emergency, and that the lockers, the cabinet and
the seal drawer are all separate keys.

13.4. New drivers from hired-truck vendors are shown the south gate routine by
the guard and the Temple Street timing by the shift lead before their first
booking.

13.5. The words used on site follow the company glossary. A new joiner who hears
a word they do not know is expected to ask, on any shift, and nobody at
Coimbatore is to laugh at the question.

## Peak season

Leave during the vaccine and dairy peak months is capped at one person per shift
per site. The cap is published in March so it is not a surprise in June.

## 17. Changes to this curriculum

17.1. Revision 1 (January 2025) set out the programme for the second intake. Revision 2 (June 2026) shortened the programme, raised the stipend in the floor months and set the ratio on live equipment after the first group completed.

17.2. The engineering pool lead reviews the curriculum each May with the workshop staff and two site managers.

17.3. Apprentices and mentors are asked at the end of each module what should change, and their answers are read at the review.

## 10. On live units

10.1. On a live unit — a working reefer, a cold room with stock in it, a customer's freezer — an apprentice is never the only pair of hands. Live means anything holding product or able to start without warning, and it is the real kit apprentices are here to learn on.

10.2. One qualified technician supervises at most three apprentices on live equipment. On a pharma chamber the ratio is one to one.

10.3. Night work is part of the job later, not at first. No apprentice is put on a night roster before month nine, even with a supervisor. From month nine an apprentice may be rostered at night with a qualified technician on the same job.

10.4. Apprentices never isolate, lock out or restore power on their own until they have passed the electrical module, and never on a pharma chamber during the programme.

10.5. An apprentice who is asked to do something on a live unit that this curriculum forbids says no, and tells the mentor the same day. Saying no is never held against the apprentice.

## 14. Safety on the floor

14.1. The safety rules of the site always apply. Where a site rule and this curriculum differ, the stricter one wins.

14.2. Apprentices wear their safety gear on every job, including short ones.

14.3. Refrigerant cylinders are carried upright and strapped in vehicles. Apprentices never carry a cylinder in a bus or on a motorcycle.

14.4. Brazing is done only with a permit and a fire watch, at the workshop and on site alike.

14.5. Any injury, however small, is reported to the mentor the same day and written in the site's accident book.

## Order cut-off for next-day vans

Orders received by 16:00 go on the next day's vans, and orders received after
16:00 go the day after. The cut-off moved from 17:00 on 1 September 2025, when

# Taloja freezer store card: blast cell, order cut-off, gas leak siren

Pinned at the Taloja order desk. This card covers three things: the arrival
probe and the blast cell, the order cut-off for next-day vans, and where to
line up when the gas leak siren sounds.

## 6. A day in the office

6.1. The office takes orders from customers by e-mail and through the customer
portal. Each order names the delivery points, the cases and the delivery window
for every stop.

6.2. The order desk builds the next morning's van plan from the orders in hand.
The plan is checked by the afternoon shift lead before it is published to the
van drivers at 19:00.

6.3. The cut-off decides which van an order joins. Anything received by 14:00 goes out the following day; anything after that goes the day after. An
order marked urgent after the cut-off is passed to the site manager, who may add
it to a van if there is room and the customer has agreed to pay for a special
drop.

6.4. Until 11 January 2026 the line was drawn at 15:00; it moved an hour earlier when the first outbound wave moved to 05:00.

6.5. Orders received on a Saturday after the cut-off go out on Monday. The site
does not run outbound vans on Sundays except before Diwali and Christmas, when
the site manager publishes a special plan.

6.6. A customer who changes an order after it has joined a van plan is told
that the change will go out on the next plan, not the current one. The order
desk does not reload a van that has been picked.

6.7. Every order and every change is kept in the portal. The order desk never
works from a phone call alone; a call is followed by an e-mail before anything
is picked.

## 2. The work

2.1. Quillfern collects the customer's frozen products from the Chakan factory,
stores them and delivers them to restaurants, caterers and retailers in Pune
and Mumbai.

2.2. Pune deliveries go out from Quillfern's own stock. Mumbai-bound stock is
cross-docked at Quillfern's Bhiwandi site and goes out on the next morning's
vans.

2.3. Call-off times for Mumbai deliveries are those printed in the site handbook of the cross-dock that ships them.

2.4. Waiting charges on the customer's own vehicles at the cross-dock are billed at the site's published rate less 20 per cent.

2.5. Pallets are exchanged one for one at the cross-dock. Exchange units that arrive unfit on the customer's own vehicles are charged at the site figure, with no discount.

2.6. Quillfern does not sell, promote or price the customer's products and does
not take orders from the customer's buyers directly.

## 15. Review of this handbook

15.1. The site manager reviews this handbook every June and after any serious
incident, audit finding or change to the building.

15.2. Revision 3 of June 2026 recorded the new apron free window, the larger cell
and the earlier order cut-off, and moved the genset rules into their own
section.

15.3. Suggestions from staff go to the site manager at any time. Each one is
answered, whether or not it is taken up.

15.4. A revised handbook replaces every earlier copy in the office, the guard
cabin and the canteen on the day it is issued.

# Western Frozen Cross-Dock Handbook

How the western frozen cross-dock is run, written for the people who work there
and for anyone from another site who is sent to help in a busy week. The site
moves frozen food from manufacturers' trailers to city delivery vans for Mumbai,
Thane and Navi Mumbai. It is a cross-dock first and a store second: stock is
meant to come in, be checked, be sorted and go out, and the building is sized
for that and nothing more. Company rules on temperature, driving and hygiene
apply here as everywhere; this handbook says how they are carried out in this
building, with these doors, this yard and this traffic.

# Consolidated Service Terms, Contract CN-31

The terms on which Quillfern Cold Logistics Pvt. Ltd. stores and delivers frozen
products for Saptagiri Foods Pvt. Ltd., as they stand after the two amendments.
This consolidation is prepared by Finance for the people who run the account. It
replaces nothing; the signed agreement and its amendments remain the legal
record, and where this text and the signed record differ, the signed record
applies.

## 1. Parties and how to read this

1.1. The parties are Quillfern Cold Logistics Pvt. Ltd. ("Quillfern") and
Saptagiri Foods Pvt. Ltd. ("the customer"), a maker of frozen parathas, samosas
and snacks with a factory at Chakan.

1.2. The agreement began on 1 April 2025 and runs until either side ends it under section 10.

1.3. Amendment 1 took effect on 1 October 2025 and changed the payment terms.
Amendment 2 took effect on 1 April 2026 and changed the liability cap. Both are
folded into the text below and listed in section 15.

1.4. Clause numbers here follow this consolidation, not the original agreement.
A clause quoted from the signed record carries its original number.

## 12. Insurance

12.1. Quillfern insures the customer's stock in its care up to the contract-year
total in section 7.2.

12.2. The customer insures its stock before handover and after delivery.

## Gas leak siren

1. Stop forklifts where they stand and switch off the engines.
2. Line up at the main gate car park. Do not go back for stock or phones.
3. Wait for the plant lead's all clear in person.

## 10. Ending the agreement

10.1. Either side may bring it to an end by giving 120 days' written notice.

10.2. Either side may end it at once if the other fails to pay, or fails to
perform a material obligation, and does not put it right within 30 days of a
written demand.

10.3. On ending, Quillfern returns the customer's stock to Chakan or to a place
the customer names in Pune, at the customer's cost, within 15 days.

## 11. Disputes

11.1. The parties first try to settle a dispute between their account managers,
then between their directors.

11.2. A dispute not settled within 45 days goes to a sole arbitrator in Pune.

## 13. Audit and records

13.1. The customer may audit the records about its own stock twice a year on
ten working days' notice.

13.2. Records are kept for three years after the end of the agreement.

# Service Partner Onboarding Standard

## 1. What this standard is for

1.1. Quillfern buildings and vehicles are kept running by outside firms as much as by our own staff. Refrigeration engineers, generator agents, the people who service dock doors and levellers, pest controllers, cleaners, electricians, calibration laboratories and fire-equipment agents all come through our gates, and some of them work on the very plant that keeps customers' stock in range.

1.2. This standard says how such a firm becomes an approved service partner, what it must keep up to stay approved, and how it leaves the list. It applies to every site opened from 2025 onwards and to every firm that is newly approved anywhere in the company from the date of this revision.

1.3. It does not cover suppliers of goods, such as seals or forms, who deliver to Stores and never work on site. Those are approved under the purchasing rules.

1.4. It is written for Procurement, which keeps the list; for site managers, who call partners in; for QA, which approves partners who work near product; and for the engineering pool, which judges the technical competence of partners who work on plant.

1.5. "Partner" in this standard means a firm, not a person. The people the firm sends are its technicians.

## 4. First cooling at a new site

4.1. A unit arriving at a new site is cleaned inside, powered and closed with
nothing in it. The controller is set to the hire's set point.

4.2. The unit must pull down to its set point and then hold its range, empty,
for the stability hold before any stock goes in. The current hold is 24 hours.

4.3. Revision 2 of February 2026 doubled the hold from 12 to 24 hours after the Satara campaign unit drifted on its second night. The drift came from a
controller probe that had been knocked out of its clip in transit; it showed
only after the first night's cold soak.

4.4. During the hold the engineer checks the controller log at least twice,
including once after dark.

4.5. The customer is told on booking that the unit cannot take stock on its
first day on site. A customer who needs stock in on day one is offered an
earlier placement date, not a shorter hold.

4.6. At the end of the hold the engineer signs the placement sheet and hands
the customer's lead the key and the duty phone number.

## 3. Before anybody calls them

3.1. A firm that is not on the approved list may not be given a work order, a gate pass or access to any site, even for a small job, even for a quotation visit inside a product zone.

3.2. A site that needs a firm not yet on the list proposes it to Procurement on the partner proposal form, with the reason, the work and the sites concerned.

3.3. In a genuine emergency, where no approved partner can attend and stock is at risk, the site manager may call in an unapproved firm once. The technician is escorted throughout, the job is limited to the emergency, and Procurement is told within one working day. A second call to the same unapproved firm is not an emergency.

3.4. Approval normally takes four weeks for Category A, two for B and one for C, counted from receipt of a complete set of papers.

3.5. A firm is told plainly why it was not approved, if it was not.

## 14. Outside help

14.1. Several outside firms work in the building: the security contractor, the pest contractor, the cleaning contractor, the generator's service agent and the calibration laboratory. Each is approved by QA before its first visit and reviewed once a year.

14.2. The pest contractor visits on the first Thursday of each month and on call after any sighting. Bait stations are numbered on the wall plan in the QA office, and nobody moves one to make room for stock.

14.3. The cleaning contractor cleans the offices, the gowning room and the floors of the goods-in and dispatch bays. Chamber floors are cleaned by store staff only, so that nobody unfamiliar with the racking works in a chamber.

14.4. Refrigeration work on the chambers is done only by a firm approved under the company's arrangements for cooling-plant service partners. A technician who arrives without his induction card is not let in, however urgent the fault.

14.5. Calibration certificates from the laboratory are filed against the instrument's number in the document system. An instrument whose certificate is missing is treated as out of calibration.

## 9. When we call them

9.1. Partners agree to attend within a set time, which is written into their agreement. Times run from the moment the site's call is logged by the partner's desk, not from the moment the site first tried to call.

9.2. For a Category A partner, an emergency — a plant fault with stock at risk — is attended on site within four hours, at any hour of any day. An urgent fault, where stock is not yet at risk, is attended within twenty-four hours. A routine job is attended at the agreed slot.

9.3. Category B partners attend emergencies within eight hours. Category C partners work to agreed slots only.

9.4. The site logs the call time and the arrival time on the work order, and the partner's score at the year end is built partly from those times.

9.5. A partner that cannot meet an emergency time says so at once, so that the site can call the next partner on the list.

## 8. Putting away and picking

8.1. Putaway is directed by the warehouse system and confirmed by a scan at the rack location. A pallet put away without a scan is treated as lost until it is found and scanned.

8.2. Picking follows first-expiry-first-out. A picker who finds that the system has directed a later-expiry batch ahead of an earlier one stops and calls the shift QA officer. The system is not overruled on the floor, and it is not trusted blindly either.

8.3. Pickers do not open outer cartons inside the chambers. Part-carton picks are made at the picking table in WIC-2's anteroom, under the anteroom's own logger.

8.4. A dropped carton is set aside on the damage shelf, photographed and written up, whatever it looks like from outside. Vials break inside cartons that look perfect, and pre-filled syringes crack without a sound.

8.5. Dispatch staging is limited to what fits on the two dispatch-bay trolleys. The vehicle waits for the stock, never the other way round, and a vehicle that is not at loading temperature when it reverses onto the bay is sent away to cool down.

8.6. Two people check every outbound pallet against the picking list before it is wrapped: the picker and a second person who did not pick it. Both initial the list.

## 6. References

6.1. Category A and B firms give two references from customers for whom they have done similar work in the past two years. At least one reference is spoken to by phone.

6.2. A reference from a relative of the firm's owner, or from another firm under the same ownership, does not count.

6.3. Procurement writes a short note of each reference call and files it.

6.4. A bad reference does not automatically stop approval, but it is discussed with the firm and the note of that discussion is filed with the reference.

## 14. Changes to this manual

14.1. Revision 2 (February 2026) lengthened the stability hold after a campaign
unit drifted.

14.2. Revision 3 (July 2026) added the long-hire daily charge and the rule that
a move within a site is a new placement.

14.3. The pool lead reviews this manual every January.

# Pharma Store Quality Manual, West Zone

## 1. Purpose and reach

1.1. The store at Changodar, on the south-west edge of Ahmedabad, is the first Quillfern building that holds medicines and nothing else. It opened in September 2025 in a leased shed inside a pharmaceutical estate off the Sarkhej–Bavla highway. From its first week its customers — two vaccine makers, a biologics firm and three hospital groups in Gujarat — asked for a written quality system they could audit against. This manual is that system. It says how the store keeps product fit for the patient, how it proves that it did so, and who answers when it did not.

1.2. It is written for the people who work in the building: receiving clerks, pickers, dispatch staff, the shift QA officers, the engineering technician and the store manager. It is also written for auditors, who will read it more carefully than anyone on the floor and who should be able to find, somewhere in it, the reason for every record the store keeps.

1.3. Where this manual and a company-wide procedure disagree about a temperature limit, a notification window or a quarantine rule, the company procedure applies and this manual is corrected at its next revision. The manual sets no temperature limit of its own; it says how those limits are kept in this building, by these people.

1.4. Revision 3 is in force from 11/05/2026. The summaries written while the store was being fitted out are withdrawn and kept only as history. Earlier revisions of this manual are withdrawn from the shared drive on the day a new one is issued.

## 15. Customer audits

15.1. Customers may audit the store on ten working days' notice, and for cause at shorter notice. The RP or the QA lead hosts every audit; the store manager joins for the operational parts.

15.2. An auditor may see any record about the customer's own stock and any part of the building. An auditor may not see another customer's stock records or another customer's audit reports.

15.3. The store answers each audit finding within 20 working days with a corrective action, an owner and a date. Answers are written by the QA lead and signed by the RP.

15.4. Findings from customer audits are added to the store's own corrective action register, so that one customer's finding fixes the problem for every customer.

15.5. A customer may ask to observe a mock recall or a self-inspection walk. The request is granted where the customer's own batch is chosen or where the walk does not expose another customer's records.

## 18. Audit of Stores

18.1. Finance audits the Nagpur store twice a year without notice, counting a
sample of lines chosen on the day.

18.2. QA audits the numbered stock once a year, from the manufacturer's delivery
note to the gate register and back to the stubs.

18.3. Findings are written up by the auditor and answered by Nalini Patil within
ten working days, with an owner and a date for each action.

18.4. A finding that repeats from one audit to the next is escalated to the
Nagpur DC manager and to Finance.

## 11. Complaints from the person at home

11.1. A patient who complains to a rider is given the Nirmaya care-desk number.
The rider writes down what was said and tells the hub lead before the end of the
shift.

11.2. Complaints that reach Quillfern directly are passed to Nirmaya's care desk
the same day, with the rider's note and the run sheet.

11.3. A complaint about a rider's behaviour or riding goes to the hub lead and
to HR. The rider is told what the complaint says and is asked for his account
before anything is decided.

11.4. Quillfern does not reply to a patient in writing. Written replies come
from Nirmaya.

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

## 5. Instruments that travel south

5.1. Coimbatore has no calibration chamber and no bench master logger. Those
live at Nagpur. What Coimbatore does have is one lab-certified hand-held
thermometer, serial HP-C00, kept locked in the DC manager's cabinet.

5.2. Every hand-held thermometer in daily use at Coimbatore is checked against
HP-C00 every 14 days: both tips go into the same stirred jug of crushed ice and
water, and the two readings must agree within 0.5 C. The shift lead writes both
readings on QCL-F-12 and sends a photograph of the sheet to the Nagpur QA desk.

5.3. The shorter interval is deliberate. Coimbatore has no bench to catch a
drifting instrument quickly, and a second jug check costs nothing but ten
minutes.

5.4. HP-C00 itself goes to Metrosure Labs, Pune, by courier every 12 months.
While it is away, the Nagpur QA desk sends a loan instrument ahead of it, so the
site is never without a certified thermometer.

5.5. USB loggers are not checked at Coimbatore at all. Every spare logger for a
Coimbatore red sleeve is checked at the Nagpur bench and arrives in its sleeve
already stickered. A logger that has been out of date on the shelf is sent back
to Nagpur, never re-used on the strength of a local jug check.

5.6. Infrared guns are used at Coimbatore only to find a warm carton quickly.
They are never the reading that decides anything.

## Handheld thermometer checks

Every handheld thermometer in daily use at Hosur is checked against the
certified thermometer every 7 days, in a stirred jug of ice and water. The two
readings must agree within 0.5 C.

## 6. The last ten metres

6.1. The rider parks where the two-wheeler is safe and visible, takes the pouch
from the carrier, shuts the lid at once and walks to the door. The carrier is
never left open while the rider is away from it.

6.2. Patients do not always hear the bell. The rider waits ten minutes and rings twice, the second call at least five minutes after the first. If there is
still no answer the pouch goes back into the carrier, the rider tells the hub,
and the hub lead calls the patient to re-slot.

6.3. Insulin is never left with anyone else unless the order itself names an alternate receiver. A neighbour, a watchman or the shop next door is not an
alternate receiver because they offer, however well the rider knows them.

6.4. An alternate receiver named on the order gives the same OTP as the patient
would. The rider writes the receiver's name on the slip.

6.5. The rider never enters a flat. Pouches are handed over at the door, and a
patient who cannot come to the door is visited by Nirmaya's care team, not by
the rider.

6.6. The rider photographs the pouch at the door, never the patient and never
the inside of the home, and uploads the photograph before moving off.

## Leaving insulin with a neighbour or watchman

If the patient is out, the insulin may be left with a neighbour or the building watchman, as long as that person shows photo ID and signs the delivery slip.

## 10. Privacy

10.1. Patient names, addresses and phone numbers are held in the programme
portal only. Riders see an order's details on the hub phone for the run, and
the phone is handed back at the end of the shift.

10.2. Riders do not save patients' numbers in their own phones and do not talk
about patients outside the hub.

10.3. Delivery photographs show the pouch and the door number, nothing else.
They are deleted from the hub phone after upload.

10.4. Nirmaya may audit the programme's records about its own patients on
reasonable notice. No other customer sees them.

## 7. Things that come back

7.1. Pouches come back to the hub when the patient is not reached, when the OTP
is not given, when the carrier's clock runs out, or when the freeze indicator
has tripped.

7.2. Undelivered pouches are logged at the hub on the returns sheet with the
reason and the time. They are held in the red box beside the store door and collected by the customer's own pharmacist the next working day; none goes back into saleable stock.

7.3. The red box is not refrigerated storage for future drops. Nothing is taken
out of it by hub staff once it has gone in.

7.4. A pouch that has been opened by anyone outside the hub is treated the same
as an undelivered one, and the rider writes on the returns sheet who opened it.

7.5. Empty carriers and packs come back on every run. A rider who loses a pack
reports it the same shift.

## 11. Inland from the coast

11.1. The site at Bhubaneswar exists to bring the DC's stock to customers in Odia-speaking markets the next morning, and to collect stock from Kalinga Biologicals and from Odisha food makers for the DC.

11.2. It is a cross-dock. Goods arriving on the nightly trunk run are sorted and loaded onto local vans for delivery the same morning. Goods collected locally wait for the next night's trunk run back to the DC.

11.3. No pallet stays at the satellite for more than 36 hours from arrival. A pallet still there at hour 30 is reported to the DC manager, who decides whether it goes back on the next trunk run or out on a special van.

11.4. Because nothing is stored there, the satellite does not hold a storage licence for medicines, and pharma stock passes through it only in the trunk vehicle without being unloaded (section 18).

11.5. The site's staging hall is mapped like a room, though it is not a store, because stock stands in it during sorting.

# East Coast Region Operating Plan 2026-28

## 1. Why the east coast

1.1. Quillfern has grown along an arc from the west into the centre of the country, and its customers have asked for years to be served on the east coast as well. Three things decided the matter in 2025. A shrimp exporter in the Godavari delta offered a five-year volume commitment if we would hold its frozen stock near the port. A vaccine maker opening a fill-finish line near Bhubaneswar asked for a cold distribution partner inside the state. And the growth of organised food retail in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha meant that frozen and chilled lanes we were already being asked to quote would pay for themselves.

1.2. This plan describes the region we are building: one distribution centre at Visakhapatnam, which people on the ground call Vizag, and one inland satellite at Bhubaneswar. It covers the calendar, space, people, power, weather, port work, fleet, money and the measures by which the region will be judged in its first two years.

1.3. It is written for the region's own managers, for the head-office teams who support them, and for the board, which approved the investment in March 2026. It replaces the outline written in 2025, which was prepared before the site was chosen.

1.4. Company-wide procedures apply in the region from the first day. Nothing in this plan relaxes a temperature rule, a driving rule or a quality rule because the region is new.

## 8. Heavy days on the road

8.1. The insurer's exposure on any single vehicle is capped. The most it will pay for all goods on one vehicle on one trip is Rs. 1.2 crore, however many consignments are on board.

8.2. A full vaccine load easily goes past that figure, and so does a frozen load of premium seafood. Any dispatch whose total declared value on one vehicle is above Rs. 1.2 crore is declared to the broker in writing at least 48 hours before the vehicle leaves. The broker then gets the insurer's agreement to a higher figure for that trip, or tells us to split the load.

8.3. Fleet planners check the declared value of every pharma critical and every high-value frozen load when they build the week's plan, and send the list of trips over the figure to the claims desk on Thursday.

8.4. A trip that goes over the figure without a declaration is still covered up to Rs. 1.2 crore. Anything above that is uninsured, and the site manager who allowed the load explains why in writing.

8.5. Splitting a load costs a second vehicle and a second crew. Planners should prefer splitting to asking for a higher figure only where the second vehicle is already on the road; the broker's higher figure usually costs less than an empty run.

## 14. Risks we can see

14.1. The anchor customer is a single exporter. If Godavari Aqua's export market falls, the frozen block is half empty. The plan reduces that risk by signing at least two more frozen customers before the end of 2027.

14.2. Storms may close the region for days at a time. Section 9 sets the response.

14.3. Skilled refrigeration technicians are scarce on this coast. Two places on each intake of the company's technician programme are reserved for people from the region, who return to it on completion.

14.4. The vaccine maker's start date may slip. Pharma space is not filled with food while it waits; it stays empty.

14.5. Port congestion may hold containers at the DC longer than planned. The container plugs in section 10 are the buffer.

Prepared before the Visakhapatnam plot was chosen, to size the investment for
the board's first look.

## 19. Review

19.1. The region head reviews this plan each quarter with the DC manager and Finance, and issues a revision when a date, a figure or a decision changes.

19.2. Revision 1 (March 2026) was approved with the investment. Revision 2 (July 2026) fixed the first-receipt date, the hiring numbers and the storm-season fuel stock after the site visit by the insurers' engineer.

19.3. The superseded outline of 2025 is kept in the plan file for history and must not be quoted to customers.

## Bhubaneswar satellite

- Cross-dock only. No pallet stays more than 48 hours.

## 17. What changed from the 2025 cover

17.1. The 2025–26 cover was placed with the same insurer on different terms, and its summary note is withdrawn. Staff who learned the old figures should unlearn them.

17.2. The deductible rose, the intimation window shortened, the machinery-stoppage threshold came down, the single-vehicle figure went up, and the survey threshold went up. The current figures are in sections 5 to 9 of this procedure and nowhere else.

17.3. SRCC cover was added by endorsement for the first time.

17.4. The desk lead reviews this procedure each February, before renewal, and issues a revision whenever the policy terms change.

## 16. Keeping the file

16.1. Each claim file is kept, complete, for eight years from the date of final settlement or rejection, whichever comes later. Files involving a court case or arbitration are kept until three years after the case ends, if that is longer.

16.2. Scanned files live in the Finance document store under the TPC26 number. Paper originals are boxed by policy year and kept in the Finance archive room.

16.3. Physical evidence — seals, logger files, damaged packaging — is kept until the claim is closed, then for one more year, and is then disposed of with the desk lead's signature.

16.4. A file is never weeded to save space. If storage runs short, the desk lead asks Finance for more.

## 2. The two sites

2.1. The Visakhapatnam DC stands on a leased plot of 4.2 acres in the Atchutapuram industrial area, south-west of the city, about 18 km by road from the port's outer gate. The building is a new pre-engineered shed with a cold block, a frozen block, a small controlled-room-temperature store, a dispatch canopy and a two-storey office.

2.2. The satellite at Bhubaneswar is a smaller leased unit in the Mancheswar industrial estate. It has two chilled docks, two frozen docks, a staging hall held at +4 C and a site office. It is a cross-dock, not a store.

2.3. The two sites are about 440 km apart by the coastal highway. A nightly trunk run links them.

2.4. The DC is the region's centre: its manager is the senior manager in the region, its QA lead covers both sites, and its engineering team maintains the satellite's plant.

2.5. Both leases run for fifteen years with a right to renew. The landlord at Atchutapuram built the shell to our drawings; the fit-out, racking and refrigeration belong to Quillfern.

## 15. Visitors and audits

15.1. Every visitor signs the visitor book at the gate cabin and wears a visitor
badge for the whole visit. A visitor who has not signed in is not shown round,
whoever they say they are.

15.2. Customer auditors are escorted by the DC manager or a shift lead from the
gate to the gate. They may look at any room and any record they ask for, but
they do not handle stock and they do not enter a cold room without a freezer
jacket from the rack by the corridor.

15.3. Photographs inside the cold block are taken only with the DC manager's
permission, and only of the thing being audited. A customer's stock is never
photographed for another customer.

15.4. Auditors from the landlord's insurer visit once a year. They look at the
building, the fire equipment and the roof units, not at the cold chain. The DC
manager keeps the fire extinguisher service tags and the roof unit service
sheets in one folder for them.

15.5. After any audit the DC manager writes a short note of what was asked,
what was shown and what was promised, and sends it to Revathi Iyer and Farhan
Qureshi the same week. Promises made to an auditor are kept in that note, not
in anyone's memory.

15.6. School and college groups are not shown round the cold block. Requests
for such visits are passed to Pune HQ.

## 3. Getting a vehicle in and out

3.1. Reefers use the south gate. The east gate is for dry grocery only unless
the DC manager approves an emergency move, as the old wiki page also said.

3.2. School traffic on Temple Street blocks the turn into the south gate between
07:45 and 08:30. Drivers are told on booking to arrive either before 07:30 or
after 08:40. A reefer is never queued across Temple Street; if the apron is
full, the driver goes round the block and comes back.

3.3. Security holds each vehicle outside the south gate until the previous one
has cleared the apron. The apron takes one reefer and one van at a time, no
more, because a reversing reefer cannot see a second one parked behind it.

3.4. Bookings are made in Dockwise, which Coimbatore joined on 1 February 2026.
The grace table and the cancellation rule are the company rule, not a local
one, and are not repeated here.

3.5. Frozen loads are placed before lunch. After about 13:00 the afternoon sun
lies across the outer apron, drivers open their doors to check paperwork, and
the frozen body loses cold it cannot spare.

3.6. Reversing on the apron after dark needs a spotter with a torch, whatever
the vehicle's camera shows. The apron lights are on a timer that the landlord
controls, and they have twice failed to come on in the monsoon.

## 12. Fleet for the region

12.1. The region starts with 14 owned reefers: eight chilled and six frozen, all new, delivered to the DC in November 2026. Peak demand is met with hired reefers from approved vendors, up to nine at a time.

12.2. The nightly trunk run between the DC and the satellite uses two owned reefers and two drivers on each vehicle, whatever the day's departure time, because the run is long and mostly at night.

12.3. Local deliveries around Visakhapatnam and around Bhubaneswar are made by small chilled vans hired with drivers.

12.4. A fleet planner based at the DC builds the region's plan. Fleet Control's national desk remains the controller for vehicles on the road.

12.5. A second set of tyres, belts and reefer spares is stocked at the DC, because the nearest dealer workshop for the reefer units is several hours away.

## 18. Things left out on purpose

18.1. The satellite does not store medicines and does not unload them. Pharma stock for Odisha customers either travels direct from the DC in a sealed vehicle that passes through the satellite's yard without opening, or is delivered by the DC's own vehicle. No passive shipper, no cross-dock exception and no customer's urgency changes this.

18.2. The region does not handle live seafood, fresh fish on ice or any product that is not packed and labelled.

18.3. The region does not offer customs clearance as a service. The exporter's own agent clears its goods; we provide the space and the supervision of stuffing.

18.4. The DC does not open a retail counter or sell surplus stock locally.

## 15. Who leads

15.1. The region head is K. Srinivasa Rao, based at the DC, reporting to the Chief Operating Officer.

15.2. The DC manager is Swagatika Mohanty. The satellite's site lead reports to her.

15.3. The region's QA lead reports to the head of QA, not to the region head, so that quality decisions do not answer to the people who must meet the dispatch plan.

15.4. Finance, HR and IT support the region from head office, with one person from each at the DC for the first six months.

15.5. Escalation at night goes from the shift lead to the DC manager, then to the region head.

## 8. Power

8.1. Each K7 has a hot-swap battery that can be changed without switching off. Spare charged batteries sit in the charging bay of each rack.

8.2. Batteries wear out, and a worn one dies at the worst moment of a pick. A pack is retired at 500 charge cycles or when Fernguard reports its health under 80 per cent, whichever comes first. Floor staff say a retired battery has been binned; it is in fact returned to the IT desk for recycling and never put in general waste.

8.3. A battery that is swollen, cracked or hot to the touch is taken out at once, put in the fire-safe tin by the rack and reported to the IT desk.

8.4. Batteries are not charged anywhere except in the cradle rack. Chargers brought from home are not used.

8.5. At the end of each shift every K7 goes back in its cradle, charged or not.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

## 3. Power

3.1. A unit needs a three-phase supply of 415 V, 32 A, through the pool's own
weatherproof socket, which the customer's electrician fits before the unit
arrives.

3.2. Every campaign hire also has a standby genset of the pool's own, wired
through an automatic transfer switch. The transfer switch must bring the standby set on line within 30 seconds of mains loss. The changeover is tested
at commissioning by pulling the mains isolator.

3.3. Long hires at sites with a reliable supply and their own standby may use
the site's standby instead of the pool's, if the pool engineer has tested the
changeover and written the result on the placement sheet.

3.4. The genset's fuel is the customer's responsibility on a campaign hire. The
pool engineer shows the customer's staff how to read the gauge and how to call
for fuel before the tank is low.

3.5. Extension leads, adaptors and shared sockets are never used.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 6. Who may use one

6.1. A K7 may be used only by a person with a login issued by the IT desk. Logins are personal; a shift lead does not sign in for a picker so the picker can start sooner.

6.2. Contract and agency workers do not get permanent logins. Agency staff on the scanners are some of the busiest users on a peak night, and each one is given a temporary sign-in for the shift at the shift lead's request to the desk. The desk issues them a day credential that stops working twelve hours after it is first used. A new one is issued for each shift worked.

6.3. Personal phones are a separate matter. Many staff would rather scan with their own phone than walk to the rack, and on the pilot some did. No personal phone may run the scanning app or hold a Quillfern login, even for one shift when a K7 has failed; the user takes a spare from the cradle rack or waits.

6.4. Customer staff and auditors may look at a K7's screen with a Quillfern user beside them. They do not operate it.

6.5. Trainees from the Waluj workshop use a K7 only with their trainer's login running, and only for the exercises in their module.

# Containerised Unit Operating Manual

How the engineering pool's containerised cold rooms are placed, powered,
started, used, moved and looked after. The units are hired out to customers who
need cold space where Quillfern has no building: hospitals running vaccination
campaigns, a dairy cooperative's collection centre in the flush season, a
programme that needs a small store in a city neighbourhood. The manual is for
the engineers who place and service the units and for the customer's people who
use them day to day.

## 10. Alarms and the duty phone

10.1. The controller calls the duty phone for a high or low temperature, a door
left open, a power failure and a controller fault.

10.2. The pool engineer on duty answers the duty phone at all hours and calls
back the customer's lead within 15 minutes.

10.3. A temperature alarm is handled under the company's excursion rules. The
customer's staff do not move stock out of the unit unless the engineer tells
them to.

10.4. Each alarm and its outcome are written in the pool's alarm log.

## 9. The engineer's calendar

9.1. Every unit has a compressor hour meter. Every 1,000 hours on the compressor meter, or every four months if that comes first, the unit gets a full visit.

9.2. A full visit covers the refrigerant charge, the condenser coil, the fans,
the door seal, the heaters, the drain, the controller probe and the alarm call.

9.3. The engineer writes the meter reading and the work done on the unit's
service card, which hangs inside the door, and in the pool's own log.

9.4. A unit that misses a visit is taken off hire at the end of its current
booking until the visit is done.

9.5. Controller probes are checked against a calibrated reference at every full
visit.

## 11. What is left of the load

11.1. Damaged goods remain the customer's property until a claim is paid; after payment, anything left belongs to the insurer. Neither the site nor the claims desk may treat what is left as Quillfern's to sell.

11.2. Medicines are never disposed of as salvage, whatever condition they appear to be in and whatever the insurer suggests. They are destroyed under QA control with a destruction certificate, and the certificate goes into the claim file in place of a salvage account.

11.3. Food that cannot be supplied to the customer may be sold for animal feed or processing, but only to a buyer the insurer approves in writing, and only after the surveyor has released it. The proceeds are paid to the insurer or deducted from the claim, as the broker directs.

11.4. Staff may not buy damaged goods, take them home or give them away, even when the goods are about to be destroyed anyway. A carton of ice cream taken off a damaged pallet is theft from the customer, whatever its future.

11.5. The salvage account lists what was sold, to whom, for how much and on what date, or what was destroyed and on whose certificate.

# Kandla export reefer cover: notice to insurer, deductible, reefer breakdown hours, surveyor threshold, salvage of damaged pharma, settlement days

The cover on export reefer containers moved between Gandhidham and Kandla port
under policy EXR-26. This note covers notice to the insurer, the deductible,
reefer breakdown hours, the surveyor threshold, salvage of damaged pharma and
settlement days.

## Salvage of damaged pharma

Damaged pharma cartons may be sold as salvage, through a buyer the insurer
approves, once the surveyor has released them.

## 10. Paper the insurer wants

10.1. A complete claim file holds: the intimation and its acknowledgement; the dispatch note and the customer's value schedule; the seal photographs and the register entries; the temperature download and, where relevant, the controller event log; photographs of the goods; the delivery receipt with any remarks written on it; the first information report where there was one; the letter to the carrier where a hired vehicle was involved; QA's disposition; the survey report or desk assessment; and the salvage account.

10.2. The complete file is sent to the insurer, through the broker, within 45 days of the date of discovery. If something is still missing at day 40, the desk sends what it has with a list of what is to follow and a date for each item.

10.3. One extension of 30 days may be asked for in writing, through the broker, before the 45 days run out. A second extension is not asked for; if the file cannot be finished in 75 days, the desk lead decides whether to abandon the claim and records why.

10.4. Copies are sent, originals are kept. Seals, damaged packaging and logger files are offered to the surveyor for inspection but are not posted to anyone.

10.5. Every document carries the TPC26 file number in its top corner, written in ink on paper copies and in the file name for scans.
