## 8. Heavy days on the road

8.1. The insurer's exposure on any single vehicle is capped. The most it will pay for all goods on one vehicle on one trip is Rs. 1.2 crore, however many consignments are on board.

8.2. A full vaccine load easily goes past that figure, and so does a frozen load of premium seafood. Any dispatch whose total declared value on one vehicle is above Rs. 1.2 crore is declared to the broker in writing at least 48 hours before the vehicle leaves. The broker then gets the insurer's agreement to a higher figure for that trip, or tells us to split the load.

8.3. Fleet planners check the declared value of every pharma critical and every high-value frozen load when they build the week's plan, and send the list of trips over the figure to the claims desk on Thursday.

8.4. A trip that goes over the figure without a declaration is still covered up to Rs. 1.2 crore. Anything above that is uninsured, and the site manager who allowed the load explains why in writing.

8.5. Splitting a load costs a second vehicle and a second crew. Planners should prefer splitting to asking for a higher figure only where the second vehicle is already on the road; the broker's higher figure usually costs less than an empty run.

## 18. Review of this manual

18.1. The Fleet head reviews this manual every April, alongside the annual review
of the Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy, and sooner after any crash or serious
exception that shows a gap in it.

18.2. Drivers and controllers send suggested changes to Fleet Control at any
time. Suggestions are read at the next Nagpur driver meeting.

18.3. A revised manual replaces every earlier copy at the Fleet Control desk, the
gate cabins and the driver rest room on the day it is issued.

## 4. Taking over a vehicle

4.1. The driver taking over a vehicle walks round it with the driver handing
over, or with the shift lead if the vehicle was parked empty.

4.2. The walk-round covers tyres and wheel nuts, lights, mirrors, the reefer
unit's display and alarm light, the rear door hasp, the cab locker and the red
sleeve, the fire extinguisher, and the wheel chocks.

4.3. Any damage found on the walk-round is photographed and written on the
takeover sheet before the vehicle moves. Damage found later is presumed to have
happened on the later driver's watch.

4.4. The cab card is checked for the current Fleet Control, QA desk and
Compliance-Red numbers. A cab card printed before the Tessaline cutover is
replaced before the vehicle leaves.

4.5. The driver checks that the Tessaline unit shows the vehicle's own asset
number. Units have been swapped between vehicles in the workshop and not
re-labelled.

## Notice to insurer

Written notice goes to the insurer within 3 days of discovering a loss.

## Settlement days

The insurer pays an agreed claim within 15 days of the survey report.

## Surveyor threshold

The insurer appoints a surveyor for any loss estimated above Rs. 1 lakh.

## 5. Taking a booking

5.1. A booking needs the product class, the quantity in the unit the rate card
uses, the pickup and delivery points, the earliest and latest delivery time, and
the name of the person who will receive.

5.2. The agent checks that the booked vehicle can carry the product class. RF-120
is frozen only; RF-119 takes pharma only with a passive shipper; RF-118 takes
pharma and dairy but never frozen.

5.3. The agent books the dock through Dockwise for Nagpur, Guwahati and
Coimbatore alike. A phone slot at Guwahati is confirmed in Dockwise the next
working day.

5.4. Pharma critical bookings that would need a night segment are passed to
Fleet Control before they are confirmed to the customer, because a night pharma
run needs two named drivers.

5.5. A booking the customer changes after 15:00 the day before is treated as a
new booking.

## Half two: passive shippers

Pharma pallets may not be staged on an open dock beyond a short limit unless a
validated passive shipper is used; the limit and the exception are clause 8.2 of
[the SOP](01-sop-temperature-excursion.md).

Quillfern has been refusing bookings it could have taken, including chilled
pharma on [RF-119](17-reefer-RF-119-asset-file.md), which has no shipper cradle
and therefore cannot take pharma critical stock without one. The pilot puts
twelve validated passive shippers at Nagpur from August 2026.

Hire is charged to the customer per shipper per trip at the rate printed on
[the H2 2026 rate card](12-rate-card-2026-h2.md). Finance added that line to the
card when this project was approved, so the card and the project were signed in
the same week.

## 10. Emergency cold for a customer's kitchen

10.1. Restaurant chains sometimes ask for emergency dry-ice packing when their
own freezer fails. Customer service takes the request; the DC decides whether it
can be done.

10.2. The agent does not promise a time. The DC tells the agent when the packing
can be ready, and the agent passes that on.

10.3. Emergency dry-ice packing is billed at a minimum of 10 kg per request,
whatever smaller quantity the kitchen asks for, and the per-kg price is the one
on the rate card in force.

10.4. Dry ice is never sent in a customer's own car unless the customer's driver
signs the dry-ice safety note at the gate. Customer service sends the note to
the customer with the confirmation.

10.5. Pharma customers are not offered dry-ice packing as an emergency measure.

## 6. Where the truck is

6.1. Customers ask where their vehicle is more than they ask anything else.

6.2. Customer service gives an ETA only from Fleet Control's board, rounded to
30 minutes, and never calls the driver.

6.3. If the board shows no position, because of a dead zone, the agent says that
the vehicle is in an area without signal and gives the last known position and
time. The agent does not guess.

6.4. A customer who has the driver's number and calls him directly is asked, the
next time customer service speaks to them, to call customer service instead.
Drivers answer only when parked.

6.5. A late vehicle is reported to the customer as late as soon as Fleet Control
says it will miss its window. The reason is given in plain words and without
blame.

## 8. How marks are given

8.1. Every module ends in a theory paper and a practical task. The practical — a hands-on test on real equipment in the workshop or on site — counts for more, because the trade is learned with the hands.

8.2. A practical passes at 70 per cent and a theory paper at 60 per cent; a failed module is repeated with the next intake. An apprentice may repeat no more than two modules in the whole programme.

8.3. Practical tasks are marked against a written checklist by a trainer who did not teach the module, and the checklist is shown to the apprentice beforehand. Safety items on the checklist are pass-or-fail: an apprentice who skips lockout, for example, fails the task whatever else they did well.

8.4. Marks are given back within a week, with the marker's comments. An apprentice who disputes a mark asks the workshop lead for a second marking.

8.5. The final assessment at the end of the programme is held with an examiner from the apprentice's ITI, and leads to the Quillfern certificate of completion.

## 3. The calendar

3.1. The apprenticeship runs as one continuous programme with no break between the classroom and the floor. Months one to six are mostly in the workshop; months seven onwards are mostly on site, with a day a week back at Waluj.

3.2. From the January 2026 intake the programme lasts 18 months; the 2024 and 2025 intakes served 24. The shorter programme was possible because the workshop now has its own reefer body, cold room and generator, so that practical work no longer waits for a site to lend equipment.

3.3. Apprentices join in two intakes a year, so that there is always a senior group on site while a junior group is in the workshop. Each intake opens on the first working day of January or July and takes twelve trainees, no more. A thirteenth applicant who passes is offered the next intake rather than squeezed in.

3.4. Public holidays follow the Maharashtra list for apprentices at Waluj and the local list for apprentices placed at a site.

3.5. An apprentice who is ill for more than four weeks in a row may move to the next intake and pick up from the module they left.

## Module notes

- **M2** walks through [the pink card](30-pharma-night-dispatch-checklist.md) on a real vehicle at the gate. A controller may not dispatch a night pharma run alone until Col. Sandhu or the Fleet head's deputy has signed the practical.
- **M3** covers how stock leaves quarantine under [the green binder](31-quarantine-release-and-return-procedure.md), including when the quarantine dwell limit forces an escalation. Written test, pass mark 80%. Drivers do not attend M3; they never release stock.
- **M4** uses [the Sunday sheet](32-reefer-washdown-and-sanitation-procedure.md). Each trainee times one full CCT with a stopwatch on a real body before signing off.
- **M5** shows planners how each factor of the lane risk score is marked and why dead zones are scored at all.
- **M6** gives every new joiner [the house word list](33-cold-chain-glossary.md) in their first week and 30 minutes with a shift lead to go through it.

## Marks and attendance

Practical tasks pass at 65 per cent. Attendance must be at least 80 per cent.

## 9. Turning up

9.1. Attendance is taken twice a day, at the workshop gate and after lunch, and on site by the mentor. Missed classes count against the apprentice whatever the reason, except leave approved in advance and documented illness.

9.2. Anyone present for less than 85 per cent of a module's sessions repeats that module, whatever their marks. Good marks do not make up for missed practice, because the practice is the point.

9.3. Lateness of more than fifteen minutes counts as half a session missed.

9.4. An apprentice who is going to be absent phones the trainer or mentor before the session starts. A text message is accepted only when the trainer has replied to it.

9.5. Three unexplained absences in a module lead to a meeting with the workshop lead, and a fourth to a written warning.

## 12. When someone else was driving

12.1. When goods are lost or damaged in a hired vehicle, Quillfern and its insurer have a right to recover the loss from the vehicle's owner. That right is easily lost through delay.

12.2. The site manager, with the claims desk, sends the hired-truck vendor a letter holding it responsible for the loss within 72 hours of the date of discovery. The letter goes by registered post and by e-mail to the address on the purchase order, names the dispatch note and the loss, and says that Quillfern and its insurers reserve all rights. A phone call, a message to the driver or a remark on the delivery note does not count.

12.3. Without that letter, the insurer may reduce what it pays by whatever it says it could have recovered, and it usually says the whole amount.

12.4. Once the insurer has paid, it takes over the claim against the vendor in Quillfern's name. The claims desk gives the insurer's lawyers whatever records they ask for, and the site manager makes witnesses available.

12.5. A vendor who pays Quillfern directly before the insurer has settled is told that the money will be accounted for in the claim. It is never kept quietly as a credit against the next invoice.

## 16. Gifts and conflicts

16.1. Nobody at Quillfern accepts a gift, a meal, travel or entertainment from a partner or a firm proposing to become one, beyond token items worth less than Rs. 1,000 in all in a year, such as a diary or a box of sweets at Diwali.

16.2. Anything above that is declined, or, where declining would cause offence, handed to HR and recorded.

16.3. A member of staff with a family or financial interest in a partner declares it to Procurement and takes no part in that partner's approval, scoring or work orders.

16.4. Partners are told these rules when they are approved, and asked to tell Procurement if anyone at Quillfern asks them for anything.

## 6. A day in the office

6.1. The office takes orders from customers by e-mail and through the customer
portal. Each order names the delivery points, the cases and the delivery window
for every stop.

6.2. The order desk builds the next morning's van plan from the orders in hand.
The plan is checked by the afternoon shift lead before it is published to the
van drivers at 19:00.

6.3. The cut-off decides which van an order joins. Anything received by 14:00 goes out the following day; anything after that goes the day after. An
order marked urgent after the cut-off is passed to the site manager, who may add
it to a van if there is room and the customer has agreed to pay for a special
drop.

6.4. Until 11 January 2026 the line was drawn at 15:00; it moved an hour earlier when the first outbound wave moved to 05:00.

6.5. Orders received on a Saturday after the cut-off go out on Monday. The site
does not run outbound vans on Sundays except before Diwali and Christmas, when
the site manager publishes a special plan.

6.6. A customer who changes an order after it has joined a van plan is told
that the change will go out on the next plan, not the current one. The order
desk does not reload a van that has been picked.

6.7. Every order and every change is kept in the portal. The order desk never
works from a phone call alone; a call is followed by an e-mail before anything
is picked.

## 1. Why the site exists

1.1. Until 2024 Quillfern's frozen customers in the Mumbai region either sent
their own trailers all the way to restaurant back doors or paid for cold-store
space they did not need. Neither worked. Long trailers cannot turn in the lanes
of Dadar or Bandra, and a cold store charges for weeks when the customer wants a
night.

1.2. The cross-dock at Bhiwandi opened on 7 October 2024 in a leased shed on the
service road of the Mumbai–Nashik highway. It takes full trailers from brand
owners in the evening and sends the same stock out the next morning on small
frozen vans that can reach a restaurant's back door.

1.3. Nothing is meant to stay longer than 48 hours. A pallet that is still on the
floor at hour 48 is reported on the morning call, and its owner is told the
next day's plan for it before noon.

1.4. The site does not handle vaccines, insulin or any other medicine. A trailer
that arrives with pharma stock on it is not unloaded. The shift lead calls the
customer, and the trailer leaves with its seal intact and a note on the gate
log.

1.5. Dairy is accepted only frozen: ice cream, frozen paneer cubes and frozen
desserts. Chilled milk and fresh paneer go to sites that have a chilled room;
this one has only an anteroom held at marshalling temperature.

1.6. The site has no retail counter and sells nothing to the public. People who
walk in from the service road asking to buy frozen stock are turned away at the
gate, politely.

## 4. The first hour at the scene

4.1. People first. Nobody risks injury to protect stock, look at a seal or take a photograph. Where there has been a crash, the vehicle and the road are made safe and emergency services are called before anyone thinks about the load.

4.2. Once it is safe, the driver or the receiving shift lead photographs the vehicle from all four sides, the seal before it is cut, the inside of the body when the doors are opened, the damaged goods, and any label or batch number that can be read. Photographs carry the date and time, and they are sent to the site manager the same hour.

4.3. Nothing is moved except to protect people or to stop further damage, such as moving chilled stock into a working cold room. Whatever is moved is photographed first and written down.

4.4. Nothing is sold, given away, thrown away or destroyed. Damaged stock goes to quarantine like any other doubtful stock, and stays there until QA has decided and, where it applies, the surveyor has seen it.

4.5. Cut seals, broken packaging, the driver's paperwork and the temperature download are kept together in a bag marked with the dispatch note number. Police matters — theft, a crash with injury, a hijack — need a copy of the first information report, and the site manager asks for it on the day.

## 3. Before anybody calls them

3.1. A firm that is not on the approved list may not be given a work order, a gate pass or access to any site, even for a small job, even for a quotation visit inside a product zone.

3.2. A site that needs a firm not yet on the list proposes it to Procurement on the partner proposal form, with the reason, the work and the sites concerned.

3.3. In a genuine emergency, where no approved partner can attend and stock is at risk, the site manager may call in an unapproved firm once. The technician is escorted throughout, the job is limited to the emergency, and Procurement is told within one working day. A second call to the same unapproved firm is not an emergency.

3.4. Approval normally takes four weeks for Category A, two for B and one for C, counted from receipt of a complete set of papers.

3.5. A firm is told plainly why it was not approved, if it was not.

## 8. North-east monsoon and the afternoon sun

8.1. Coimbatore's heavy rain comes with the north-east monsoon, from October to
December, not in the June to September months that set the calendar at Nagpur
and Guwahati.

8.2. Rain cover over rear pallets is used at Coimbatore from October to December
whenever it is raining on the apron. The site owns six tarpaulins for this.

8.3. Coimbatore does not bill the customer for rain cover. The monsoon handling
line on the rate card is a Guwahati charge and is not quoted for Coimbatore
loads. Customer service agents who copy the Guwahati line onto a Coimbatore
quotation create a credit note later.

8.4. The hot months are March to May. In those months the afternoon rule in
section 3.5 is enforced strictly, and the wash pad is used before 11:00 so that
washed bodies are not left drying in the midday sun with their doors open.

8.5. The cold block wall sweats in the monsoon. Anything stored against it on
the dry side is moved 30 cm away from the wall from October onwards.

## 9. Insulin without spare cold

9.1. Coimbatore holds no passive shippers, no gel packs and no conditioning
cabinet. The passive shipper pilot is at Nagpur only, and it does not extend to
Coimbatore until a later project is approved.

9.2. Because there are no shippers, insulin at Coimbatore is never staged on an
open dock beyond the SOP limit. Insulin moves from CBE-PHARMA straight into a
reefer body that is already at loading temperature, and the reefer waits for
the insulin, never the other way round.

9.3. A customer who asks Coimbatore for a shipper-packed consignment is told
that the site cannot pack one. The account manager may arrange for a
shipper-packed consignment to come from Nagpur.

9.4. Coimbatore does not stock blue-cap or white-cap packs of any kind, and does
not freeze packs in CBE-FROZEN for customers. A customer's own packs returned
with a consignment go back with the customer's return challan.

6.4. The two-person figure is lower at Coimbatore than elsewhere because the
path from the shed to the apron crosses the wash pad, which is wet for most of
the day.

6.5. Dry ice never goes into CBE-PHARMA, never into the closed dairy room, and
never into a cab. Unused pellets go back to the chest in the same shift.

## 10. Training and drills

10.1. Every warehouse shift lead, fleet controller, and customer service agent
who handles cold-chain accounts must complete excursion training once each
calendar year. New joiners must complete the same training before they are
assigned unsupervised night duty.

10.2. Nagpur shall run one night-shift drill every quarter because it is the
central hub and handles the largest mix of pharma, dairy, and frozen movements.
Guwahati and Coimbatore shall each run at least two drills per year. A drill
must include one missing-record problem, not only a simple high-temperature
alarm.

10.3. Training records must show attendance, scenario, trainer, questions raised
by staff, and any local confusion found during the drill. Repeating a slide deck
without recording staff questions is not enough evidence for this SOP.

10.4. If a drill finds that staff are using a shortcut, hiding an alarm, calling
the wrong group, or relying on an obsolete document, QA must open a corrective
action. The corrective action may be simple, but it must name the obsolete habit
plainly.

## 4. Immediate containment

4.1. Stop movement of the affected pallet, tote, crate, reefer body, or room bay.
Do not load additional customer stock into the affected compartment.

4.2. Attach a red sleeve to the stock or truck file. The red sleeve contains the
customer intimation form, red hold tags, seal tape, and one spare calibrated
logger. If there is no physical sleeve, print form QCL-F-09 and write RED
SLEEVE MISSING at the top.

4.3. Move warehouse stock to quarantine bay Q-3 at Nagpur, Q-G2 at Guwahati, or
Q-C1 at Coimbatore. Truck stock must remain sealed unless QA instructs unloading
for product safety.

4.4. Photograph the sensor display, seal number, dock clock, and pallet labels.
The first four photographs must be uploaded before anyone debates stock
disposition. Do not wait for the manager to arrive.

4.5. Do not warm, chill, re-ice, ventilate, or hide the probe in order to make a
display look normal. Corrective measures may protect product, but the record
must continue to show the product environment honestly.

4.6. If a reefer unit is unstable on the road, the driver shall stop at a lit
fuel plaza or toll rest area, call Fleet Control, and keep the engine running
unless there is a fire, police order, or personal safety threat.
question: coimbatore site - who's in charge

answer_text:
## Before loading

1. Two drivers are named on the dispatch note before departure, as clause 2.3 of the [Driver Hours and Road Safety Policy](08-driver-hours-and-safety-policy.md) requires.

2. The body is run empty with its doors shut until the display holds loading temperature, and then held there for the Pre-Cool Hold Time (PCH) set by the qualification record for that route. Where no qualification record exists, the PCH is 45 minutes.

3. The red sleeve is in the cab locker and holds a spare calibrated logger. No logger, no departure: a hand-held thermometer is not a substitute.

4. Where the qualification record requires a backup passive shipper, its SCT is written in the shipper register. A shipper with no SCT entry is not a backup and the run waits.

## 3. Planning a week of duty

3.1. Planners build the week's duty on Thursday for the following Monday to
Sunday. Each driver's weekly rest is placed first, then night segments, then
day runs.

3.2. The limits the plan must respect are in the Driver Hours and Road Safety
Policy. A plan that meets them only if nothing goes wrong does not meet them.

3.3. A lane with a qualification record is planned with that record open, so
that its relief point, its pre-cool hold time and any two-driver condition are
on the plan and not in someone's memory.

3.4. Festival shuttle rosters with split rest are planned only after the Fleet
head has approved the roster in writing, and only for the festival named.

3.5. The plan is published to drivers by Friday noon. A driver who sees a
problem with his week tells Fleet Control on Friday, not on the morning of the
run.

3.6. Leave requests go to the planner by the 20th of the previous month. Late
leave is granted where cover exists, and cover is never found by stretching
another driver's hours.

## 5. Temperatures

5.1. The customer's products are kept at -18 C or colder in storage and in
transit.

5.2. The customer pre-cools each trailer before loading at Chakan and sends the
pre-cool record with the trailer.

5.3. Product that turns up above minus 12 is brought down to temperature at the cross-dock, and that work is invoiced to the customer.

5.4. Quillfern is not liable for product damage caused by temperatures before
handover. Each party may inspect the other's temperature records for its
stock.

## 2. The Fleet Control desk

2.1. Fleet Control sits at Nagpur DC and answers extension 301 at all hours. At
night one controller is on duty, with the Fleet head's deputy on call.

2.2. Fleet Control owns the dispatch note, the vehicle's route and the driver's
duty plan. A shift lead can hold a vehicle at the gate, but only Fleet Control
can change a route or a driver.

2.3. Every call from a driver is logged in the driver call log with the time,
the place and what was said, including calls that come to nothing. The paper
log is kept alongside the Tessaline record because network coverage is patchy
on several lanes.

2.4. Fleet Control does not pass customer pressure to a driver. A customer who
wants a location or an arrival time asks customer service, and customer service
asks Fleet Control.

2.5. Each controller hands over at 08:00 and 20:00, with every open exception,
every vehicle on the road with a pharma critical load, and every vehicle off
road for repair named aloud.

## 14. Training and coaching for drivers

14.1. Every new owned-reefer driver rides two supervised runs with an experienced
driver before driving alone. One of the two is a night run.

14.2. The supervised runs cover the cab card, the takeover walk-round, the seal
routine, the red sleeve, the gate checklist for pharma runs and the way to speak
to Fleet Control on the phone. The experienced driver signs the new driver's
training sheet at the end of each run.

14.3. Telematics coaching calls are held within two working days of an alert, as
the policy says. The coach asks what happened before saying anything about what
should have happened.

14.4. Drivers who complete a year with no safety non-conformance receive a
certificate from the Fleet head, presented at the Nagpur driver meeting. The
certificate carries no money and is not tied to arrival times.

14.5. The Nagpur driver meeting is held on the last Saturday of each month in
the driver rest room. Attendance is paid duty time. Drivers on the road that day
receive the notes on their phone.

# Pharma Critical Night Dispatch Checklist

Worked through at the gate by the Fleet controller and the shift lead together before any pharma critical vehicle leaves a Quillfern DC between 22:00 and 05:00. Both sign. One signature is not a dispatch.

## 3. Commitments on both sides

3.1. The customer commits to 1,800 pallet movements in each calendar month; any month that falls short is charged Rs. 300 for each movement not made.

3.2. A pallet movement is one pallet received or one pallet dispatched. A pallet
received and dispatched in the same month counts twice.

3.3. Quillfern commits to hold enough frozen space in Pune for 900 of the
customer's pallets at any one time, and to give 30 days' notice before reducing
it.

3.4. Months in which Quillfern could not take the customer's stock, for reasons
on Quillfern's side, are not counted for the shortfall charge.

## 14. Risks we can see

14.1. The anchor customer is a single exporter. If Godavari Aqua's export market falls, the frozen block is half empty. The plan reduces that risk by signing at least two more frozen customers before the end of 2027.

14.2. Storms may close the region for days at a time. Section 9 sets the response.

14.3. Skilled refrigeration technicians are scarce on this coast. Two places on each intake of the company's technician programme are reserved for people from the region, who return to it on completion.

14.4. The vaccine maker's start date may slip. Pharma space is not filled with food while it waits; it stays empty.

14.5. Port congestion may hold containers at the DC longer than planned. The container plugs in section 10 are the buffer.

## 16. How the region will be judged

16.1. In its first two years the region is measured on: deliveries on time, which is planned at 96 per cent from month four; temperature excursions per thousand pallets moved; customer complaints; safety incidents; and money against plan.

## 11. Racking and the floor

11.1. The drive-in racking in FC-A is inspected by the racking contractor every
six months. Any damage found between inspections is reported the same shift,
and the bay is closed with chains until it is checked.

11.2. Reach trucks keep to the marked aisles. Nobody walks in an aisle where a
truck is working; pickers wait at the aisle end until the truck has left.

11.3. Pallets are placed so that no carton overhangs the pallet edge. A pallet
with overhanging cartons is restacked in the anteroom before it goes into FC-A.

11.4. The floor of FC-A has a heated sub-floor to stop frost heave. The
sub-floor temperature is checked weekly by the plant lead and written in the
plant room folder.

11.5. Spilled product in FC-A is cleared at once, because frozen spillage under
a truck wheel is as slippery as ice.

## 14. Paper we keep

14.1. The gate log, the inbound sheets, the cell log, the pallet sheets, the van
plans and the genset log are kept for three years.

14.2. Records about a pallet that was held, destroyed or disputed are kept for
seven years, with the photographs.

14.3. Paper sheets are scanned at the end of each week and filed in the site
folder. The paper originals go to the archive room in the office.

14.4. A missing sheet is written as missing in the weekly scan index, never
rewritten from memory.

## 2. The micro-hub

2.1. The Kothrud micro-hub is a ground-floor unit off Paud Road with a covered
loading lane for two-wheelers and a packing room behind the shutter.

2.2. Stock at Kothrud sits in MCR-4, taken on long hire from the engineering pool. The hub staff do not service it; the engineering pool's own people do,
on their own calendar.

2.3. The packing room holds the packing bench, the carrier rack and PF-K1, the
fridge in which carrier packs are conditioned before use. PF-K1 is not used to
store insulin, even for an hour.

2.4. The hub is open from 06:30 to 22:00 every day. It is staffed by a hub lead
and two packers on each of two shifts.

2.5. Nirmaya's pharmacist visits the hub every working morning to check stock
received from Nirmaya's distributor and to collect anything held for her.

2.6. The hub lead keeps the keys to the store, the packing room and the red
box. Keys are handed over at the shift change against a signature in the key
book.

## 9. The engineer's calendar

9.1. Every unit has a compressor hour meter. Every 1,000 hours on the compressor meter, or every four months if that comes first, the unit gets a full visit.

9.2. A full visit covers the refrigerant charge, the condenser coil, the fans,
the door seal, the heaters, the drain, the controller probe and the alarm call.

9.3. The engineer writes the meter reading and the work done on the unit's
service card, which hangs inside the door, and in the pool's own log.

9.4. A unit that misses a visit is taken off hire at the end of its current
booking until the visit is done.

9.5. Controller probes are checked against a calibrated reference at every full
visit.

## 1. What the programme does

1.1. Nirmaya Healthcare runs a home-care service for people with diabetes who
find it hard to collect insulin from a pharmacy. Quillfern holds Nirmaya's
insulin stock in Pune and takes each patient's order to the door on the day and
in the slot the patient booked.

1.2. The programme started on 1 August 2025 with nine riders and about 300 drops
a week. By April 2026 it had 26 riders and about 1,100 drops a week across Pune
and Pimpri-Chinchwad.

1.3. Only insulin pens, cartridges and vials are carried. Vaccines and other
cold medicines are not carried unless Nirmaya adds them by a written change
signed by both sides, and no such change has been signed.

1.4. Quillfern does not advise patients on their medicine. A patient who asks a
rider how much to take, or whether a pen is the right one, is given the Nirmaya
care-desk number printed on the delivery slip.

1.5. Nirmaya owns the stock and the patient relationship. Quillfern owns the
cold chain from the hub to the door, and is answerable for it.

## 4. Getting in

4.1. Screen lock is set centrally from Fernguard and cannot be changed on the device. Staff often complain that the scanner screen locks itself too soon on a slow pick; the setting is deliberate, because an unlocked scanner left on a pallet is an open door into customer stock records. An idle K7 now goes dark and asks for its PIN after two minutes; until the March 2026 revision the figure was five.

4.2. PINs — staff call them passcodes — are six digits and personal, and nobody else is told one, including a supervisor. Fernguard forces a new PIN every 90 days; the 2025 rules allowed 180. A passcode may not repeat any of the user's last five.

4.3. Five wrong attempts lock the user out of every K7 until the IT desk resets the account. A reset needs the user to be present with an ID card; it is never done over the phone for someone else.

4.4. Fingerprint unlock is switched off. Gloved hands made it unreliable, and a fallback to PIN was the only thing anyone used.

4.5. A user who believes someone else has seen their PIN asks the desk for a reset the same shift. Nobody is criticised for asking.

## 5. Getting in and out

5.1. The personnel door is the only way into a unit. It is kept shut except
while someone is passing through it with stock.

5.2. The door has a strip curtain behind it and a plastic step outside. Staff
take what they need, close the door, and then sort or count outside, not in the
doorway.

5.3. The door switch is wired to the controller. The controller sounds after 90 seconds ajar and calls the duty phone after three minutes.

5.4. The customer's staff cannot silence the door sounder; only closing the
door does. A door that will not close is reported to the duty phone at once.

5.5. Nobody stays inside a unit with the door shut. The inside handle opens the
door from inside even when it is padlocked outside, and this is checked at every
service.

# Last-Mile Programme Manual

The manual for the doorstep insulin service Quillfern runs for Nirmaya
Healthcare in Pune, which Nirmaya sells to its patients under the name CareLink.
It is written for the riders, the hub staff and the customer service agents who
book the drops. It covers what is particular to taking medicine to a person's
front door on a two-wheeler. Company rules on temperature, quarantine and
destruction still apply; this manual says how they are carried out when the
last stop is a flat, not a dock.

## 13. Records

13.1. The placement sheet, the service cards, the alarm log and the controller
logs are kept for three years, or seven where a temperature alarm was raised
during a pharma hire.

13.2. Controller logs are downloaded at every service visit and at the end of
every hire.

## 13. Bikes and kit care

13.1. The two-wheelers are leased and serviced by the leasing company every
3,000 km. The hub lead books the service.

13.2. The rider checks tyres, brakes, lights and the carrier rack before every
shift and writes the check on the shift sheet.

13.3. A two-wheeler with a fault is not ridden. The hub keeps one spare machine
for that reason.

13.4. Helmets are replaced after any fall, whether or not they look damaged.

## 12. The customer's people

12.1. The customer names a lead for each unit. The lead is shown the door, the
controller display, the duty phone and the genset gauge at placement.

12.2. The lead keeps a simple sheet of who went in and when, and the sheet is
collected at each service visit.

12.3. Nobody under 18 goes into a unit.

# Containerised Unit Operating Manual

How the engineering pool's containerised cold rooms are placed, powered,
started, used, moved and looked after. The units are hired out to customers who
need cold space where Quillfern has no building: hospitals running vaccination
campaigns, a dairy cooperative's collection centre in the flush season, a
programme that needs a small store in a city neighbourhood. The manual is for
the engineers who place and service the units and for the customer's people who
use them day to day.
